86.

### What must a family trust document before distributing income at year-end?

A resolution making beneficiaries presently entitled to trust income is only effective for tax if it is made by 30 June, or earlier if the deed requires. If it isn’t effective, the trustee or other beneficiaries may be assessed instead, and a trustee may be taxed at the top rate. Build the distribution file from the deed, beneficiary position, income calculation and trustee decision.

- Check the deed and timing requirements, prepare the relevant income and distribution schedules, and retain resolutions.
- Use the existing trust example to separate arithmetic from missing documents and unresolved entitlement.

The tool cannot validate a deed or cure a late or ineffective trustee decision.

Trusts · Trustee resolutions · Trust distributions example

The bold answer was checked on 23 November 2026.

Link to question 86

87.

### How do dividends and franking credits affect my tax return?

A franking credit is tax the company has already paid on the dividend. Include the dividend and franking credit in your return; the credit reduces your tax, and an eligible individual gets any excess refunded. If your franking credits for the year total $5,000 or more, you must have held the shares at risk for at least 45 days (90 for preference shares). Reconcile the dividend statement to cash received, the franked or unfranked amount and franking credits.

- Record any foreign, trust or other adjustments and the relevant holding period evidence.
- Use the ATO investment and imputation guidance to determine what appears in the return.

A stated franking credit does not automatically establish entitlement to use the offset.

Investments and assets · Refund of franking credits for individuals

Link to question 87

88.

### Does providing a company car or paying an employee’s private expenses create FBT?

FBT applies if a company car is used or available for an employee’s private use, and reimbursing or paying for an expense an employee incurs can be an expense payment fringe benefit. FBT is 47% of the grossed-up taxable value for FBT years ending 31 March. Identify the benefit, recipient, private use and FBT year before valuing anything.

- Gather vehicle records or expense invoices, employee contributions and any claimed exemption evidence.
- Apply the appropriate valuation method and reconcile the resulting taxable value to the FBT workpaper.

The existing worksheet grosses up supplied taxable values; it does not decide whether a benefit or exemption exists.

Fringe benefits tax (FBT) · FBT rate and gross-up rates on this site · How FBT applies to cars · Expense payment fringe benefits · Experimental tax worksheets and supported years

Link to question 88

89.

### What information do I need to prepare an ATO payment plan proposal?

A payment plan must clear the debt in the shortest possible fixed period, with weekly, fortnightly or monthly instalments. General interest charge keeps accruing daily, you must pay new tax debts on time, and each account with an overdue debt, such as income tax and activity statement accounts, must be paid in full or have its own plan. Prepare a proposal that shows how the debt and ongoing obligations could be paid.

- Reconcile the ATO debt, outstanding lodgements and available cash, and prepare a realistic payment forecast.
- Use the ATO support route to discuss terms and retain any accepted arrangement.

A forecast does not establish acceptance, interest relief or removal of other obligations.

Paying the ATO · Payment plans · 13-week cash forecast

The bold answer was checked on 16 November 2026.

Link to question 89

90.

### Could my related businesses be grouped together for NSW payroll tax?

Businesses can be grouped for NSW payroll tax through related corporations, common employees, common control, tracing of interests, phoenix operators or subsuming smaller groups. Only one group member claims the tax-free threshold, against the group’s combined wages. Assess the relationships between businesses against the NSW grouping rules.

- Prepare an ownership and control diagram, shared-employee details and financial relationships.
- Document each grouping test and any exclusion application, then reconcile group wages.

Separate company names or accounts do not by themselves prevent payroll tax grouping.

Revenue NSW payroll tax · What is payroll tax grouping?, Revenue NSW

91.

### Which expenses can I claim for a rental property?

Loan interest, council rates and qualifying repairs and maintenance may be deductible for income-producing use. A depreciating asset costing $300 or less may qualify for an immediate deduction only if used predominantly to produce non-business assessable income and the set and identical or substantially identical asset cost tests are met. Check the second-hand residential asset restrictions before claiming. Other depreciating assets, eligible capital works and borrowing expenses have separate deduction rules. Apportion private use. Separate rental income, private use, borrowing costs, repairs and capital items before claiming expenses.

- Gather agent statements, invoices, loan interest, ownership details and rental availability records.
- Apportion costs where required and reconcile the deduction schedule to the supporting documents.

The treatment depends on the expense and property use; a rental label alone does not establish deductibility.

Property and land · How to claim rental expenses · Income Tax Assessment Act 1997, section 40-80 · Income Tax Assessment Act 1997, section 40-27

Link to question 91

92.

### Is work on my rental property a repair, an improvement or a depreciating asset?

Qualifying repairs and maintenance for income-producing use may be immediately deductible. Initial repairs for defects that existed when you acquired the property, improvements and replacements of an entire unit of property are capital. Assess any deduction under the depreciating asset or capital works rules separately. Eligible expenditure may form part of the CGT cost base. For property acquired after 7.30 pm (ACT time) on 13 May 1997, and for expenditure after 30 June 1999 on property acquired earlier, the cost base is reduced by capital works deductions claimed or claimable. Capital expenditure does not automatically produce a deduction over several years. Review what the work did to the property and when the relevant damage or condition arose.

- Keep invoices, scope of work, purchase condition and dates; split distinct components where supported.
- Assess repair, capital works and depreciating asset treatment separately and update the relevant schedules.

Cost alone does not distinguish a repair from an improvement or initial repair.

Property and land · Repair and maintenance expenses · Income Tax Assessment Act 1997, section 110-45

The bold answer was checked on 4 November 2026.

Link to question 92

93.

### How do I work out the capital gain when I sell an investment property?

The capital gain is the capital proceeds less the cost base. An Australian resident individual who owned the property for at least 12 months can usually reduce the gain by the 50% CGT discount. For a CGT event on or after 1 July 2027, the first enacted stage of reform treats gains that accrue from that date differently: cost base indexation replaces the discount for assets held at least 12 months, and a minimum 30% tax can apply to certain net capital gains of individuals. Gains accrued before then keep their existing treatment, such as the discount, but the pre-CGT exemption does not cover gains accruing from that date. An owner can choose to keep the current rules for an eligible new residential dwelling or affordable housing. Build the capital gains calculation from the relevant event, proceeds and adjusted cost base.

- Gather purchase and sale contracts, costs, ownership and occupancy history, and capital works records, and for a property acquired before 1 July 2027 and sold on or after that date, its market value immediately before that date, where required.
- Review any exemptions, adjustments, residency and discount conditions before calculating the net result.

A sale price minus purchase price calculation can omit material tax adjustments.

Capital gains tax · How to calculate your CGT · Capital gains tax reform · Experimental tax worksheets and supported years

The bold answer was checked on 27 September 2026.

Link to question 93

94.

### How do capital losses and the CGT discount affect tax on shares I sell?

Apply capital losses first. An Australian resident individual who owned the shares for at least 12 months can then reduce the remaining gain by the 50% CGT discount. For a CGT event on or after 1 July 2027, the first enacted stage of reform treats gains that accrue from that date differently: cost base indexation replaces the discount for assets held at least 12 months, and a minimum 30% tax can apply to certain net capital gains of individuals. Gains accrued before then keep their existing treatment, such as the discount, but the pre-CGT exemption does not cover gains accruing from that date. Calculate each gain or loss, apply eligible capital losses, then consider any available discount.

- Retain trade records, cost base adjustments, holding periods and carried-forward loss balances, and for shares acquired before 1 July 2027 and sold on or after that date, each holding’s market value immediately before that date, where required.
- Reconcile the final calculation to the year’s CGT schedule and keep the remaining loss record.

The bounded worksheet assumes the gains, losses and discount eligibility have already been established.

Capital gains tax · How to calculate your CGT · Capital gains tax reform · Experimental tax worksheets and supported years

The bold answer was checked on 27 September 2026.

95.

### Do I owe tax when I sell, swap or spend cryptocurrency?

Often, yes. Selling crypto or swapping one crypto asset for another is a CGT event, so a gain can be taxable. Review each crypto disposal and income event, including swaps and spending, rather than only withdrawals to cash.

- Export exchange and wallet activity, fees and Australian dollar values with dates.
- Reconcile transfers between your own wallets separately from transactions that require tax review.

The tax treatment depends on the activity and event; this site does not import wallets or classify transactions.

Crypto asset investments · Crypto asset transactions

The bold answer was checked on 27 September 2026.

96.

### How do I report ETF distributions and their tax adjustments?

Declare ETF distributions, including amounts reinvested through a distribution reinvestment plan. Your ETF tax statement, such as an AMMA statement, shows the amounts to report and where, and non-assessable amounts mostly adjust the cost base of your units. Use the fund’s annual tax statement and any AMMA statement to reconcile the distribution components.

- Match cash, reinvestments, capital gains, foreign income and credits to the statement.
- Record cost base increases or decreases and carry them into the investment register.

Cash received alone can differ from the amount and components that belong in the tax return.

### What records does my accountant need for an SMSF annual return and audit?

Trustees must appoint an approved SMSF auditor each year, at least 45 days before the SMSF annual return is due. The auditor needs a statement of financial position and an operating statement before starting, and any requested information within 14 days; the audit must be finished before the return is lodged. Prepare the financial records and trustee evidence needed for both the return and the independent audit.

- Gather bank and investment records, valuations, contributions, pensions, minutes, member balances and supporting agreements.
- Reconcile opening and closing balances and resolve the auditor’s record requests before finalising the return.

This checklist does not perform an SMSF audit or certify compliance.

ATO self-managed super funds · Your SMSF auditor

### When does an investment property become liable for land tax in NSW?

For owners entitled to the general threshold, NSW land tax for the 2026 land tax year applies when the combined taxable value of their non-exempt NSW land exceeds $1,075,000. Some trusts and related companies do not qualify for that threshold, and foreign-owner surcharge land tax has no tax-free threshold. Check ownership, land values, exemptions and any surcharge conditions for the relevant NSW land tax year.

- Reconcile all relevant NSW landholdings, ownership interests and valuation notices.
- Use Revenue NSW’s current assessment guidance and retain the calculation and exemption evidence.

Purchase price and one property’s value alone do not establish the full land tax position.

Land tax · Preparing for the 2026 land tax year, Revenue NSW · Land tax thresholds and rates, Revenue NSW

### Does a Hunter Valley coal mining employer pay the Coal LSL levy?

Yes, for eligible employees in the black coal mining industry. The employer reports and pays the levy monthly, currently 2.7% of each eligible employee’s eligible wages. The levy depends on whether each employee is an eligible employee in the black coal mining industry, then on that employee’s eligible wages for the month.

- List each employee’s role and check it against the Coal LSL eligible employee guidance.
- Work out each eligible employee’s eligible wages for the month using the section 3B formula that applies.

The calculator does not decide whether an employee is eligible; it calculates the levy on the wages you supply.

Before engaging anyone for tax work, check that they are listed on the Tax Practitioners Board register. Shortlist providers against the work you need and verify the relevant registrations.

- Check the TPB register for tax or BAS services, and ask who prepares and reviews the work.
- Request a sample reporting pack, Xero experience, cash forecast process, responsibilities and a written scope.

Location or software certification alone does not demonstrate the quality of advice or forecasting.

# GST calculator: exclusive, inclusive and GST amounts

Source: https://duguid.com.au/tools/business-calculators/gst/

> Enter an amount with or without GST and get the GST component, the exclusive amount and the inclusive amount at 10%, rounded once to cents, in your browser.

# GST calculator

Work out GST, the GST-exclusive amount and the GST-inclusive amount for a wholly taxable supply at 10%, rounded once to cents.

Published 20 September 2026. Last checked 13 November 2026. Boundary cases added 5 November 2026.

JavaScript is required for interactive calculations. The formula, assumptions and source links remain available below.

GST inputs

Amount (AUD) Amount includes GST

Calculate Fictional example: the first boundary case below. Change the inputs and calculate your own. Inputs: amount $110.00, includes GST. Excluding GST $100.00 GST $10.00 Including GST $110.00

## How the GST calculator works

The GST calculator takes one amount for a wholly taxable supply and works out the GST, the GST-exclusive amount and the GST-inclusive amount. For a wholly taxable amount at 10% GST, exclusive amount / 10 gives GST; inclusive amount / 11 gives its GST component. Each result rounds once to cents.

The 10% rate and the one-eleventh fraction come from ATO: How GST works and the A New Tax System (Goods and Services Tax) Act 1999.

## What the GST calculator does not decide

The GST calculator does not decide whether a supply is taxable, whether you must be registered for GST or what a BAS should report. Mixed, GST-free and input-taxed supplies need classification first.

Half a cent of GST rounds up | $0.05 excluding GST | Exclusive $0.05, GST $0.01, inclusive $0.06
GST below half a cent rounds to nil | $0.01 including GST | Exclusive $0.01, GST $0.00, inclusive $0.01

# Gross profit margin and markup calculator

Source: https://duguid.com.au/tools/business-calculators/margin/

# Margin and markup calculator

Gross profit, margin and markup from sales and direct cost, on a consistent GST basis and matching period.

Published 20 September 2026. Last checked 13 November 2026. Boundary cases added 5 November 2026.

JavaScript is required for interactive calculations. The formula, assumptions and source links remain available below.

Margin and markup inputs

Sales (AUD) Direct cost (AUD)

Calculate Fictional example: the first boundary case below. Change the inputs and calculate your own. Inputs: sales $100.00, direct cost $80.00. Gross profit $20.00 Margin 20.00% Markup 25.00%

## How the margin and markup calculator works

The margin and markup calculator works out gross profit, margin and markup from one sales figure and one direct cost figure. Gross profit = sales − direct cost. Margin = gross profit / sales × 100. Markup = gross profit / direct cost × 100. A zero denominator leaves that percentage undefined.

No statutory rate or threshold is applied. Gross profit and margin follow Business Queensland: break-even and profit; markup follows Business Queensland: pricing products and services.

## What the margin and markup calculator does not decide

The margin and markup calculator does not set a price, test whether direct cost is complete or adjust for GST. Use a consistent GST basis and matching period for both figures.

# Break-even sales calculator: units and sales

Source: https://duguid.com.au/tools/business-calculators/break-even/

> Work out contribution per unit, break-even units (rounded up) and break-even sales from fixed costs, price and variable cost per unit, in your browser.

# Break-even sales calculator

Whole units and sales required to cover fixed costs from price and variable cost per unit.

Published 20 September 2026. Last checked 13 November 2026. Boundary cases added 5 November 2026.

JavaScript is required for interactive calculations. The formula, assumptions and source links remain available below.

Break-even sales inputs

Fixed costs for the period (AUD) Selling price per unit (AUD) Variable cost per unit (AUD)

Calculate Fictional example: the first boundary case below. Change the inputs and calculate your own. Inputs: fixed costs $1,000.00, selling price $30.00 per unit, variable cost $18.00 per unit. Contribution per unit $12.00 Break-even 84 whole units, or $2,520.00 in sales

## How the break-even calculator works

The break-even sales calculator works out how many whole units, and how much in sales, cover the fixed costs for a period. Contribution per unit = price − variable cost per unit. Required units = fixed costs / contribution, rounded up. Required sales = whole units × price. Price must exceed variable cost per unit, or no break-even exists.

No statutory rate or threshold is applied. The definitions follow Business Queensland: break-even and profit.

## What the break-even calculator does not decide

The break-even sales calculator does not forecast demand or say that the units can be sold. It uses one price and one variable cost, so use one product or a stable representative mix and a consistent GST basis.

## Boundary cases

Each row is a test: scripts/business-calculators.test.mjs runs this calculator on these fictional inputs and fails if the result differs from the one shown.

Case | Inputs | Result
Part of a unit rounds up to a whole unit | Fixed $1,000.00, price $30.00, variable $18.00 | Contribution $12.00, 84 units, sales $2,520.00
A price equal to variable cost never breaks even | Fixed $1,000.00, price $18.00, variable $18.00 | Refused: price must exceed variable cost per unit to reach break-even

Required hourly rate before GST from annual costs, target profit and billable hours.

## How the hourly pricing calculator works

The hourly pricing calculator works out the hourly rate that covers your annual costs and target profit. Required hourly rate = (annual costs + target annual profit) / annual billable hours, rounded up to the next cent so the hours cover the total. Include owner remuneration in costs if it must be covered before profit. Exclude non-billable time from hours. The result is before GST.

# Fixed fee pricing calculator for accountants and advisers

Source: https://duguid.com.au/tools/business-calculators/fixed-fee/

> Price a fixed fee from hours or cost and margin, with GST, monthly instalments adding to the cent and the effective hourly rate, calculated in your browser.

# Fixed fee pricing calculator

A fixed fee from estimated hours at a rate or a cost and margin, with GST, monthly instalments that add up to the cent and the effective hourly rate.

Published 15 November 2026. Last checked 15 November 2026.

JavaScript is required for interactive calculations. The formula, assumptions and source links remain available below.

Fixed fee pricing inputs

Estimated hours for the work Hourly rate or cost per hour, before GST (AUD) Target margin on the fee (%) Monthly instalments Round the fee up to The cent The next $10 The next $50 The next $100

Add GST at 10%

Enter a 0% margin when the rate already includes your profit. The hourly pricing calculator works out a rate from annual costs, target profit and billable hours; with a target profit of $0 it gives your cost per hour.

Calculate Fictional example: the first boundary case below. Change the inputs and calculate your own. Inputs: 18.5 hours at $95.00 an hour, 40% margin, fee rounded up to the next $10, GST added, 12 monthly instalments. Fee before GST $2,930.00 GST $293.00 Fee including GST $3,223.00 First instalment $268.62 Instalments 2 to 12, each $268.58 Effective hourly rate before GST $158.38

## How the fixed fee pricing calculator works

The fixed fee pricing calculator turns an estimate of hours into a fee you can quote before the work starts. Enter your hourly rate with a 0% margin, or your cost per hour with the margin you want the fee to carry: fee = hours × rate / (1 − margin). A margin is a share of the fee, so a 40% margin on a $95 cost is $158.33 an hour, not the $133 a 40% markup would give. The fee then rounds up to the cent or to the next $10, $50 or $100, so rounding never takes it below your rate or margin.

GST at 10% is added to the fee when you tick the box, and the fee including GST is split into monthly instalments. Each instalment is the total divided evenly and rounded down to the cent; the first instalment also carries the cents left over, at most one cent for each instalment after it. The instalments add up to the fee to the cent, every instalment after the first is the same amount for a recurring payment, and if the engagement ends early the client has paid at least an even share of the fee for each month paid. The effective hourly rate is the fee before GST over the hours, so you can see what rounding and the margin earn an hour.

## What the fixed fee pricing calculator leaves out

The fixed fee pricing calculator prices one piece of work. For several services or entities, price each and add the fees. It does not suggest a market rate, allow for work beyond the hours you estimated, or decide whether your supply is taxable: add GST only if you are registered for GST and the supply is taxable.

Each row is a test: scripts/business-calculators.test.mjs runs this calculator on these fictional inputs and fails if the result differs from the one shown.

## How the budget variance calculator works

The budget variance calculator compares one actual figure with one budget figure. Difference = actual − budget. Percentage = difference / absolute budget × 100. A zero budget has no percentage comparison. Positive income differences are favourable; positive cost differences are unfavourable.

No statutory rate or external source is applied. The favourability convention is the usual management-accounting one.

## What the budget variance calculator does not decide

The budget variance calculator does not say why a difference arose or whether it matters. Explain causes from the records.

Monthly payment $954.09 Last payment, 1 July 2031 $954.35 Number of payments 60 Amount financed $60,000.00 Annual nominal rate 7.5% Balloon, due 1 July 2031 $18,000.00 Total paid, with the balloon $75,245.66 Total interest $15,245.66 The last payment is $954.35, not $954.09: it is what the balance needs after each period’s interest is rounded to the cent.

Download schedule CSV

## How the loan repayment schedule calculator works

The calculator sets out a loan payment by payment, weekly, fortnightly, monthly, quarterly or yearly. Give any 3 of the regular payment, the amount financed, the number of payments and the annual nominal interest rate, with the balloon, and it works out the fourth. Each row shows the date, the balance before the payment, the payment, the interest since the last payment, the principal repaid and the balance after it.

The period rate is the annual nominal rate divided by the payments a year: 52 for weekly and 26 for fortnightly, so a year of weekly payments is taken as 52 weeks. Payments in arrears fall at the end of each period, the first one period after the start date. Payments in advance fall at the start, the first on the start date, so the first carries no interest. A balloon, or residual, is due at the end of the last period: with the last payment in arrears, or a period after it in advance. It can be an amount or a percentage of the amount financed, rounded half up to the cent.

Each period’s interest is rounded to the cent, so the last payment differs from the others by the cents that rounding leaves. In advance, the last payment leaves the balloon’s value a period before it falls due, rounded to the cent, and the balloon row’s interest is the rest of the balloon. The payment is the same as a spreadsheet’s PMT with the balloon as the future value and type 1 for advance.

The amount financed is the payments and balloon discounted at the rate, rounded half up to the cent. The number of payments is found by running the payment until one would take the balance to the balloon; that payment is the last and is smaller. The interest rate is found by bisection between 0% and 100% a year: halving 48 times leaves it within 0.0000000000004% a year of the rate at which the payments and balloon, discounted, equal the amount financed. The page refuses payments and a balloon that add up to less than the amount financed, which no rate of nil or more fits, payments that would need more than 100% a year, and a payment that never covers a period’s interest.

Download schedule CSV saves the inputs, totals and every row as plain figures.

## What the loan repayment schedule calculator leaves out

The calculator assumes a rate that does not change, payments on the same day of each period and no fees. It does not work out GST, stamp duty or the tax treatment of the interest or the asset. Lenders that accrue interest daily, or count a weekly year as 365 days, give slightly different figures. The result is not a lender’s quote.

## How the hire purchase and chattel mortgage schedule works

The calculator sets out a hire purchase agreement or a chattel mortgage payment by payment from the amount financed, weekly to yearly, in arrears or in advance, with any balloon or residual. Give any 3 of the regular payment, the amount financed, the number of payments and the annual nominal rate, and it works out the fourth. Under Division 240 the interest in each payment is the hirer’s notional interest at the implicit rate; working out the rate from the agreement’s payments finds that rate.

The calculator totals the interest, the finance charge, by income year from 1 July to 30 June, and sets out a journal for each payment: debit the liability with the principal, debit interest expense with the interest and credit the bank with the payment. The balloon has its own line. Download schedule CSV saves the schedule, the income years and the journal as plain figures.

The australian-accounting command hire-purchase-schedule works the same agreement monthly. It keeps every instalment as the agreement states it and puts the cents of rounding into each month’s interest, and it lists a month that runs across 30 June apart rather than sharing it. This page keeps the interest of each period rounded on its own and puts the cents into the last payment, so on the same agreement the two can differ by a few cents.

## What the hire purchase and chattel mortgage schedule does not cover

The schedule does not work out GST, the GST credit or the car limit: it starts from the amount financed. Record the asset at its cost and the liability at the amount financed when the agreement starts; a deposit, trade-in, fees and stamp duty are yours to add. It does not state the income tax treatment of a chattel mortgage, which the sources applied do not cover, or of an early payout. It assumes a rate that does not change and payments on the same day of each period.

Leases are not covered: a lessee’s lease under AASB 16 is not worked here. Confirm the treatment with the agreement, the financier’s statements and a registered tax agent.

Download schedule CSV

## How the AASB 16 lease calculator works

The calculator measures a lessee’s lease under AASB 16 at commencement and sets out each income year to the end of the lease. The lease liability is the payments not yet paid, with any residual value guarantee you expect to pay or purchase option you are reasonably certain to exercise, discounted at the rate you enter: the rate implicit in the lease or, if that cannot be readily determined, your incremental borrowing rate. A payment in advance falls on the commencement date, so it goes into the right-of-use asset’s cost, not the liability. The asset’s cost adds payments made before commencement, less incentives received, initial direct costs and the estimated cost to dismantle, remove or restore.

Each period’s interest is the period rate on the liability. The schedule sets out every payment’s interest and principal, which are the journal for that payment, and the income year table gives each year’s interest, payments, straight-line depreciation and the liability and asset at 30 June. Depreciation is an equal amount each payment period over the lease term, or each month over the useful life where ownership transfers. Download schedule CSV saves the tables as plain figures.

With the comparison on, the page puts the same asset under hire purchase at your rate and bought outright, beside the lease, for each income year to the year the lease term ends: cash paid with GST, GST credits, deductions, the tax they save at your rate and the net cost. The lease deducts its payments when they are paid. Hire purchase deducts its notional interest and, like buying, the asset’s decline in value. The tax value left at the end is what can still be deducted after it: the residual if a lease buys the asset, and the asset’s adjustable value otherwise.

## What the AASB 16 lease calculator does not cover

The calculator does not decide whether a contract is or contains a lease, the lease term, the discount rate or whether a purchase option is reasonably certain. It flags a short-term lease but not a lease of a low-value asset, which paragraph 5(b) also lets the lessee expense. It does not remeasure a lease: a change in an index or rate, a lease modification, a reassessed term or option, an early payout, or variable payments that do not depend on an index or rate. It does not separate non-lease components, apply the revaluation or fair value models, impairment, a sale and leaseback, a lessor’s accounting, not-for-profit concessionary leases or deferred tax.

The comparison does not discount the cash flows, value the asset at the end of the term, apply the prepayment rules to a payment in advance, the luxury car lease rules (it refuses a car above the car limit), small business simplified depreciation or an instant asset write-off, or an asset first used after the commencement date. It takes GST credits on the payment dates rather than at the end of each tax period, and the tax saved at 30 June of each year. Confirm the treatment with the agreement, the financier’s statements and a registered tax agent or auditor.

## How the rental property calculator works

The rental property calculator works out one owner’s rental income and deductions for one residential property and one income year, on the lines of the ATO’s rental property worksheet (Rental properties guide 2026, Example 33). Rent and other rental income are assessable (section 6-5). Co-owners who are not in a business of letting share income and expenses by legal interest, whatever they agree between them (TR 93/32), so the calculator takes the whole property’s amounts and multiplies them by your interest. Your loans are entered as your own and are not divided.

An expense of the property for the whole time you held it in the year, such as rates, insurance or repairs, is apportioned by the days it was let or available for rent on commercial terms over the days you held it. An expense solely for renting, such as agent commission or advertising for tenants, is not (the guide’s time-based method and Example 34). Travel is shown but not deducted: section 26-31 denies it to an individual not in a business of letting from 1 July 2017. Interest on a loan used partly for the rental is the interest times the principal used for the rental over the total principal, then the time-based share (TR 2000/2 paragraphs 15 and 16).

Capital works are 2.5% of the construction expenditure a year, or 4% for a building begun from 18 July 1985 to 15 September 1987 or taken to have begun before 16 September 1987 under section 43-220, times the days used over 365. The deduction is never more than the construction expenditure not yet deducted (sections 43-25, 43-210 and 43-240). Each asset’s decline in value is taken as you enter it, at your interest and the time-based share, and is nil where section 40-27 denies it for a second-hand asset or one used privately. The borrowing expenses line is the year’s figure from the borrowing expenses calculator. Each line is rounded to the cent, where the guide’s examples round to the dollar. The calculator reproduces Example 33: deductions of $20,193.33 and a net rent of −$10,893.33, the guide’s $20,629 less the $436 of travel its Note 2 says needs an exception.

Given your other taxable income for 2024-25 to 2026-27, the calculator works out the tax at the resident scale with and without the net rent, its cents dropped as a return shows them, and the difference.

## Choices the rental property calculator makes

The calculator makes 2 counting choices the ATO gives no worked example for, as the rental-property command of the australian-accounting calculators does. The use period of capital works counts both its first and last day (section 43-230(2)). The time-based share applies to a decline in value you enter, as it does to the other lines. The 4% rate for a residential building begun from 18 July 1985 rests on the guide’s Table 1, not on a provision read. A building begun from 22 August 1979 to 17 July 1985 qualifies only if it was intended on completion for short-term traveller accommodation or non-residential use, so the calculator refuses it rather than give nil.

## What the rental property calculator does not cover

The calculator works the income years 2020-21 to 2026-27 and refuses 2027-28, from which section 26-155 can limit residential rental deductions. It refuses a holiday home whose costs section 26-50 denies (TR 2026/1), a loan redrawn or drawn further in the year (TR 2000/2 paragraphs 23 to 25), an asset acquired on 9 May 2017, the day section 40-27 starts at 7.30 pm, and the effect on tax before 2024-25. It also refuses works or an asset first used after you first held the property in a year it was not available every day, as the days of rental use are then not known.

Not covered: a business of letting; a company, trust or other entity; letting part of a dwelling or at less than market rent; GST on short stays; the 4% rate for build to rent or short-term traveller accommodation; vacant land under section 26-102; a tax loss under Division 36; and the Medicare levy, the surcharge, offsets and study loan repayments. The calculator never derives construction expenditure from a price or a valuation. A value or total of $70,368,744,177,664 or more is refused, as the page cannot show it to the cent. Have a registered tax agent confirm the result before you lodge.

## How the borrowing expenses calculator works

The borrowing expenses calculator works out the deduction for costs of borrowing money, such as loan establishment fees, mortgage registration and lender’s mortgage insurance, under section 25-25 for up to 3 loans and every income year of each. Each year’s maximum is what is left of the expenditure over the days left in the period of the loan, times those days in the year, rounded to the cent. The deduction is that maximum times the year’s income use, which can change from year to year.

A loan repaid early ends its period that day. The remaining expenditure becomes the maximum for that year before apportionment. A loan that refinances an earlier one spreads its own expenses from its own first day. When everything incurred for borrowing in a year comes to $100 or less of income use, it is deducted that year instead.

The optional accounting column sets the same expenses against the loan under AASB 9: the effective interest rate that discounts the loan’s monthly payments to the amount borrowed less the expenses, the expenses recognised each year by that rate, the write-off when a loan is extinguished, the 10% test for a refinancing with the same lender, and the amortised cost at 30 June. Beside each year’s section 25-25 amount it shows the difference, and what tax and accounting each still carry at 30 June.

For the same-lender test, enter the part of the borrowing expenses paid to the lender or on its behalf. Enter zero if there were none. Leave fees received blank if there were none. Exclude fees paid to third parties for your own account from the 10% test.

## What the borrowing expenses calculator does not cover

The calculator does not decide which costs are borrowing expenses rather than interest or a capital cost of the property, or how much of the money is used to produce income: you state those. It refuses a loan first drawn before 1 July 2017, an income year after 2027-28, a holiday home or other leisure facility unless subsection 26-50(3) applies all year (whether the anti-avoidance rule in subsection 26-50(7) stops it applying is yours to decide), and a refinancing whose dates do not meet. It works years after 2027-28 under section 25-25 as read and marks them projected. It does not apply the vacant land or residential loss limits, interest deductions, redraws, Division 7A loans or debt forgiveness.

### Vacant land and residential loss limits

The result shows the section 25-25 amount before any applicable limit. Section 26-102 can limit deductions for vacant land holding costs incurred from 1 July 2019, including ongoing costs of borrowing to acquire the land. From 2027-28, section 26-155 can restrict deductions for residential accommodation. Check whether either limit or an exception applies to your costs.

The accounting column takes every expense as integral to the effective interest rate, fixed monthly payments in arrears and the expected life you give, and shares a month’s amortisation across 30 June by days. It does not work a modification under 10%, a variable rate repricing, fair value through profit or loss, AASB 112 deferred tax or the AASB 123 capitalisation period. Confirm the result with the ATO’s Borrowing expenses page or a registered tax agent before relying on it.

## How the depreciation pools calculator works

The calculator works one of 3 Division 40, Subdivision 328-D or Division 43 worksheets for an income year from 2020-21 to 2026-27. A low-value pool declines by 18.75% of the low-cost assets and second element costs added in the year, and by 37.5% of the previous closing pool balance and the low-value assets added (section 40-440). The 2 parts are added before rounding. Termination values reduce the closing balance, and any excess over it is assessable income (section 40-445).

A general small business pool first adds the opening balance, the year’s additions and cost additions, less termination values (subsection 328-210(2)). An amount above zero and below the year’s low pool value threshold is deducted in full and the pool closes at zero: $20,000 from 2023-24, and no limit from 2020-21 to 2022-23. An amount below zero is assessable income (section 328-215). Otherwise the deduction is 30% of the opening balance and 15% of the additions and cost additions (section 328-190), each rounded to the cent. The ATO’s example of Loretta’s pool, with a $100,000 opening balance, $28,000 of additions and an $8,000 sale, gives a $34,200 deduction and an $85,800 closing balance.

A capital works deduction is your construction expenditure times the days used over 365, at 4% for a part used in the 4% manner or else 2.5%, then reduced to the taxable use and limited to the undeducted construction expenditure (section 43-210, or section 43-215 for works begun from 16 September 1987 to 26 February 1992). The ATO’s example 29 in Rental properties 2026, $115,800 for 346 days at 2.5%, gives $2,744.

## What the depreciation pools calculator does not cover

The calculator does not decide which assets may go into a pool, whether you are a small business entity that chose simplified depreciation, or each asset’s taxable use: you enter the amounts after those choices. It does not work out temporary full expensing of individual assets from 2020-21 to 2022-23, the instant asset write-off or backing business investment, and refuses the one 2020-21 small business pool case where the 57.5% rate could apply. It leaves out the change of business use adjustment, roll-over relief, the car limit and balancing adjustments outside a pool. For capital works it refuses works begun before 16 September 1987 and the 4% rate for works begun before 27 February 1992, and does not decide whether the works qualify, work out the undeducted construction expenditure or split it amongst co-owners. Results are planning estimates: check them against your records and the ATO’s guidance.

# Division 7A minimum yearly repayment calculator

Source: https://duguid.com.au/tools/business-calculators/div7a/

> The Division 7A minimum yearly repayment on an amalgamated loan for one income year, from its balance, that year’s benchmark rate and the remaining term.

# Division 7A loan calculator

Minimum yearly repayment, interest and principal on one amalgamated loan.

Published 13 November 2026. Last checked 13 November 2026.

JavaScript is required for interactive calculations. The formula, assumptions and source links remain available below.

Division 7A minimum yearly repayment inputs

Loan not repaid at the end of the previous income year (AUD)

Income year (benchmark rate) 2026-27 (8.77%) 2025-26 (8.37%) 2024-25 (8.77%) 2023-24 (8.27%) 2022-23 (4.77%) 2021-22 (4.52%) 2020-21 (4.52%) 2019-20 (5.37%)

Remaining term (whole years)

The years and rates are those in the Division 7A benchmark rate table, for a company whose income year ends on 30 June. Round a remaining term that is not a whole number up to the next whole year.

Calculate Fictional example: the first boundary case below. Change the inputs and calculate your own. Inputs: 2026-27 income year at the 8.77% benchmark rate, $1,000.00 not repaid at 30 June 2026, 1 year remaining. Minimum yearly repayment $1,087.70 Interest for the year, if repaid on 30 June $87.70 Principal, if repaid on 30 June $1,000.00

## How the Division 7A minimum yearly repayment calculator works

The Division 7A minimum yearly repayment calculator works out the least a borrower must repay on one amalgamated loan in one income year after the year the loan was made. It applies the formula in subsection 109E(6) of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1936: the loan not repaid at the end of the previous income year, times the year’s benchmark interest rate, divided by 1 minus (1 ÷ (1 + the rate)) raised to the remaining term in years.

The interest for the year is the benchmark rate on the whole balance, and the principal is the rest of the repayment. That split assumes the whole repayment is made on the last day of the income year. The ATO works interest out from the daily balance, so a repayment made earlier in the year carries less interest and more of it reduces the principal.

The ATO’s worked example on Loans by private companies takes $55,000 at 5.95% with 7 years remaining and gives $9,835 to the nearest dollar; this calculator gives $9,834.92 for those figures.

## What the Division 7A minimum yearly repayment calculator does not cover

The calculator does not decide whether a payment or loan is a Division 7A loan, whether the loan agreement complies, whether a shortfall is a deemed dividend or how much of it, or how a distributable surplus limits one. It works one income year only, with no repayment schedule, and none for the year in which the loan was made. It takes the balance as you enter it: it does not work it out from the loans made, repayments made before the lodgment day or the previous year’s interest, and it does not combine several loans. It does not handle an income year that ends on a day other than 30 June. Subsection 109E(5) lets regulations set another amount, and this calculator applies the formula only. Confirm the figures with the ATO Division 7A calculator and decision tool or a registered tax agent.

## Common questions

### What is the Division 7A benchmark interest rate for 2026-27?

For a company with a 30 June year end, the Division 7A benchmark interest rate is 8.77% for 2026-27 and 8.37% for 2025-26 under section 109N(2) of the ITAA 1936.

### What is the difference between this page and the Division 7A loan schedule calculator?

The Division 7A minimum repayment calculator works out one income year’s minimum yearly repayment, interest and principal; the Division 7A loan schedule calculator tracks every year over a 7-year or 25-year complying loan.

## How the FBT car calculator works

The FBT car calculator values one car’s fringe benefits for the FBT year from 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027, which has 365 days. Under the statutory formula, the taxable value is the car’s base value times 20%, times the days it was used or available for an employee’s private use, divided by 365, less what the employee contributed. The base value is the cost price plus non-business accessories fitted later; if the employer or an associate first held the car before 1 April 2022, only two-thirds of the cost price counts.

Under the operating cost method, the taxable value is the year’s operating costs times the private use share, 100% less the business use percentage, less contributions. The method applies only if the employer elected it and kept log book and odometer records; without them the business use percentage is nil. If the statutory formula gives a lower value, the calculator uses that value, as subsection 10(5) of the Act requires.

The taxable value is then grossed up: at the Type 1 rate, 2.0802, if the employer, or another provider, is entitled to a GST credit for providing the car, or the Type 2 rate, 1.8868, if not, as section 2.3 of the guide’s chapter 2 sets out. FBT is 47% of the grossed-up value. The FBT return for the year ending 31 March 2026, read 15 November 2026, asks for whole dollars at each taxable value and grossed-up amount and works the FBT from the total of all benefits, so a return’s figures can differ from these by the cents.

Example 28 in section 7.8 of the ATO’s guide for employers takes a $60,000 car available for 182 of 365 days, with $1,000 of fuel paid by the employee. It shows $5,983 at step 4, leaving out the cents of $5,983.56, and a taxable value of $4,983; this calculator gives $4,983.56. Example 31 in section 7.9 takes $19,580 of operating costs, 75% business use and a $2,000 contribution, and gives $2,895; this calculator gives $2,895.00 when the statutory formula value is higher.

## How the FBT car calculator checks the electric cars exemption

For a battery electric, hydrogen fuel cell electric or plug-in hybrid car, the calculator checks the electric cars exemption in section 8A, one condition to a row. The car must be provided to a current employee, first both held and used by anyone on or after 1 July 2022, and have had no luxury car tax payable on its first retail sale or on any other sale or import before the benefit. A first retail sale after 31 March 2027, such as a dealer’s demonstrator sold later, comes after every benefit in the year, so its luxury car tax does not count. A first retail sale within the year after the car was first held and used may come between the year’s benefits, so the calculator refuses one on which luxury car tax was payable: that tax does not affect a benefit provided before the sale. For the first retail sale, the calculator compares the luxury car tax value, the price with GST and any accessories sold with the car but without luxury car tax, with the fuel-efficient threshold for the financial year of the sale: $91,661 for 2026-27, and $91,387 for 2024-25 and 2025-26. A plug-in hybrid also needs a commitment made before 1 April 2025 for a period that began before then and includes the benefit, no new commitment since for a period that includes the benefit, such as an optional extension, a break in the novation, changed lease payments or residual value, or a new employer, and an exempt car benefit before that day. When every condition is met, the taxable value and FBT are nil, and the result shows the value before the exemption, which still counts towards the employee’s reportable fringe benefits amount unless the car is a pooled or shared car.

The ATO’s Electric cars exemption page gives 3 examples, each a boundary case below: Shelly’s car, first used on 1 April 2022, is not exempt; John’s, held from 15 June 2022 but first used on 5 July 2022, is exempt; GHI Co’s $85,000 car was above 2022-23’s $84,916 threshold when first sold, so it is not. Its plug-in hybrid page’s Simon, whose lease runs from 1 April 2024 to 31 March 2027, stays exempt; Tony’s break in his novation from 1 May 2025 is a new commitment, so his car is not.

## What the FBT car calculator does not cover

The calculator does not decide whether a vehicle is a car, whether a benefit arises, or whether the work vehicle exemption or a reduction applies. For the electric cars exemption it does not decide the kind of car, its dates, its luxury car tax value or a plug-in hybrid’s commitments, which you state. It takes the fuel-efficient threshold, so it does not cover a car that was not fuel-efficient under the Luxury Car Tax Act when first sold, or a car never sold at retail in Australia, such as one its user imported, and it reads a value above the threshold as luxury car tax payable, so a supply exempt from that tax is not covered either. The changes announced on 5 May 2026 for electric cars from 1 April 2027 were not law when read on 19 November 2026; they are listed under announced, not yet law. It does not work out operating costs: add deemed depreciation, at 25% of the car’s depreciated value for a car acquired on or after 10 May 2006, and deemed interest at the statutory interest rate on the ATO’s FBT rates and thresholds page, both apportioned to the days held. It values one car for one FBT year. It does not work out a leased car value, apply the older statutory percentages kept for commitments made before 10 May 2011, or work out the reportable fringe benefits amount or FBT for other benefits. On 15 November 2026 chapter 7 of the ATO’s guide said it was being reviewed after the Full Federal Court’s decision of 27 March 2026 in SEPL Pty Ltd as trustee of the SFT Trust v Commissioner of Taxation [2026] FCAFC 36, on whether the directors of a discretionary trust’s corporate trustee were employees and whether their cars were provided in respect of employment, a question this calculator leaves to you. Confirm the figures with the ATO’s guide or a registered tax agent.

# FBT car parking calculator: threshold test and 5 methods

# FBT car parking calculator

The $11.48 threshold test, then the taxable value by any of the 5 methods, for the FBT year ending 31 March 2027.

Valuation method Commercial parking station method Market value method, elected, with a valuer’s report Average cost method, elected 12-week register method, elected Spaces method, elected Highest of the lowest all-day fees of commercial parking stations within 1 km on Wednesday 1 April 2026, the year’s first business day (AUD) Station, market value or average cost: number of benefits Station or market value: each benefit’s value, the lowest all-day fee on its day or the valuer’s amount (AUD) Average cost only: lowest all-day fee on the year’s first day with a benefit (AUD) Average cost only: lowest all-day fee on the year’s last day with a benefit (AUD) 12-week register only: value of the benefits it records as if kept this year, after employee contributions (AUD) 12-week register only: days from the first to the last day in the year a benefit was provided 12-week register only: FBT year it was first valid for, the year ending 31 March Spaces only: daily rate amount of each space, by the station, market value or average cost method, before contributions (AUD) Spaces only: days in each space’s availability period Spaces only: number of spaces Spaces only: employees the election covers at the start of the parking period Spaces only: employees the election covers at the end of the parking period Spaces only: eligible spaces at the start of the parking period Spaces only: eligible spaces at the end of the parking period Every method but the register: total employee contributions (AUD)

Calculate Fictional example: the first boundary case below. Change the inputs and calculate your own. Inputs: commercial parking station method, first business day fee $12.36, 22 benefits at $12.36, employee contributions $0.00. Gross taxable value $271.92 Employee contributions applied $0.00 Excess contributions $0.00 Taxable value $271.92

## How the FBT car parking calculator works

The FBT car parking calculator values the car parking fringe benefits an employer provides at one work car park in the FBT year from 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027. It first applies the threshold test: a benefit arises only if a commercial parking station within 1 km charged a lowest all-day fee of more than $11.48 on Wednesday 1 April 2026, the first business day of the year. Enter the highest of the nearby stations’ lowest fees that day. At $11.48 or less, no car parking benefit arises and the taxable value is nil.

Where a benefit arises, the calculator values it by the method you choose. The commercial parking station method values each benefit at the lowest all-day fee charged nearby on its day; the market value method at a qualified valuer’s arm’s length amount; the average cost method at the average of the lowest fees on the first and last days a benefit was provided. Each takes off employee contributions, never below nil. The 12-week register method grosses a register’s 12 weeks up to a year: the register value × 52 ÷ 12 × the days in the availability period ÷ 366. The spaces method values each space at its daily rate amount × its days ÷ 366 × 228, scales the total down where fewer employees than spaces are covered, and takes off contributions.

This page opens on example 13 in section 16.2.4.4 of the ATO’s guide for employers: Rent-a-spot’s $272 monthly fee over 22 business days is $12.36 a day, above the $11.48 threshold. With Rent-a-spot the only station within 1 km, an employee who parks on each of those 22 days receives 22 benefits worth $271.92. The guide works the daily rate, not a total. The tests also hold the guide’s example 15, $18.50 a benefit by the average cost method, example 17, $5,416.67 by the register method, and example 18, $1,061.31 by the spaces method, each at its own year’s threshold.

The method is the employer’s choice, made by election for every method but the commercial parking station method; the calculator values the method chosen and does not recommend one.

## What the FBT car parking calculator does not cover

Apart from the threshold test, the calculator does not decide whether a car parking benefit arises. It does not check that a car was parked for more than 4 hours between 7 am and 7 pm at premises the employer controls near the employee’s primary place of employment, that the car was used to travel between home and work that day, and that a facility is a commercial parking station within 1 km by the shortest practicable route. It does not check that a fee is representative (sections 39AA and 39AB) or set at arm’s length (subsection 39E(2)), or that an election, valuer’s report or register is valid; it checks only a register’s age, not the 10% increase rule in subsection 39GF(3). Nor does it check that the numbers of employees and spaces behind the spaces method’s reduction are representative (subsection 39FB(6)). Under the station, market value and average cost methods it takes contributions off in total, which is right only where no benefit’s contribution is more than that benefit’s value: an excess on one benefit does not reduce another. It does not apply exemptions, such as the small business exemption in section 58GA, the exempt employers or the disabled persons’ parking exclusion. It values one work car park: under the commercial parking station method it takes one value for every benefit, and under the spaces method one group of spaces sharing a daily rate amount and availability period. It does not split the value between Type 1 and Type 2 benefits, gross it up or work out FBT. Confirm the figures with the ATO’s guide or a registered tax agent.

# FBT expense payment calculator: otherwise deductible rule

## How the FBT expense payment calculator works

The FBT expense payment calculator values one expense payment fringe benefit in the FBT year from 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027: your payment of an employee’s expenditure to a third party, or your reimbursement of it. An external expense payment is valued at the payment, less any contribution the employee made towards it, or at the reimbursement. Where the employee could have deducted the expenditure at once, the otherwise deductible rule reduces the value: the gross deduction is the expenditure × the share that would be deductible; the notional deduction is that less the deduction for the part the employee bore. The taxable value is the payment less the contribution and the notional deduction, never below nil.

Where the employee bought goods or a service that you, or an associate, sell to customers in the ordinary course of business, the payment is an in-house expense payment. The calculator values the goods or service by the in-house rule that applies to the seller, as if the seller’s sale to the employee were an in-house benefit (section 22A), and takes off the part of the expenditure the employee bore, the expenditure less your payment net of their contribution, then the part of the employee’s $1,000 in-house reduction for the year that their other in-house benefits have not used, outside salary packaging.

This page opens on the first example in section 9.4 of the ATO’s guide for employers: an employee spends $500, 80% for work, and you reimburse $250 without regard to the business share. The gross deduction of $400 less the employee’s deduction of ($500 − $250) × 80% = $200 leaves a notional deduction of $200, so the taxable value is $250 − $200 = $50. The tests also hold the guide’s second section 9.4 example and its section 9.3 in-house example.

## What the FBT expense payment calculator does not cover

The calculator does not decide whether an expense payment fringe benefit arises or whether an exemption applies, such as a no-private-use declaration (section 20A), accommodation away from home (section 21), car expenses (section 22) or the exemptions in Division 13. It does not apply the otherwise deductible rule to an in-house expense payment (subparagraph 24(1)(b)(i)): choose 0% and $0 for one. It does not value airline transport, a car expense, whose otherwise deductible amount follows the car substantiation rules, an expense paid for an employee and an associate jointly, whose reduction is limited to the employee’s interest, the reduction for entertainment of others in section 63A, the living-away-from-home food reduction in section 63, or several payments for the same expenditure (subsection 22A(4)). It does not check the documentary evidence, declaration or travel diary the otherwise deductible rule needs (paragraphs 24(1)(c) to (e)) or work out the employee’s deduction. It values one benefit: the $1,000 in-house reduction is for all of an employee’s in-house fringe benefits in the year, so enter what the others have not used. Goods or services you buy and give an employee, or buy on your credit card, are property or residual benefits, not expense payments. It stops at the taxable value and does not gross it up or work out FBT. Confirm the figures with the ATO’s guide or a registered tax agent.

# FBT loan calculator with the otherwise deductible rule

Source: https://duguid.com.au/tools/business-calculators/fbt-loan/

> A loan fringe benefit’s taxable value for the FBT year ending 31 March 2027: interest at 8.27% less interest accrued, then the otherwise deductible rule.

# FBT loan calculator

A loan fringe benefit’s taxable value: interest at 8.27% less interest accrued, then the otherwise deductible rule.

Published 17 November 2026. Last checked 17 November 2026.

JavaScript is required for interactive calculations. The formula, assumptions and source links remain available below.

FBT loan inputs for the FBT year 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027

Total of the loan’s daily balances for the days the employee owed it in the year (AUD) Interest that accrued on the loan for the year (AUD) Share of the loan used to produce the employee’s assessable income (%) Deduction the employee could claim for the interest that accrued (AUD)

A balance of $50,000 owed every day of the year totals $50,000 × 365 = $18,250,000. Enter 0% income use for a loan to an associate, or where the employee has not given you the loan declaration subsection 19(1) requires (an employee credit or share loan benefit needs none): the reduction then does not apply.

Calculate Fictional example: the first boundary case below. Change the inputs and calculate your own. Inputs: daily balances totalling $18,250,000.00, interest accrued $2,000.00, 60% income use, deduction for the interest accrued $1,200.00. Notional interest at 8.27% $4,135.00 Gross taxable value $2,135.00 Gross deduction $2,481.00 Notional deduction $1,281.00 Reduction applied $1,281.00 Taxable value $854.00

## How the FBT loan calculator works

The FBT loan calculator values one loan fringe benefit for the FBT year from 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027. The notional interest is the interest the loan would have earned at the statutory interest rate, 8.27%, on its balance at the end of each day: the total of the daily balances × 8.27% ÷ 365. The gross taxable value is the amount by which that exceeds the interest that accrued on the loan for the year, never below nil.

Where the employee, not an associate, would have been able to deduct interest on the loan, the otherwise deductible rule reduces the value. The gross deduction is the notional interest × the share of the loan used to produce the employee’s assessable income. The notional deduction is the gross deduction less the deduction the employee could claim for the interest that accrued. The taxable value is the gross taxable value less the notional deduction, never below nil.

Section 8.8 of the ATO’s guide for employers works a $50,000 loan at 4% for the whole year, 60% used for interest-bearing investments, at the 5.65% rate of 2016-17: $825 less a $495 reduction, a taxable value of $330. This page opens on the same loan at 8.27%: notional interest of $4,135.00 less $2,000.00 accrued is $2,135.00; the gross deduction of $2,481.00 less the $1,200.00 deduction for the interest accrued leaves $1,281.00; the taxable value is $854.00. Run at 5.65%, the same steps give the guide’s $330, and its section 8.5 example’s $325; the tests hold both.

## What the FBT loan calculator does not cover

The calculator does not decide whether a loan fringe benefit arises or whether an exemption in section 17 applies, such as a loan at an arm’s length rate by a lender to the public or an advance for work expenses accounted for within 6 months. It does not treat deferred or unpaid interest, which can be a further loan or a debt waiver fringe benefit, a loan made before 1 July 1986 or a housing loan made before 3 April 1986, which can take a lower rate, a car loan, whose otherwise deductible amount follows the car substantiation rules in subsection 19(1), or a loan provided jointly to an employee and an associate. It does not work out the employee’s deduction, and it does not check the declaration the rule requires. A loan fringe benefit carries no GST credit, so it is grossed up at the Type 2 rate, 1.8868; this calculator stops at the taxable value and does not gross it up or work out FBT. Confirm the figures with the ATO’s guide or a registered tax agent.

Calculate Fictional example: the first boundary case below. Change the inputs and calculate your own. Inputs: 50/50 split method, meal entertainment expenses $4,000.00. Taxable value, 50% of the expenses $2,000.00

## How the meal entertainment calculator works

The meal entertainment calculator values an employer’s meal entertainment fringe benefits for the FBT year from 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027, where the employer has elected to value them under Division 9A. Both methods start from the year’s total expenses for providing meal entertainment to everyone, employees, associates and clients alike, less contributions from employees and their associates that the employer did not reimburse.

Under the 50/50 split method the taxable value is half those expenses. Under the 12-week register method it is those expenses × the register percentage: the value of the meal entertainment fringe benefits the register records for employees and their associates, over the value of all the meal entertainment it records. A register kept for 12 weeks in the year ending 31 March 2027 is valid for that year and the 4 after it. The calculator refuses a register first valid before the year ending 31 March 2023, or one that ceased to be valid because a year’s expenses rose more than 20% above those of its first valid year.

The ATO’s guide for employers describes both methods but works no example in figures. This page opens on example 18 of the ATO’s FBT return 2026 instructions, $4,000 of meal entertainment under the 50/50 split: $2,000. For the register method, the tests work a register of $1,000 of fringe benefits out of $3,000 of meal entertainment from the Act: the register percentage shows as 33.33% but applies as a third exactly, so $900 of expenses gives $300.00.

When the register method is chosen, the result also shows the 50/50 split figure for the same expenses. Which method to elect, if either, is the employer’s choice; the calculator does not recommend one.

## What the meal entertainment calculator does not cover

The calculator does not decide what is meal entertainment, whether the election is available or made, or whether a register meets the record and representative period rules in sections 37CC and 37CE. It does not value meal entertainment provided under a salary packaging arrangement, which cannot be elected, or entertainment valued by its actual cost as an expense payment, property or residual benefit. It does not apply exemptions; under the 50/50 split the property benefits and minor benefits exemptions do not apply. It does not take a register whose first valid year had nil expenses or check whether a later register replaced this one, split the value between Type 1 and Type 2 benefits, gross it up or work out FBT. Confirm the figures with the ATO’s guide or a registered tax agent.

# FBT property calculator

A property fringe benefit’s taxable value by the in-house or external rules, the otherwise deductible rule and the $1,000 in-house reduction.

## How the FBT property calculator works

The FBT property calculator values one property fringe benefit, goods or other property you give an employee in the FBT year from 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027. An in-house benefit is goods identical or similar to those you, or an associate, sell in the ordinary course of business; any other property is an external benefit. Choose the rule that applies to the property. Under a salary packaging arrangement an in-house benefit takes the notional value. Goods you make take the lowest arm’s length price where you sell identical goods to the trade, 75% of the lowest public price where you sell them to the public, and otherwise 75% of the notional value. Goods you buy for your business take the lesser of the arm’s length purchase price and the notional value. The calculator takes the employee’s contribution off, never below nil, and shows any excess, which does not reduce another benefit.

Where the employee would have had a once-only income tax deduction had they bought the property themselves, the otherwise deductible rule reduces the value. The gross deduction is the value before the contribution × the share of use that would be deductible; the notional deduction is that less the deduction for the contribution. For an in-house benefit outside salary packaging, the calculator then takes off the part of the employee’s $1,000 in-house reduction for the year that their other in-house benefits have not used.

This page opens on the desk example in section 17.3 of the ATO’s guide for employers: a desk you make and sell to the public for at least $900, which an employee buys for $500, has a taxable value of 75% × $900 − $500 = $175. The tests also hold the guide’s other section 17.3 and 17.5 examples.

## What the FBT property calculator does not cover

The calculator does not decide whether a property fringe benefit arises or whether property is in-house. Nor does it apply an exemption, such as property consumed on your premises on a working day (section 41), a minor benefit (section 58P) or an eligible work-related item such as a portable electronic device (section 58X). It does not value airline transport (paragraph 42(1)(ab)), a car property benefit, whose otherwise deductible amount follows the car substantiation rules, a benefit provided jointly to an employee and an associate, whose reduction is limited to the employee’s interest, or an expense payment, which has its own calculator. It does not check the declaration the otherwise deductible rule needs (paragraph 44(1)(c)) or work out the employee’s deduction. It values one benefit: the $1,000 in-house reduction is for all of an employee’s in-house fringe benefits in the year, so enter what the others have not used. It stops at the taxable value and does not gross it up or work out FBT. Confirm the figures with the ATO’s guide or a registered tax agent.

## How the vehicle classifier works

The vehicle classifier works out whether one vehicle bought in 2025-26 or 2026-27 is a car for income tax, GST and FBT, and what follows. The designed load is the gross vehicle mass on the compliance plate less the basic kerb weight, or the stated payload, which must agree with them. Under section 995-1 of ITAA 1997, a motor vehicle other than a motor cycle is a car if designed to carry a load under 1 tonne and fewer than 9 passengers, the driver counted.

For a car, the classifier asks whether it was designed principally to carry passengers. A passenger body was. A dual cab was if its seats, at 68 kg each (MT 2024), weigh more than the load left. For a single cab ute or panel van the answer turns on factors the page does not weigh (TD 94/19). The dual cab test is MT 2024’s, for FBT; no ATO ruling applies it to the car limit. So for a passenger body section 40-230 caps the cost to depreciate at the car limit, after any GST credit, and for a dual cab, a single cab ute or a panel van the car limit is not decided here; the page still gives a cost after the credit that is within the limit, as the limit would not reduce it. Section 69-10 of the GST Act caps the credit at 1/11 of the limit.

## Luxury car tax, the GST credit and FBT

Luxury car tax has its own car: a load under 2 tonnes and fewer than 9 passengers. The tax can apply above the threshold for its fuel consumption, unless it is a commercial vehicle not designed principally to carry passengers. For utes the classifier uses LCTD 2023/1’s simplified method, the ATO’s compliance approach: seats at 68 kg weighing less than half the load at supply, which is the designed load less any accessories then fitted. That approach says when the ATO will not review a sale, not whether the vehicle is a commercial vehicle in law, so it does not lift the GST credit cap: above the car limit the credit on a ute or van that is a car is not decided here. At exactly half, the 2 tests part: MT 2024 counts a dual cab as designed for passengers only when its seats weigh more than the load left, whilst LCTD 2023/1’s method needs them to weigh less than half the load. A 5-seat dual cab with a 680 kg load can therefore be exempt from FBT, whilst luxury car tax and the GST credit cap are not decided here.

For FBT, a single cab ute, a panel van, a dual cab not designed principally for passengers and any vehicle that is not a car can be exempt only if an employee’s private use was work-related travel or minor, infrequent and irregular use. You state that fact; the classifier never concludes it. A car designed principally for passengers gives a car fringe benefit, which the FBT car calculator values.

TD 94/19’s 4-wheel drive wagon, with 5 seats and an 865 kg load, carries passengers; at $75,000 in 2025-26 the ATO’s instant asset write-off page gives a $6,334 credit and a $68,666 cost, or the $69,674 car limit without a credit. MT 2024’s dual cab has 340 kg of passengers against 260 kg left. LCTD 2023/1’s example 5, a dual cab with 5 seats and 960 kg, is one the ATO will not review for luxury car tax. TD 2006/40’s $5,182 credit is $5,182.64 here, with its cents.

## What the vehicle classifier does not cover

The classifier does not decide whether private use was minor, infrequent and irregular, or whether a dual cab, single cab ute or panel van was designed mainly for carrying passengers for the car limit. Nor does it decide whether a ute or van is a commercial vehicle for the GST credit cap, whether a modification permanently changed a vehicle’s design (MT 2033 and LCTD 2023/1 paragraphs 16 to 30), or the principal purpose of a truck, bus or other body under 1 tonne, which turns on factors it does not weigh. Where LCTD 2023/1’s simplified method is not met it says the question is not decided here, and that method assumes a ute the Australian Design Rules class as a goods vehicle. It does not cover cars fitted out to carry people in wheelchairs, emergency vehicles, motor homes and campervans, taxis and limousines, leases and hire, a dealer quoting an ABN, a partly creditable purchase, or a year before 2025-26. It does not work out decline in value, luxury car tax payable or the taxable value of a fringe benefit. A classification is not advice: confirm it with the ATO’s guidance or a registered tax agent.

## How the PCG 2021/4 risk scorer works

Practical Compliance Guideline PCG 2021/4 sets out how the ATO rates the risk that an individual professional practitioner (IPP) does not return enough of their professional firm’s profit in their own hands. The scorer first asks the 2 gateways. If the arrangement is not commercially driven (Gateway 1) or has a high-risk feature (Gateway 2), it gives no score, because paragraph 12 makes the risk assessment framework unavailable.

It then scores up to 3 factors from 1 (lowest risk) to 6 (highest), using Table 1 at paragraph 76: the share of the whole of firm group profit entitlement the IPP returns personally, the total effective tax rate paid by the IPP and associated entities on that income, and, if you choose, the IPP’s remuneration as a percentage of a commercial benchmark for their services. It adds the scores and places the total in the green, amber or red zone of Table 2 at paragraph 78. If the IPP returns the whole entitlement, paragraph 81 makes the arrangement low risk and no other factor is scored.

The scorer reproduces the scores and zones of all 12 case studies in the guideline’s appendix. Case study 1 opens the page: Nicolas returns $330,000 of a $600,000 entitlement, 55% and a score of 4, and he and his company pay $189,367 of tax on it, 31.56% and a score of 3, so his aggregate of 7 is green. In case study 7, Jacinta’s $360,000 against a $350,000 benchmark adds a factor 3 score of 3, for an aggregate of 10 against all 3 factors, also green.

## What the PCG 2021/4 risk scorer does not cover

The scorer does not decide whether the guideline applies: whether the IPP provides professional services or manages the firm and is an equity holder, whether the firm’s income is personal services income and whether the structure is legally effective (paragraph 28). It does not test the gateways; it takes your answers. It does not work out the entitlement, the tax for each entity under paragraph 85, a part-time IPP’s full-time equivalent (paragraph 71) or a commercial benchmark; the PCG 2021/4 allocation calculator works out each recipient’s tax. A green zone is not a ruling: PCG 2021/4 does not change the law, Part IVA can still apply, and the ATO may still review an arrangement whose profit allocation drifts (paragraph 107). Confirm the assessment with the guideline or a registered tax agent.
