## How the PCG 2021/4 allocation calculator works

The PCG 2021/4 allocation calculator works out the tax each recipient of a professional firm’s profit pays on it, then scores the 3 risk assessment factors from those figures. It takes the IPP and up to 5 associated entities, each with its firm income, firm-related deductions and other income.

For an individual it applies the year’s resident scale, and for a company the year’s company rate. Paragraph 85 counts the larger of the tax on the firm income alone and the extra tax the firm income adds to the recipient’s other income. In example 4 of the guideline, an associate with $100,000 of firm income and $50,000 of other income pays $40,567 on both and would pay $6,717 without the firm income, so $33,850 counts, more than the $22,967 on the firm income alone.

Factor 1 is the IPP’s share of the total firm income, factor 2 the tax counted over that income, and factor 3, if you choose it, the IPP’s firm income against your benchmark. The scores and zone then follow Tables 1 and 2. The calculator reproduces the effective tax rate and scores of the guideline’s case studies 1 to 12 and example 4, and the tax in examples 5 and 6. For Bernie in case study 4 and Frank in case study 5 the resident scale gives $1 more tax than the guideline prints; the rates and scores are the same.

## What the PCG 2021/4 allocation calculator does not cover

The PCG 2021/4 allocation calculator does not tax a non-resident, a person under 18 on trust income (Division 6AA), a trustee taxed under section 98 or 99A, a superannuation fund or fringe benefits: it refuses them. Paragraphs 72, 73 and 95 to 99 count superannuation contributions and FBT in the effective tax rate but do not say how they count in factor 1, so work those out yourself and use the risk scorer. It applies no tax offset, such as the low income tax offset or a franking tax offset, because the guideline’s examples apply none; where your tax paid differs, use the risk scorer with your own figure.

It offers 2022-23 to 2026-27, the years since the guideline applied from 1 July 2022 (paragraph 17), and 2020-21 for the guideline’s examples. It does not test the gateways or decide whether the guideline applies (paragraph 28), and it takes each figure as you enter it, with no full-time equivalent for a part-time IPP (paragraph 71) and no commercial benchmark of its own. A green zone is not a ruling: Part IVA can still apply (paragraphs 36 and 37). Confirm the assessment with the guideline or a registered tax agent.

# GIC payment plan calculator

What a tax debt costs by equal instalments, against paying it now, with GIC compounding daily.

Calculate Fictional example: the first boundary case below. Change the inputs and calculate your own. Inputs: debt $1,000.00, first instalment 1 Oct 2026, 3 monthly instalments, 11.51% a year assumed after December 2026. Paid in full now $1,000.00 Each instalment but the last $336.56 Final instalment, 1 Dec 2026 $336.56 Total paid on the plan $1,009.68 GIC on the plan, over paying now $9.68

## How the GIC payment plan calculator works

The calculator compares paying a tax debt in full today with paying it by equal instalments. It works day by day from the first instalment to the last. Each day, the unpaid debt and any unpaid GIC grow by that day’s rate: the quarter’s annual GIC rate divided by 365, or 366 in a leap year, as sections 8AAC and 8AAD of the Taxation Administration Act 1953 set out. It finds the equal instalment that clears the debt and its GIC on the last instalment day, rounds it down to the cent, and lets the final instalment pay what is left. The GIC is the total paid on the plan less the debt.

In the example the page opens with, a $1,000 debt is paid in 3 monthly instalments from 1 October 2026, all at the October to December 2026 rate of 11.51%. Paying $336.56 on 1 October leaves $663.44, which grows by 31 days of GIC to $669.96 by 1 November. Paying $336.56 then leaves $333.40, which grows by 30 days to $336.56 on 1 December, the final instalment. The plan costs $1,009.68, so $9.68 of GIC over paying now.

## What the GIC payment plan calculator does not cover

The calculator does not work out the debt, its due date or any GIC that accrued before the plan starts; enter the debt as it stands on the first instalment day. It does not model a missed or late instalment, a plan the ATO varies, a GIC remission, a refund offset against the debt or the deductibility of GIC. Rates after December 2026 are your assumption until the ATO publishes them. The ATO sets the instalments of an actual plan, and its figures may differ by cents from these. Confirm the amount payable with the ATO or a registered tax agent.

Fictional example: the first boundary case below. Change the inputs and calculate your own. Inputs: GIC on $10,000.00 due 21 November 2025, to 30 June 2026. GIC to 30 June 2026 $676.86 Paid in the period $0.00 Owing at the end of that day, with GIC $10,676.86 Days of GIC 222 days Before remission: the Commissioner may remit GIC (TAA 1953 s 8AAG), SIC (TAA Sch 1 s 280-160) and administrative penalties (s 298-20), which this calculator does not estimate.

## How the ATO penalties and interest calculator works

The calculator works one question at a time, with the same rules, rounding and refusals as the ato-interest-penalties command in the australian-accounting calculators. GIC compounds daily from the due day on the unpaid amount and unpaid GIC, at each quarter’s annual rate divided by 365, or 366 in a leap year (sections 8AAC and 8AAD). A payment reduces the balance before that day’s charge. SIC compounds the same way on the additional tax, at the GIC rate less 4 points, from the day the first assessment’s tax was due to the day before the amended assessment’s notice (sections 280-100 and 280-105). Both are worked exactly and rounded to the cent once.

The failure to lodge penalty is 1 penalty unit for each 28 days or part of 28 days late, at most 5, each at the unit applying when its period starts: $330 to 30 June 2026 and $364 from 1 July 2026. It is doubled for a medium entity, times 5 for a large entity and times 500 for a significant global entity (section 286-80). The statement penalty is 75%, 50% or 25% of the shortfall for intentional disregard, recklessness or a failure to take reasonable care, or 60, 40 or 20 penalty units with no shortfall. A position not reasonably arguable gives 25% where its shortfall is more than the greater of $10,000 and 1% of the return’s income tax. The base amount is increased 20% where section 284-220 applies and reduced 80%, to nil or 20% for a voluntary disclosure (section 284-225).

The ATO pays simple interest at the base interest rate, the GIC rate less 7 points, on a payment of income tax, SIC, a compulsory study loan repayment or an FS assessment debt made more than 14 days early, to the end of the due day (sections 8A to 8C), and on relevant tax overpaid because of a decision and then refunded, from the later of the notice and the payment (sections 9 and 10). The interest rounds to the cent, and under 50 cents is not paid.

In the example the page opens with, $10,000 due on 21 November 2025 and unpaid to 30 June 2026 grows by 222 days of GIC at 10.61%, 10.65% and 10.96% to $10,676.86: $676.86 of GIC.

## What the ATO penalties and interest calculator does not cover

Every amount is before remission: the Commissioner can remit GIC, SIC and penalties, and the calculator does not estimate that. It does not work scheme penalties, the trust and partnership items of section 284-90, Division 296 GIC, a payment refunded before its due day or interest on a running balance account surplus. It refuses days without a published rate: GIC after 31 December 2026 unless you assume a rate, which makes the result an estimate, and SIC and credit interest after that day. The October to December 2026 base interest rate of 4.51% is the published GIC rate less 7 points; the ATO’s credit interest page lists quarters only to September 2026. The behaviour behind a shortfall, whether a position is reasonably arguable, whether a disclosure was voluntary and the entity’s size are your facts; the calculator does not decide them. Confirm the amount with the ATO or a registered tax agent.

# Division 296 tax calculator for 2026-27, above $3 million

Source: https://duguid.com.au/tools/business-calculators/division-296/

## How the Division 296 tax calculator works

The Division 296 tax calculator works out one person’s Division 296 tax for 2026-27, the first year it applies. Tax arises when the total superannuation balance at 30 June 2027 is greater than $3,000,000 and the year’s total superannuation earnings are greater than nil. The share of the balance above $3,000,000 times the earnings gives taxable superannuation earnings, taxed at 15%. Above $10,000,000, the share above that threshold times the earnings gives the very large superannuation balance earnings component, taxed at a further 10%.

The Explanatory Memorandum to the Treasury Laws Amendment (Building a Stronger and Fairer Super System) Bill 2026 works 2 examples. Jordan has $4,000,000 at the end of 2026-27 and $100,000 of earnings: 25% of the balance is above $3,000,000, so taxable superannuation earnings are $25,000 and the tax $3,750. Kelly has $12,000,000 and $500,000 of earnings: 75% and 16.67%, so $375,000 taxed at 15% ($56,250) and $83,350 at 10% ($8,335), $64,585 in all. This calculator opens on Jordan’s figures, and both are among its boundary cases.

## What the Division 296 tax calculator does not cover

The calculator works out one year from the balance and earnings you supply. It does not project a balance, compare a withdrawal or set tax inside super against tax outside it: those turn on future earnings, contributions and withdrawals that no source states, and choosing between them is financial advice. It covers 2026-27 only. From 2027-28 the thresholds are indexed (paragraphs 296-30(b) and 296-35(b)) and the balance just before the start of the year counts too, and those figures are not yet published.

It does not work out the total superannuation balance, a fund’s Division 296 fund earnings or how they are attributed to each interest (sections 296-55 to 296-75), or the earnings of defined benefit and other interests under section 296-70. Only tax attributable to a defined benefit interest can be deferred to a debt account. It does not cover temporary residents who depart Australia (sections 296-195 to 296-205), the notice of assessment, payment or release authorities. The ATO assesses the tax from what funds report, and the notice of assessment sets the amount. Confirm the figures with the ATO or a registered tax agent.

## How the Division 7A loan schedule calculator works

The Division 7A loan schedule calculator sets out a complying loan from a private company year by year, from the first income year after the year it was made to the end of its term. Each year it works the minimum yearly repayment under subsection 109E(6) at that year’s benchmark rate, the interest at that rate, how much of the repayment reduces the loan and the balance left at 30 June. Leave the repayments blank to pay the minimum each year; enter more in any year to see the later minimums fall and the loan end sooner.

In the last year the minimum is the balance and a full year’s interest. A repayment on 30 June carries that day on the reduced balance, so repaying the loan then needs a day’s interest less than the minimum; a blank entry repays the loan and no more, and a repayment that repays the loan is no shortfall.

If a year’s repayment is less than its minimum, subsection 109E(1) takes the company to pay a dividend of the shortfall at the end of that year, limited by section 109Y to its distributable surplus. The schedule stops at that year. The heading of subsection 109E(1) speaks of the first year in which a payment falls short, and the sources applied do not say how later years are worked.

The minimum for a single year matches the Division 7A minimum yearly repayment calculator. The ATO’s worked example on Loans by private companies takes $55,000 at 5.95% over 7 years for $9,835 and then $50,430 at 5.45% over 6 years for $10,079, to the nearest dollar; those years are before the published rates this page holds.

## What the Division 7A loan schedule calculator does not cover

The calculator does not decide whether a payment is a loan, whether the agreement is in writing before the lodgment day or charges at least the benchmark rate, or whether a mortgage meets the 110% test: it takes the term you choose. It works only a loan whose written term is the maximum, 7 or 25 years: subsection 109E(6) counts the remaining term from the loan’s own term, so a loan agreed for fewer years has higher minimums than this page shows. It refuses a loan made before 4 December 1997, which Division 7A reaches only once its term or amount is varied (subsection 109D(5)); a loan made before 1 July 2020, whose first year is before the ATO rates it holds; a loan made through an interposed entity (Subdivision E); a loan that refinances another or was extended under a mortgage, whose term subsections 109N(3A) to (3D) and 109E(3A) and (3B) reduce or restart; and a repayment made between 30 June and the lodgment day for the year the loan was made, which the ATO takes off the loan and also counts in the next year.

It assumes each repayment is made on 30 June and that the company’s income year ends on 30 June. A repayment made earlier in a year carries less interest. It does not apply section 109Q, which lets the Commissioner disregard a shortfall that would cause undue hardship, section 109R, which disregards a repayment funded by a new loan from the company, section 109Y’s limit or the regulations that subsection 109E(5) allows. It does not combine loans with different terms: each is a separate amalgamated loan with its own schedule.

The funding dividend is arithmetic on the marginal rate you give. It does not check that the company has the profits or franking credits to pay it, and it is not advice on whether to repay by dividend, salary or cash. Future benchmark rates are not known: the figures from 2027-28 rest on your assumption. Confirm the figures with the ATO Division 7A calculator and decision tool or a registered tax agent.

## How the CGT concessions checker works

The CGT concessions checker takes one capital gain from selling an asset used in a business and works through Division 152 in the order the Act sets. It first tests the basic conditions in subsection 152-10(1): at least one of a CGT small business entity, the maximum net asset value test or a passively held asset, and the active asset test. Each of the 4 concessions then has its own conditions, and the result says, for each, whether it is open and which provision decides it.

A CGT small business entity carries on a business, or is winding one up, and has an aggregated turnover under $2 million: for the previous year, as likely for the year of the sale at its first day or the day the business started (unless both of the 2 years before were $2 million or more), or for the year of the sale at its end. For a partnership asset, the partnership is tested, not the partner. The net asset value test counts the market value of the CGT assets of you, your affiliates and the entities connected with you, less the liabilities and provisions related to them; an individual leaves out personal use assets, the main residence (except the share subsection 152-20(2A) counts for its use to produce income), super and life insurance (section 152-20).

The active asset test counts the days from the purchase contract to the sale contract, or to an earlier end of the business when the sale came within 12 months of it, both days included. An asset owned 15 years or less must have been active for at least half of those days; one owned more than 15 years, for at least 7.5 years. Because 7.5 years is 2,736 to 2,746 days, depending on the leap days and months the periods span, a total from 2,736 to 2,745 is refused: count it in years and months.

The 15-year exemption needs 15 years of continuous ownership before the sale and an individual aged 55 or over who is retiring, or one permanently incapacitated; for a company or trust, the individual is its significant individual, and it must have had one for a total of 15 years. When it applies, the whole gain is disregarded and the other concessions are not needed. Otherwise the 50% reduction applies automatically, and the retirement exemption and roll-over can follow in either order.

## What the CGT concessions checker does not cover

The checker says which concessions are open, and gives no advice. It does not work out the capital gain or the amount each concession takes off it. It does not cover:

- sale contracts from 1 July 2027, when Schedule 1 to the Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Act 2026 changes Division 152, and before 1 July 2020;
- a share in a company or an interest in a trust, which must also meet the look-through conditions in subsection 152-10(2);
- a depreciating asset, whose gain is disregarded (section 118-24) or comes from CGT event K7, which section 152-10(1) excludes;
- CGT events other than a sale, including CGT events D1, J2, J5 and J6, and rights to partnership income or capital (subsection 152-10(2C));
- working out aggregated turnover, net value, affiliates, connected entities and small business participation percentages, which it takes from you;
- involuntary disposals and relationship breakdown roll-overs, which can extend the ownership and active periods (sections 152-45 and 152-115);
- public entities, which cannot choose the retirement exemption (subsection 152-305(3)), look-through earnout rights, and substituted accounting periods.

## How the PSI rules checker works

The PSI rules checker takes one individual’s personal services income for one income year and works through Part 2-42 in the order the Act sets. Each step on the result names the section it applies and what it found.

Income that is not mainly a reward for the individual’s personal efforts or skills is not PSI (subsection 84-5(1)), and income received as an employee or office holder falls outside Division 85 (subsection 85-35(1)). So does a payment to a religious practitioner by an entity carrying on an enterprise, for work in their religious vocation done as a member of a religious institution (subsection 85-35(2) and section 12-47 of Schedule 1 to the Taxation Administration Act 1953); check any other PSI they earn as a contractor. A personal services business determination in force settles the question (subsection 87-15(1)). Otherwise the results test comes first: if at least 75% of the PSI is paid for a result, with the plant and tools supplied and liability for defects, the PSI rules do not apply, however much comes from one payer (section 87-18).

If 80% or more of the PSI comes from one payer and its associates, the other 3 tests cannot be self-assessed and only a determination keeps the rules away (subsection 87-15(3)). The checker still works them out, because the Commissioner weighs them for a determination: 2 or more unrelated payers that engaged the individual or entity through offers to the public (section 87-20), principal work by others of at least 20% by market value or an apprentice for half the year (section 87-25), and qualifying business premises all year (section 87-30).

The checker reproduces the conclusion of each worked example in TR 2022/3 that reaches one on a test it applies, and of the matching examples on the ATO’s PSI pages.

## How to enter payers in the PSI rules checker

Enter each payer once, with its associates’ payments added in: the payer is whoever must pay under the contract, so a labour hire firm or agency is the payer, not its client (TR 2022/3 paragraphs 69 to 72). Payers that are associates of each other count as one payer too, as section 87-20 counts only payers that are not associates of each other: put them in one row, or choose the first of their rows under ‘Same payer as’ in each later one. Linked rows count as one payer in the unrelated clients test too, so 2 payers that are each an associate of a third, but not of each other, count once there; that can only make the test harder to pass. Count each Australian government agency as its own payer (section 87-35) and leave out income received as an employee. If the individual works through their own company, partnership or trust, choose that entity as who receives the income, even if it pays them a salary. Tick ‘Paid for a result’, ‘Supplies plant and tools’ and ‘Liable for defects’ only where the contract or industry custom makes it so (subsection 87-18(4)). The results test counts income, not payers, and a tick covers all of that row’s PSI: where only part of a payer’s PSI meets all 3, enter that part in a row of its own and choose the payer’s first row under ‘Same payer as’, so the 80% rule and section 87-20 still count one payer. For the market value of principal work by others, count work by any individual or entity engaged, an individual associate included, but not by an associate that is a company, partnership or trust, nor, for an entity, by an individual whose PSI it receives; a partner counts only if they earn no PSI through the partnership (subsections 87-25(1), (2) and (2A); TR 2022/3 paragraphs 110 to 116). With more than 5 payers, put the smallest together in one row only where every answer is the same; that can only make a test harder to pass.

## What the PSI rules checker leaves to you

The checker does not decide whether income is mainly a reward for personal efforts or skills, whether a contract pays for a result, whether an offer to the public won the work, who is an associate or what principal work is worth. These turn on facts and judgement, so it takes your answers and says so on each step; TR 2022/3 sets out the factors at paragraphs 34 to 49 and 77 to 148.

The checker does not allocate expenses across PSI, business income and other income. Division 85 limits deductions to the extent they relate to PSI (subsection 85-10(1)) but sets no method for the split, and TR 2022/3 leaves deductions to other rulings (paragraphs 6 and 31), so any split is practice rather than law. It does not work out the amount attributed under Division 86, PAYG withholding or a deduction for a net PSI loss.

The checker does not apply the agent rules when they could apply (section 87-40), decide a determination, which is the Commissioner’s (sections 87-60 and 87-65), or test Part IVA, which can still apply to a personal services business (TR 2022/3 paragraph 160). Several individuals working through one entity are tested one at a time (paragraph 76). Confirm the result with the ruling or a registered tax agent.

## How the casual and overtime pay calculator works

The calculator works one employee’s gross pay for one pay period from the rates you enter, then the super guarantee on the part that is ordinary time earnings. Ordinary hours are paid at the base hourly rate, plus the casual loading as a percentage of it for a casual. Each penalty or overtime line is its hours at the percentage of the base rate you enter, such as 150% for time and a half. Each hour is entered once, as an ordinary hour or on one line. Annual leave is paid at the base rate with any leave loading. Each amount is worked exactly and rounded to the cent once.

Ordinary time earnings are the pay for ordinary hours, the casual loading, penalty rates and shift loadings on ordinary hours, paid leave and a leave loading, unless the whole loading is paid for overtime the employee would have worked; a loading paid only partly for that is counted in full. Pay for overtime hours is not ordinary time earnings. For a payday from 1 July 2026, the super guarantee is 12% of qualifying earnings, which here are the ordinary time earnings in the pay; for a payday from 1 July 2025 to 30 June 2026, it is 12% of the ordinary time earnings under the quarterly rules. The calculator does not work out when the fund must receive the contribution: the SGC and Payday Super calculator does. The calculator refuses a pay whose ordinary time earnings alone exceed the maximum contribution base.

## What the casual and overtime pay calculator does not cover

The calculator applies no award, enterprise agreement or minimum rate, and does not check that the rates you enter meet one: the Fair Work Ombudsman’s pay guides and Pay and Conditions Tool give award rates. It does not decide which hours are ordinary hours or overtime, whether a casual loading compounds with a penalty rate, or how an award rounds its rates; enter those as your award or agreement states them. It does not check whether the employee or the earnings are excluded from the super guarantee. It leaves out allowances, commission, bonuses, salary sacrifice, other qualifying earnings, PAYG withholding, payroll tax and workers compensation, and it does not track the maximum contribution base across a quarter or year: it assumes earlier pays have not reached it. Paydays before 1 July 2025 or after 30 June 2027 are refused. The calculator follows the ATO’s view of ordinary time earnings. In Department of Education v Commissioner of Taxation [2026] FCA 898 the Federal Court held that a salary loading allowance paid on top of the salary for ordinary hours was not ordinary time earnings; the Commissioner has appealed, will not finalise the draft qualifying earnings ruling until the appeal ends, and meanwhile decides by the existing view. The outcome may change how loadings are treated. Results are planning estimates: check them against the award or agreement and the ATO’s guidance.

## How the staff cost calculator works

What counts is the value of what the contract is for, not how an invoice splits it.

## How the contractor against employee calculator works

The calculator takes one person doing the same work for the same hours for a full income year, as an employee and as a contractor. The employee is paid the salary, which includes paid leave. The leave loading is the stated rate on the annual leave pay, a 52nd of the salary for each week of leave. The super guarantee is the year’s rate on the salary and, when it is ordinary time earnings, the loading, up to the year’s maximum contributions base, which before 2026-27 applied each quarter: the page assumes even quarters. Payroll tax and the workers compensation premium are the rates you state on the salary and loading, with the super guarantee when you say it counts.

The contractor is paid the hourly rate for the hours the employee would work: the hours a week times the 52 weeks of the year less the annual and other paid leave. The business pays GST on top when the contractor is registered, and its cost includes that GST only when it cannot claim it back. Under section 12(3) of the Superannuation Guarantee (Administration) Act 1992, a person who works under a contract that is wholly or principally for their labour is an employee of the other party for the super guarantee, even with an ABN. TR 2023/4 says the contract must be with the person as an individual, give no right to delegate, subcontract or assign the work, not be for a result and be mainly for labour. When all 4 hold on your answers, the business owes the super guarantee on the labour part of the fee, which section 10A(1)(d) makes qualifying earnings. Payroll tax and workers compensation apply to the labour part only when you say the state’s law reaches the contractor, a simplification: each scheme can value the amount differently.

The take-home figures are for an Australian resident with no other income, using this site’s income tax engines. The employee’s salary and loading take income tax, the Medicare levy and any surcharge or study loan repayment, after the $1,000 standard deduction from 2026-27. The contractor’s fee less business expenses and their own deductible super is taxed the same way as a sole trader’s profit, with the small business income tax offset when you say it applies. Each amount is worked exactly and rounded to the cent once.

## Employee or contractor: what decides it

The calculator does not decide whether the person is an employee: it works both answers from your facts. Whether a person is an employee in the ordinary meaning depends on the whole relationship between the parties. Section 15AA of the Fair Work Act 2009 and the ATO’s TR 2023/4 set out the tests, and the ATO’s Employee or independent contractor pages include its decision tool. A contractor who is an employee in the ordinary meaning is owed the super guarantee on all of their ordinary time earnings, whatever section 12(3) says. Payroll tax and workers compensation each have their own tests in each state and territory. For income tax, see the personal services income checker: the PSI rules can deny a contractor deductions and the small business income tax offset.

## What the contractor against employee calculator does not cover

The calculator does not decide whether the person is an employee, whether section 12(3) applies when labour is the largest part of the fee without being more than half, or whether a contractor is in payroll tax or workers compensation: you answer those. It holds no award or agreement rates: the leave, loading, payroll tax rate and workers compensation rate are what you enter. It does not work payroll tax thresholds, grouping or deductions (see the payroll tax calculator), workers compensation by industry (see the workers compensation calculator), overtime, penalty rates, allowances, long service leave, notice or redundancy pay, or leave paid out when employment ends. It leaves out the PSI rules, Division 293 tax, excess concessional contributions, salary sacrifice, contributions tax in the fund, PAYG withholding and instalments, other income, part years, non-residents, contracts through a company or trust, labour hire and domestic or private work of 30 hours a week or less (section 12(11)). It leaves out public holidays worked, unpaid leave, when super is due, GST turnover from the contractor’s other work and each state’s rules for valuing a contractor’s wages or remuneration. A year is taken as 52 weeks. Results are planning estimates: check them against the contract, your records and the ATO’s guidance.

## How the 13-week cash forecast works

The 13-week cash forecast works out closing cash for each week and the funding gap against a buffer you set. Weekly closing cash = opening cash + receipts − payments. Each closing balance opens the next week. Funding gap = minimum buffer − lowest opening or weekly closing cash, with a floor of zero.

No statutory rate or threshold is applied. The layout follows business.gov.au: cash flow.

## What the 13-week cash forecast does not decide

The funding gap is a planning gap, not a lending decision. The 13-week cash forecast does not predict receipts or payments, and weekly totals can hide a shortage within the week. A receipt delayed beyond week 13 is reported separately and does not enter the closing balance.

The Lumbridge cash flow case works the same question with a 45-day receipt delay.

Source: https://duguid.com.au/tools/business-calculators/objection-deadline/

# Objection deadline checker

The last day to object to an income tax or FBT assessment, an amended assessment or another ATO decision, with the weekend rule.

Published 15 November 2026. Last checked 15 November 2026.

JavaScript is required for interactive calculations. The formula, assumptions and source links remain available below.

Objection deadline inputs

Decision objected to Income tax assessment Amended income tax assessment FBT assessment Amended FBT assessment Another decision for which section 14ZW sets no other period Income tax only: does item 1, 2, 3 or 3A of the table in subsection 170(1) of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 apply to the assessment? Yes: 2 years No: 4 years Day notice of the decision was given or served Amended assessments only: day notice of the first assessment for the year was given or served

Item 1 covers most individuals, and items 2 and 3 companies and trusts that are small or medium business entities; each excludes, for example, a scheme to obtain a tax benefit. Item 3A covers their requests to amend. Which item applies is not decided here.

Calculate Fictional example: the first boundary case below. Change the inputs and calculate your own. Inputs: income tax assessment, item 1, 2, 3 or 3A applies (2 years), notice given 18 November 2026. Period ends, subparagraph 14ZW(1)(aa)(i) Saturday 18 November 2028 Last day to lodge, under subsection 36(2) of the Acts Interpretation Act 1901 Monday 20 November 2028 If that day is a public holiday where the objection is lodged, or the office is closed all day, it may be lodged on the next day that is not a Saturday, Sunday or holiday. After the last day, an objection needs a written request under subsection 14ZW(2), which the Commissioner decides under section 14ZX.

## How the objection deadline checker works

The objection deadline checker gives the last day to lodge a taxation objection under section 14ZW of the Taxation Administration Act 1953. An income tax assessment allows 2 years after notice of the assessment is given when item 1, 2, 3 or 3A of the table in subsection 170(1) of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 applies, and 4 years otherwise. An FBT assessment allows 4 years. Any other decision for which the section sets no other period allows 60 days after notice is served.

An amended assessment allows whichever ends later: 60 days after notice of the amended assessment, or the 2 or 4 years after notice of the first assessment for that year. The checker shows both dates and the later one.

Each period starts the day after notice, because subsection 36(1) of the Acts Interpretation Act 1901 leaves out the day a period begins after. A 2-year period from notice given on 28 February 2026 therefore starts on 1 March 2026 and ends on 29 February 2028. When the last day is a Saturday or Sunday, subsection 36(2) lets the objection be lodged on the next day that is not a weekend or holiday. The Act’s own example: a person who has until Saturday 31 March may apply on Monday 2 April.

## What the objection deadline checker does not cover

The checker does not decide whether a decision can be objected to, which item of subsection 170(1) applies, or when notice was given, so keep the notice’s issue and receipt dates. It does not know public holidays: they differ by state and town, so check the last day and the day after it where you lodge. It does not cover private rulings, administrative penalties, retained refunds, deceased estates, specialised taxes or the other decisions for which section 14ZW sets its own period, or the time to seek review of an objection decision. Confirm the date with the notice of decision or a registered tax agent.

# PAYG instalments calculator

One quarter’s PAYG instalment by the instalment amount or the instalment rate, as notified or varied, with any credit to claim.

Published 15 November 2026. Last checked 15 November 2026.

JavaScript is required for interactive calculations. The formula, assumptions and source links remain available below.

PAYG instalment inputs for one quarter

How this instalment is worked out Option 1: pay the instalment amount at T7 Option 1, varied: an amount from your estimated tax for the year Option 2: instalment income times the rate at T2 Option 2, varied: a rate from your estimates for the year Option 1: instalment amount at T7 (AUD) Option 2: instalment income for the quarter at T1 (AUD) Option 2, not varied: instalment rate at T2 (%) Varied amount only: which of this income year’s instalments is this? Each option reads only its own fields. For a varied amount, earlier credits are those you were entitled to claim for earlier quarters, claimed or not; for a varied rate, those you claimed. Calculate Fictional example: the first boundary case below. Change the inputs and calculate your own. Inputs: instalment rate (option 2), instalment income $20,100.00 at T1, instalment rate 1.7% at T2. T1 × T2 $341.70 Instalment at T11 and 5A, whole dollars $341.00

## How the PAYG instalments calculator works

The PAYG instalments calculator works out one quarterly pay as you go instalment by the method on the activity statement. Under option 1 the instalment is the amount the ATO notifies at T7. Varying it, the first instalment of the income year is 25% of the estimated tax for the year, the second 50%, the third 75% and the fourth 100%, each less the earlier instalments. The third and fourth add back any credits you were entitled to claim for earlier instalments, claimed or not; no credit can arise before the second, so the calculator refuses one entered for the first or second. A negative result is a credit to claim at 5B.

Under option 2 the instalment is the quarter’s instalment income at T1 times the instalment rate at T2. A varied rate is the estimated tax for the year divided by the estimated instalment income, times 100. If the varied rate is lower than the rate used for the previous quarter, the earlier instalments less any credits claimed, less the earlier instalment income times the varied rate, is a credit for 5B. That comparison is with last quarter’s rate, not a new rate the ATO gives at T2. No step is rounded: only the instalment and the credit drop their cents, so 25% of an estimate of $399.99 is $99.9975, an instalment of $99.

For 2026-27, the instalment amount the ATO notifies already includes its GDP adjustment of 5%, which raises the base year’s income to allow for growth; the adjustment does not change an instalment rate. The ATO’s own example: instalment income of $20,100 at a rate of 1.7% gives $341.70, entered as 341 at T11 and 5A.

## What the PAYG instalments calculator does not cover

The calculator does not work out instalment income, the tax on it or whether you can choose between the 2 options. It does not cover monthly instalments, the 2 instalments a year some payers make, annual instalments or consolidated groups, and it does not estimate general interest charge on a variation that proves too low. It does not check whether you may claim a credit or when an instalment is due. Confirm the figures with the ATO’s PAYG instalments calculator or a registered tax agent.

Calculate

## What the inputs need

The most tax is what the lump sum can bear in the person’s return, before the Medicare levy. The amount withheld is what the fund takes out when it pays, under Schedule 12 of the withholding schedules; it is a credit against that tax. A departing Australia superannuation payment, to a former temporary resident who has left Australia, bears its own final tax.

For one lump sum from a complying fund paid on a condition of release: not an income stream commutation or a payment in breach of the payment rules. A roll-over and a payment to the trustee of a deceased estate are worked only for withholding. The fund states the interest’s value and tax free component just before the payment, and the untaxed element.

The lump sum’s tax free component is its share of the interest’s, rounded to the cent; the rest is taxable, taxed in the fund except the untaxed element. Leave that at 0 for a fund that pays tax on its income, as most do.

Needed only with an untaxed element. An untaxed element from service before 1 July 1983 is refused: part of it then becomes tax free under section 307-150.

You decide whether the person is a death benefits dependant: a spouse or former spouse, a child under 18, someone interdependent with or dependent on the member, or anyone if the member died in the line of duty (section 302-195).

Two registered medical practitioners, one a specialist, certify death is likely within 24 months. A disability superannuation benefit is refused: section 307-145 enlarges its tax free component.

The low rate cap applies only at preservation age and under 60, which from 1 July 2024 no one is. Enter the amounts counted for earlier lump sums. Other lump sums at that age in the same year share the cap, so they are refused while any is left.

### What the withholding and DASP inputs need

Withholding is worked for payments from 13 October 2020. With a TFN, a resident’s rate for each part is its ceiling rate plus the 2% Medicare levy, and the total rounds to the nearest dollar. Without one, the fund withholds 47% (45% for a foreign resident) of the taxable component, or of the untaxed element at 60 or over, ignoring cents. Without a TFN the rate turns on the payee’s age, which the calculator does not take for a death benefit, and none is stated for a member benefit under $200, so a non-dependant’s death benefit and such a member benefit are refused. The calculator assumes the payment is taxable in Australia and applies no tax treaty.

Take the components from the fund’s or the ATO’s statement. The working holiday maker rate applies when the payment includes amounts from contributions made whilst the person was a working holiday maker. An unclaimed money roll-over with an untaxed element is refused: section 5(2) taxes any excess untaxed roll-over amount in it at nil.

## How the super lump sum tax calculator works

The super lump sum tax calculator splits one lump sum from a complying fund, paid from 1 July 2020 to 30 June 2027, into its components. It gives the most income tax each part can bear before the Medicare levy. A member’s treatment turns on age on the payment day and preservation age; a death benefit’s turns on whether the person receiving it is a death benefits dependant. Each rate is a ceiling: the offsets stop the tax on a part going above it, so a person on lower marginal rates pays less, and the Medicare levy is added on top.

It also works the amount the fund withholds from the same lump sum under Schedule 12, for a payment from 13 October 2020, including from a roll-over and a death benefit paid to a deceased estate, and the final tax on a departing Australia superannuation payment in 2025-26 to 2027-28.

Its results match the super-benefit-tax command of Ryan Duguid’s australian-accounting calculators on the ATO’s examples and 532 test cases, and its super-withholding and dasp-tax commands on 613 more, refusals included.

## What the super lump sum tax calculator does not cover

The calculator does not work the tax at the person’s own marginal rates, the Medicare levy, income streams and their withholding (Schedule 13), the tax on a roll-over or a deceased estate, a tax treaty, or payments from a non-complying or foreign fund. It does not decide dependency, a terminal medical condition, the components or the elements: you state those. It refuses a disability superannuation benefit, an untaxed element from service before 1 July 1983, and other lump sums in the same year that share the low rate cap.

Confirm the result with the fund, the ATO’s guidance on super lump sums or a registered tax agent before relying on it. The redundancy and ETP withholding calculator covers employment termination payments.

# Redundancy and ETP withholding calculator for 2026-27

Source: https://duguid.com.au/tools/business-calculators/termination-payment/

> The tax-free part of a genuine redundancy payment, the ETP and whole-of-income caps, and the PAYG to withhold from an ETP under Schedule 11, for 2026-27.

# Redundancy and ETP withholding

The tax-free part of a genuine redundancy payment and the amount to withhold from an ETP under Schedule 11, for 2026-27.

Published 15 November 2026. Last checked 15 November 2026.

JavaScript is required for interactive calculations. The formula, assumptions and source links remain available below.

Inputs for one life benefit ETP paid in 2026-27

Genuine redundancy or early retirement scheme payment, before its tax-free part (AUD) Completed years of service Other code R taxable component: invalidity, or compensation for personal injury, unfair dismissal, harassment or discrimination (AUD) Code O taxable component: golden handshake, gratuity, non-genuine redundancy, severance pay, payment in lieu of notice, unused sick leave or unused rostered days off (AUD) Other taxable payments you made to the employee in 2026-27, excluding the ETP (AUD) Employee’s date of birth

For an employee who has given you their TFN. Unused annual leave, leave loading and long service leave are not ETPs and are withheld under Schedule 7, but count them in other taxable payments, as Schedule 11’s example 3 counts $50,000 of leave entitlements paid as a lump sum.

Calculate Fictional example: the first boundary case below. Change the inputs and calculate your own. Inputs: genuine redundancy or early retirement scheme payment $48,000.00 after 5 completed years of service, other code R taxable component $0.00, code O taxable component $17,678.00, other taxable payments in 2026-27 $140,000.00, born 1 Aug 1996. Tax-free limit $47,603.00 Tax-free part of the redundancy payment $47,603.00 Code R taxable component $397.00 Withhold from the code R part $127.00 Whole-of-income cap left $40,000.00 Cap for the code O part $40,000.00 Withhold from the code O part $5,657.00 Total to withhold $5,784.00 Under preservation age on 30 June 2027: 32% within each cap and 47% above it.

This is the payer’s withholding under Schedule 11, a payroll and practitioner task; it does not estimate the employee’s take-home pay or the tax assessed on their return.

## How the redundancy and ETP withholding calculator works

The redundancy and ETP withholding calculator works out how much a payer withholds from one life benefit employment termination payment (ETP) made in 2026-27. A genuine redundancy or early retirement scheme payment is tax-free up to $13,598 plus $6,801 for each completed year of service. The part above that limit is a code R ETP, as are payments for invalidity and compensation for personal injury, unfair dismissal, harassment or discrimination. The code R part is withheld at the rate within the cap up to the $270,000 ETP cap and at 47% above it.

The rest of the ETP is code O: a golden handshake, gratuity, non-genuine redundancy payment, severance pay, payment in lieu of notice, unused sick leave or unused rostered days off. Its cap is the smaller of the ETP cap left after the code R part and the whole-of-income cap, which is $180,000 less the other taxable payments you made to the employee in the year. The rate within the cap is 17% if the employee is their preservation age or older on 30 June 2027, otherwise 32%; 47% applies above the cap.

Schedule 11’s example 4 takes Alec, 30, made redundant after 5 years of service with a $48,000 genuine redundancy payment and a $17,678 gratuity, having been paid $140,000 of salary and wages in the year. It works out a $397 ETP over the $47,603 tax-free limit, withholds $127 from it and $5,657 from the gratuity within the $40,000 whole-of-income cap. This calculator opens on those figures, with a date of birth that makes Alec 30, and gives the same amounts.

## What the redundancy and ETP withholding calculator does not cover

The calculator does not decide whether a termination is a genuine redundancy, whether a payment is an ETP or which code applies. It takes the taxable component as you enter it and does not work out a tax-free component other than the redundancy limit, such as an invalidity segment. It covers one life benefit ETP for one termination: not death benefit ETPs, delayed termination payments, a later instalment for the same termination, an earlier ETP in the same year, an employee who has not given you their TFN, a foreign resident or a working holiday maker. It does not work out withholding on unused leave, which Schedule 7 covers. Confirm the figures with Schedule 11 or a registered tax agent.

# Land tax calculator

Land tax for a year in each Australian state and territory that levies it, at the general or trust rates with any foreign owner surcharge, from each revenue office’s current rates.

Published 16 November 2026. Last checked 16 November 2026.

JavaScript is required for interactive calculations. The formula, assumptions and source links remain available below.

Land tax inputs

State or territory New South Wales Victoria Queensland Western Australia South Australia Tasmania Australian Capital Territory

Total taxable land value (whole dollars) Rates General rates Trust rates (in Queensland, companies and trustees) Foreign person or absentee owner? No Yes Surcharge value, New South Wales and Tasmania only (whole dollars) All the land is in the Perth metropolitan region (Western Australia)

Enter the value the revenue office taxes, after exempt land is left out: in New South Wales the 3-year average of the land values, in Victoria and South Australia the total site value, in the Australian Capital Territory one parcel’s average unimproved value, and elsewhere the total land value of all the owner’s taxable land. The Northern Territory has no land tax.

Trust rates are a special trust’s in New South Wales, the trust surcharge rates in Victoria, those for companies and trustees in Queensland and those for land held on trust in South Australia. The calculator has none for Western Australia, Tasmania or the Australian Capital Territory.

The surcharge value is the land value the New South Wales or Tasmanian surcharge applies to, as set out below the calculator; elsewhere a surcharge applies to the taxable land value. The calculator has no foreign or absentee rates for Western Australia or South Australia.

Calculate Fictional example: the first boundary case below. Change the inputs and calculate your own. Inputs: New South Wales, total taxable land value $1,100,000.00. Land tax for the year $500.00 Rate applied $100 plus 1.6% of the value over $1,075,000

## How the land tax calculator works

The calculator applies one state or territory’s general or trust scale to a total taxable land value for a full year. Below the threshold tax is nil; the Australian Capital Territory and New South Wales special trusts have no threshold. Above it, each scale charges a base amount plus a percentage over the band threshold, except Victoria’s flat $500 from $50,000 and $975 from $100,000 up to $300,000. South Australia rounds each excess up to the next $100 and makes land tax under $20 nil (Land Tax Act 1936 (SA) s 6). Tasmania rounds to 10 cents, rounding up only if over 5 cents remain (Land Tax Rating Act 2000 (Tas) s 7). The Australian Capital Territory adds its $1,778 fixed charge to the valuation charge for the full-year amount. Scales are current on 16 November 2026: the 2026 calendar year in New South Wales and Victoria, and the 2026-27 financial year in Queensland, Western Australia, South Australia, Tasmania and the Australian Capital Territory.

Worked figures match published revenue-office examples. Revenue NSW gives $500 on $1,100,000, $9,600 for a special trust on $600,000, and $2,100 land tax plus $60,000 surcharge on $1,200,000. Victoria’s State Revenue Office gives $5,550 on $1,100,000, and $44,650 on $1,000,000 at general absentee rates. Queensland Revenue Office gives $1,300 on $680,000 and $87,000 on $6,400,000 for an individual, $106,500 on $6,400,000 for a company, $8,420 on $760,000 for a self-managed super fund trustee, and on $400,000 for an absentee or foreign company the statutory surcharge over $349,999 is $1,500.03 ($3,800.03 total). RevenueSA gives $2,670 on $1,470,000, and Tasmania’s surcharge guideline gives $8,000 on $400,000. Hand-worked checks cover the rest: $6,250 on $1,500,000 in Western Australia with $1,680 metropolitan region improvement tax, $2,500 at South Australia’s trust rates on $500,000, $3,237.50 on $600,000 in Tasmania and $7,418 on an average unimproved value of $600,000 in the Australian Capital Territory with $4,500 foreign ownership surcharge.

## Trust rates, surcharges and the metropolitan region improvement tax

Trust rates are a special trust’s rates in New South Wales, with no threshold; the trust surcharge rates in Victoria; the rates for companies and trustees, including super funds, in Queensland; and the trust rates in South Australia. Western Australia taxes a trustee’s land as if it were the trustee’s own, at the general rates.

A foreign or absentee owner pays: in New South Wales surcharge land tax of 5% of the land value of the residential land a foreign person owns, their share only and including land exempt from land tax, entered as the surcharge value; in Victoria the absentee owner surcharge of 4% of the total taxable value from $50,000 at the general rates (a Victorian absentee trust is refused because section 46IA of the Land Tax Act 2005 (Vic) apportions the surcharge by its absentee beneficiaries’ interests); in Queensland the absentee rates for an absentee individual, and for an absentee, a foreign company or the trustee of a foreign trust a surcharge of 3% of the value over $349,999 (Schedules 2 and 3 of the Land Tax Act 2010 (Qld)); in Tasmania the foreign investor land tax surcharge of 2% of the assessed land value of the foreign-owned share of residential General Land acquired on or after 1 July 2022, entered as the surcharge value (a surcharge value above the taxable land value, or a case where rounding land tax and surcharge to 10 cents separately differs from rounding their sum, is refused); and in the Australian Capital Territory the foreign ownership surcharge of 0.75% of the parcel’s average unimproved value.

Western Australia charges its metropolitan region improvement tax of 0.14% of the value over $300,000 with land tax where the land is in the Perth metropolitan region; the calculator adds it when all the land is. A surcharge and this tax are shown apart from the land tax, with the total.

## What the land tax calculator does not compute

The land tax calculator applies the scale for the rates and owner you choose. It does not decide which land is taxable, which rates apply, whether an owner is a foreign person or absentee, or what the taxable or surcharge value is; the foreign purchaser surcharge calculator applies each jurisdiction’s test of a foreign or absentee owner. These are not computed:

- New South Wales land tax exemptions and concessions, including the principal place of residence and primary production land exemptions, exemptions from surcharge land tax, and land of a company that is not its group’s concessional company, which pays 1.6% of its whole taxable value with no threshold, or 2% of it where the group’s land exceeds the premium threshold (Land Tax Act 1956, Schedule 13, Parts 3 and 4).
- Victoria land tax exemptions and concessions, exemptions from the absentee owner surcharge and vacant residential land tax.
- Queensland: exemptions and relief, exemptions from the foreign surcharge and the aggregation of land held for trusts with the same beneficiaries.
- Western Australia land tax exemptions, and the metropolitan region improvement tax on holdings only partly in the Perth metropolitan region.
- South Australia: exemptions, waiver or relief, and which land held on trust qualifies for the general rates.
- Tasmania: zero rate classifications, exemptions and rebates, including principal residence and primary production land, and which land the foreign investor land tax surcharge applies to.
- Australian Capital Territory land tax exemptions, when the foreign ownership surcharge applies, a unit’s share by its unit entitlement and the split into quarters. Land tax there applies to residential property that is not a principal place of residence.

Joint ownership, grouping of related companies and the apportionment of the tax between properties are not computed either. Confirm the figure with the revenue office’s own calculator or assessment notice before relying on it.

# Transfer duty calculator

Calculate Fictional example: the first boundary case below. Change the inputs and calculate your own. Inputs: New South Wales, dutiable value $1,350,000.00. General transfer duty $55,537.00 Rate applied $52,237 plus $5.50 for every $100, or part of $100, over $1,290,000

## How the transfer duty calculator works

The transfer duty calculator applies one state or territory’s general rates to a dutiable value. Most scales charge a base amount plus a rate for every $100, or part of $100, over a threshold, so the excess is rounded up to the next $100. Victoria takes a percentage of the excess without rounding it, and 5.5% of the whole value from $960,000 to $2 million. The Australian Capital Territory takes $4.54 per $100 of the whole value above $1,455,000. The Northern Territory uses a formula up to $525,000 and a single percentage of the whole value above it.

Where a revenue office publishes worked figures, the calculator gives the same amount. Revenue NSW’s worked examples give $55,537 on $1,350,000, $14,437 on $450,000 and $203,237 on $4,000,000; its Transfer of Land or Business Calculator gave $14,441.50 on $450,050 when tried on 15 November 2026. The Victorian State Revenue Office gives $28,070 at the standard rate on $550,000 and $19,070 on $400,000. The Queensland Revenue Office gives $31,275 on $850,000. RevenueSA’s foreign ownership surcharge example gives stamp duty of $26,830 on $600,000. The Tasmanian duty calculator gave $18,247.50 on $500,000 on 15 November 2026. For Western Australia, the Australian Capital Territory and the Northern Territory the tests work examples by hand from the published rates: $32,315.50 on $800,000 in Western Australia, $17,880 on $650,000 in the Australian Capital Territory and $23,928.60 on $500,000 in the Northern Territory.

## Duty for a first home buyer

For an eligible first home buyer, the calculator applies the state or territory’s first home buyer concession on a home, new or established, bought to live in. Each scheme’s conditions, such as citizenship or residency, never having owned a home, age and moving in within a set time, are in the sources listed and are not tested.

- New South Wales: no duty up to $800,000. Below $1 million, the duty on $800,000, scaled down evenly to nil at $1 million, comes off the general duty, with the $20 minimum.
- Victoria: no duty up to $600,000. Up to $750,000, the general duty multiplied by the value over $600,000 and divided by $150,000.
- Queensland: the home concession rate less the first home concession amount for the value’s $10,000 band, from $17,350 below $710,000 down to nil from $800,000, so no duty up to $700,000. No duty on a new home, whatever its value.
- Western Australia: no duty up to $600,000. Up to $800,000, $16.15 for every $100, or part of $100, over $600,000.
- South Australia: no duty on a new home, whatever its value. An established home pays the general rate.
- Australian Capital Territory: no duty under the Home Buyer Concession Scheme, whatever the value. The scheme is open to buyers who have not owned property in the past 5 years, not only first home buyers.
- Tasmania and the Northern Territory: no first home buyer duty concession on a home, so the general rate applies. Tasmania’s exemption for established homes ended with settlements on 30 June 2026.

The NSW Government’s 2026-27 table gives $9,796.75 on $850,000, $19,593.50 on $900,000, $29,390.25 on $950,000 and $37,227.65 on $990,000. Revenue NSW’s First Home Buyers Assistance calculator gave $38,991.06 on $999,000 and $20 on $800,001 when tried on 16 November 2026. The Queensland Revenue Office gives $6,555 on $730,000 and $24,100 on $850,000 for an established first home. For Victoria and Western Australia the tests work examples by hand: $24,713.33 on $700,000 in Victoria and $16,150 on $700,000 in Western Australia.

First home owner grants are payments to the buyer, not duty concessions; the first home owner grant calculator works them out beside this duty. The sources: New South Wales, Victoria, Queensland, Western Australia, South Australia, Tasmania, the Northern Territory’s HomeGrown Territory Grant, and the Australian Capital Territory’s First Home Owner Grant, which stopped on 1 July 2019.

## What the transfer duty calculator does not compute

The transfer duty calculator gives general transfer duty, and duty for an eligible first home buyer of a home. It applies no other concession, exemption or surcharge, does not test whether a buyer is eligible, and does not decide whether a transaction is dutiable or what its dutiable value is; the foreign purchaser surcharge calculator works out the foreign purchaser duty surcharge. These are not computed:

- New South Wales: duty on land other than residential land over $3,870,000, which the premium rate does not reach (the calculator applies it and says so in its result), the First Home Buyers Assistance Scheme on vacant land, surcharge purchaser duty for foreign persons, including foreign trusts and companies, and landholder duty.
- Victoria: the principal place of residence concession, the first home buyer concession on vacant land, the off-the-plan concession, the City of Melbourne new residential property concession and exemption, the pensioner exemption and concession, and foreign purchaser additional duty.
- Queensland: the home concession for a buyer who is not a first home buyer, the first home vacant land concession, and additional foreign acquirer duty, which also reaches companies and trusts.
- Western Australia: the concessional rate for a principal place of residence or WA business asset up to $200,000, the first home owner rate on vacant land, the off-the-plan concession or rebate, and foreign transfer duty.
- South Australia: stamp duty relief for eligible first home buyers on vacant land, seniors downsizing stamp duty relief, home buyer ex gratia relief for victim-survivors of family, domestic or sexual violence, and the foreign ownership surcharge.
- Tasmania: concessions and exemptions, and the foreign investor duty surcharge.
- Australian Capital Territory: the lower rate for an eligible owner occupier transaction (Table 1 of the determination), the Home Buyer Concession Scheme on vacant land, and the rates for commercial property.
- Northern Territory: the house and land package exemption and the home incentive schemes in Part 5 of the Act.

Duty on a trust acquisition, a landholder or corporate trustee acquisition, a lease premium or a business sale, and the land tax that follows a purchase, are not computed either. Confirm the figure with the revenue office’s own calculator or a conveyancer before relying on it.

> First home owner grants across all 8 states and territories from 1 July 2025: amount, value cap by contract date, eligibility facts and first home buyer duty.

# First home owner grant calculator

The first home owner grant in each Australian state and territory for a new home bought or built, by contract date and value cap, beside the transfer duty for an eligible first home buyer.

Published 22 November 2026. Last checked 23 November 2026.

JavaScript is required for interactive calculations. The formula, assumptions and source links remain available below.

Bought: price (Victoria: off-the-plan contract price), which tests any value cap and limits the grant where lower (NSW refuses it). Built: land plus building contract tests any value cap (Victoria caps the building contract alone); land is excluded from the lower-consideration rule, so where the building contract price is below the grant, the grant is limited to that price (NSW refuses it).

Inputs: New South Wales, contract 1 August 2026, new home bought, total value $600,000.00, every eligibility fact stated. First home owner grant $10,000.00 Value cap up to $600,000 Residence requirement you stated each applicant lives in the home for 12 continuous months, starting within 12 months Transfer duty for an eligible first home buyer $0.00 General transfer duty on the same value $21,187.00

## How the first home owner grant calculator works

The first home owner grant calculator gives the grant for a first home buyer who buys or builds a new home under a contract made from 1 July 2025 to 22 November 2026, beside the transfer duty the same buyer pays. It applies the contract-date grant and cap, paying nothing above the cap or for established homes except in the Northern Territory before 1 October 2025.

- New South Wales: $10,000; cap $600,000 for a home bought, $750,000 for land and building contract.
- Victoria: $10,000, or consideration if less, up to $750,000. For a home built the cap tests the building contract alone, so totals over $750,000 need that price entered.
- Queensland: $30,000, or the consideration if less, for a home worth under $750,000. The cap tests the greater of the price and the unencumbered value of the home and land, or for a home built the contract and the land’s value; enter that value where it differs.
- Western Australia: $10,000, or consideration if less. Cap is $800,000 south of the 26th parallel from 7 May 2026 ($750,000 before) and $1,000,000 north; enter any different cap value.
- South Australia: $15,000, or the consideration if less, with no value cap.
- Tasmania: $30,000 for contracts from 1 July 2025 to 30 June 2026, then $20,000 to 30 June 2027, or the consideration if less, with no value cap. The transaction must be completed within 24 months, or a period the Commissioner extends, and not replace a transaction for the same property, between or benefiting substantially the same parties, entered before 1 July 2025 for a 2025-26 contract or 1 July 2026 for a 2026-27 contract.
- Northern Territory: HomeGrown Territory Grant $50,000, or consideration if less, no cap. Established homes bought 1 July to 30 September 2025 get $10,000, or consideration if less. Must not replace a pre-1 October 2024 contract.
- Australian Capital Territory: $0 since 1 July 2019; the duty result applies the Home Buyer Concession Scheme.

## Eligibility facts and transfer duty

Each grant needs 4 facts, which you state and the calculator does not test. Every applicant is a person aged 18 or over. At least one applicant is an Australian citizen or permanent resident. No applicant or spouse is excluded by the prior ownership rules below. The applicants meet the residence requirement: 12 continuous months starting within 12 months in New South Wales; 12 months for at least one applicant in Victoria; 6 continuous months starting within 12 months in Queensland, Western Australia, South Australia and Tasmania; and 12 months after taking possession or completion in the Northern Territory. Without the building contract price entered, a home built also needs you to state that the price, excluding land, is at least the grant; with it entered, Queensland, Victoria, Western Australia, South Australia, Tasmania and the Northern Territory pay a lower contract price instead. A Northern Territory contract must not replace one signed before 1 October 2024. A Tasmanian transaction must be completed within 24 months, or a period the Commissioner extends, and not replace a transaction for the same property, between or benefiting substantially the same parties, entered before the 1 July starting its grant period. The calculator computes nothing until the facts a transaction needs are stated, and in Western Australia until you choose where the home is.

For a home bought, the result adds the transfer duty calculator’s duty for an eligible first home buyer and its general duty on the same value, for contracts its rates cover: from 1 July 2025 in Victoria, Queensland, South Australia and the Northern Territory, from 7 May 2026 in Western Australia, and from 1 July 2026 in New South Wales, Tasmania and the Australian Capital Territory. Earlier contracts there get the grant without the duty.

## Prior ownership rules

The sources read state these rules. New South Wales: no applicant or spouse owned a home or other residential property in Australia before 1 July 2000. Victoria: none owned one before 1 July 2000, or lived for a continuous 6 months or more in a home they owned on or after 1 July 2000. Western Australia: none owned residential property on or after 1 July 2000 and lived in it for a continuous 6 months or more beginning on or after 1 July 2004. Tasmania: none owned a residential property before 1 July 2000, or owned and lived in one for more than 6 months after 1 July 2000. For Queensland, South Australia and the Northern Territory the sources read do not set the rule out, so state the fact against the revenue office’s own eligibility rules.

## What the first home owner grant calculator does not compute

The calculator refuses a contract dated before 1 July 2025 or after 22 November 2026, and a value or building contract price below the grant amount in New South Wales, where the source read did not confirm the rule. Without the building contract price, it refuses a Victorian home built whose land and building total is over $750,000, since Victoria caps the building contract alone, and a home built unless you state that the building contract price is at least the grant. With the price entered, a contract below the grant gets the contract price, as each Act read pays the lesser of the consideration and the grant. It does not cover owner-builders, substantially renovated homes, the ADF and family violence exemptions, the Commissioner’s discretion over the residence requirement, or schemes that are not first home owner grants, such as regional building grants, shared equity schemes and Commonwealth deposit schemes. For a home built, the duty falls on the land, and the first home buyer concessions on vacant land are not computed. Confirm the grant with the revenue office or an approved agent before relying on it.

## How the concessional catch-up calculator works

The concessional catch-up calculator works out each earlier year’s unused concessional contributions cap, the shortfall of that year’s contributions below its general cap, from 2018-19. Where an earlier year’s contributions went over its cap and the balance just before it was under $500,000, it applies the unused cap of the 5 years before that one, earliest first, as subsections 291-20(4) and (5) required for that year. What is left of the previous 5 years’ unused cap is carried into the year you choose.

With a total super balance under $500,000 on 30 June before the year, the cap available is the general cap plus that carried amount. The calculator shows how much of it this year’s contributions use, any excess, and what is left of each year’s amount with the year after which it lapses. A proposed contribution is added to the contributions so far, so you can see how far it goes before it becomes excess.

The ATO’s concessional contributions cap page works Sam’s example: unused cap of $14,000, $13,000, $14,500, $13,500 and $12,500 from 2019-20 to 2023-24 gives $67,500, so his 2024-25 cap is $97,500, and contributions of $97,500 use it all with no excess. The calculator opens on his figures; the ATO says only that his balance was below $500,000, so the $450,000 is fictional.

## What the concessional catch-up calculator does not cover

The calculator works the cap only. It does not decide what counts as a concessional contribution, in which year a contribution counts, or whether a deduction notice is valid, and it does not work out the tax on excess contributions or Division 293 tax. It does not cover a defined benefit interest, or non-concessional contributions and their bring-forward. It covers 2024-25, 2025-26 and 2026-27.

Your carry-forward amounts are on ATO online services (Super, then Information, then Carry forward concessional contributions), which use the contributions your funds have reported. Confirm the figures there or with a registered tax agent before you contribute.

## How the income tax calculator works

The income tax calculator works out one individual’s tax for a full income year from 2020-21 to 2026-27: the tax on taxable income at the year’s rates, the offsets, the Medicare levy and the Medicare levy surcharge. The offsets are the low income tax offset and, for 2020-21 and 2021-22, the low and middle income tax offset. It then takes that total, and any study or training loan repayment, from the tax withheld you enter, to estimate a refund or an amount owing.

It can also work out the beneficiary tax offset, the invalid and invalid carer tax offset, the zone or overseas forces tax offset, the foreign income tax offset and the private health insurance rebate. The first 4 come off the tax but not below nil. The rebate is worked from your private health insurance statement: what you were entitled to at your tier, less the premium reduction you received, comes off the total and can make it negative; a premium reduction above your entitlement is added to the total.

An Australian resident pays nothing on the first $18,200 and then each part of taxable income at its rate. The low income tax offset of up to $700 comes off a resident’s tax, but not below nil. The Medicare levy is 2% of a resident’s taxable income; up to the low-income threshold there is none, and from there to the phase-in limit it is 10% of the income over the threshold, if that is less. The ATO’s example on Medicare levy reduction for low-income earners, read 17 November 2026, gives Angie, single with $29,000 of taxable income in 2025-26, a levy of $98.90, as this calculator does.

The Medicare levy surcharge applies to a resident without private patient hospital cover whose income for surcharge purposes is above the year’s threshold. For each day without cover it charges 1%, 1.25% or 1.5% of taxable income and reportable fringe benefits, by the tier the income falls in.

For 2026-27 the Medicare levy thresholds are those the Act held on 17 November 2026, the same as 2025-26. If Parliament raises them for 2026-27, a person just above $28,011 will pay less than shown here.

## What the income tax calculator does not compute

The calculator gives the tax of one person who was a resident, a foreign resident or a working holiday maker for the whole year. It does not compute:

- the Medicare levy reduction for families, which depends on family taxable income and dependants, or a Medicare levy exemption;
- the seniors and pensioners tax offset and its higher Medicare levy thresholds, the net medical expenses tax offset, worked out below for 2016-17 to 2018-19, or any other offset, such as for super contributions;
- for the rebate, a lifetime health cover loading, a policy for dependants only, a claim of a spouse’s share, or dependent children for a person with no spouse who maintained no dependant; for the invalid carer offset, shared maintenance, Family Tax Benefit Part B shared care or successive spouses; for the zone offset, shared maintenance or more than one area;
- a change of family or cover status during the year beyond the days without cover, a spouse’s trust income that the surcharge test adds, the net amount on which family trust distribution tax has been paid, which counts in income for surcharge purposes and in the amount the surcharge is levied on, or exempt foreign employment income, which the ATO’s surcharge page adds to income for surcharge purposes when taxable income is $1 or more;
- a first home super saver released amount, which is taxed with a 30% offset but left out of repayment income and income for surcharge purposes, or, for 2023-24 and earlier, the taxed element of a super lump sum up to the low rate cap, which a person from preservation age to under 60 could leave out of income for surcharge purposes;
- a study loan debt smaller than the repayment: the repayment cannot exceed what is still owed (section 154-20(1)(c) of the Higher Education Support Act 2003), which the calculator does not ask for;
- a part-year resident’s reduced tax-free threshold, a working holiday maker who is an Australian resident, or one with other income besides working holiday taxable income;
- tax on superannuation or employment termination remainders, income averaging, or a minor’s unearned income, worked out below for 2024-25 to 2026-27;
- Division 293 tax, excess contributions, PAYG instalments or other credits besides the tax withheld you enter.

Confirm the figures with the ATO’s Simple tax calculator or a registered tax agent.
