## How the take-home pay calculator works

The take-home pay calculator takes one salary for a year, month, fortnight or week and works out the year’s income tax, offsets, Medicare levy, any Medicare levy surcharge and any study or training loan repayment on it. Salary sacrificed to super comes off first. From 2026-27 it also takes off the standard deduction of up to $1,000 for work-related expenses. It then gives what is left for the year, a month, a fortnight and a week, and an estimate of employer super guarantee. Supply dated earnings to calculate super using the applicable quarters or paydays. Employer super goes to a fund and is separate from take-home pay.

Those take-home amounts are the year’s tax spread evenly: the year’s net amount divided by 12, 26 and 52. They are not the amounts an employer withholds each pay. For a weekly, fortnightly or monthly pay, the calculator also works the PAYG amount withheld from one pay under the year’s Schedule 1, and Schedule 8 with a study loan, and the year’s withholding less the year’s tax, which is the refund or amount owing when the tax return is assessed. Withholding does not allow for the low and middle income tax offset, so in 2021-22 the offset comes back as part of the refund: $3,000 a fortnight has $670 withheld each pay and $1,543 back. For working holiday makers, who are withheld from under another schedule, use the ATO’s tax withheld calculator.

The example on arrival is 2025-26, before the standard deduction: on $75,000 the Medicare levy is $1,500, as the ATO’s example of Matthew on What is the Medicare levy gives. In 2026-27 the same salary is $74,000 of taxable income.

When the salary includes super, the calculator splits it: at 12%, a package of $112,000 is $100,000 of salary and $12,000 of super. For the package estimate, the annual earnings limit caps the estimate of employer super.

## What the take-home pay calculator does not compute

The tax and PAYG estimates assume one employer, a salary paid evenly over the full year and no other income, deductions or offsets. Dated super can use irregular payments that add up to the year’s gross salary.

- separate tax or withholding treatment for overtime, bonuses, allowances or leave loading. PAYG estimates use 52 weekly or 26 fortnightly pays and omit withholding under scales 1, 5 and 6, withholding for working holiday makers, offsets claimed in a withholding declaration and Medicare levy variations;
- 2025-26 withholding with a study loan that mixes the 2 Schedule 8s: the year’s withholding and refund take the one from 24 September 2025 for every pay, and the component before that date is shown beside it;
- work-related deductions you claim, which reduce the standard deduction dollar for dollar except those section 25-130(3) disregards, such as professional association fees;
- salary sacrifice of anything but super, reportable fringe benefits, excess concessional contributions or Division 293 tax;
- everything the income tax calculator leaves out, such as the Medicare levy reduction for families and the seniors and pensioners tax offset;
- a family’s surcharge: this calculator works out the surcharge for a single person with no dependants, and the income tax calculator works out a family’s;
- a study loan debt smaller than the repayment, which section 154-20(1)(c) of the Higher Education Support Act 2003 caps at what is still owed;
- whether an employee is entitled to super guarantee, the lower transitional rate for employees on Norfolk Island (11% for 2026-27), or a second employer’s separate maximum contribution base;
- actual PAYG withholding from the optional dated earnings. Those entries calculate super only. Without dates, super is estimated on the year’s earnings and rounded once. For example, $260,000 from 26 fortnightly $10,000 pays beginning 8 July 2025 gives $29,400 using the quarterly caps, compared with the $30,000 annual estimate.

Confirm the figures with the ATO’s Simple tax calculator or a registered tax agent.

## How the lump sum in arrears calculator works

Salary, wages or a Centrelink or compensation payment that you receive as a lump sum, for earlier years, is taxed in the year you receive it, often at a higher rate than it would have been in the years it was for. The tax offset gives back the difference. The calculator first tests whether the arrears are at least 10% of the rest of your normal taxable income for the year. If they are, it works out the tax the arrears add this year and the tax they would have added in the years they accrued in, and the offset is the amount by which the first exceeds the second.

For the 2 latest accrual years it adds the arrears to that year’s taxable income at that year’s resident rates. Arrears from any earlier years are taxed at the average of those 2 years’ rates, so the oldest years’ arrears can share one row. Where a recent year was itself a year you got this offset for, or arrears of such a year accrued in it, its income is adjusted as the Act directs.

The ATO’s page on lump sum payments in arrears works Yan’s breakdown of arrears by year, received in 2025-26. The calculator opens on it; the ATO does not give Yan’s taxable incomes, so the $100,000, $30,000 and $17,000 are fictional. Anthony’s, Sudeep’s and Heather’s examples are among the boundary cases.

## What the lump sum in arrears calculator does not cover

The calculator works the offset for a person resident in Australia for the whole of the year of receipt and of each recent accrual year, entitled to the full tax-free threshold, for a year of receipt of 2024-25, 2025-26 or 2026-27. It does not decide what is a lump sum in arrears: it takes the arrears you enter as eligible income that accrued more than 12 months before you received it. It refuses an employment termination payment, unused leave paid on termination, a super lump sum or income stream, above-average special professional income or primary producer averaging in the year of receipt or a recent accrual year, and does not cover a minor’s income or a trustee.

It does not work out the Medicare levy or surcharge on the arrears, which have their own rules, or apply the offset against your tax. The ATO works the offset when you lodge with the amounts for each year; confirm the figures with the ATO or a registered tax agent.

## How the study and training loan repayment calculator works

The study and training loan repayment calculator works out the compulsory repayment on a HELP, VET Student Loan, Student Start-up Loan or Australian Apprenticeship Support Loan debt for one income year. It first adds up repayment income: taxable income, reportable fringe benefits, total net investment loss, reportable super contributions and exempt foreign employment income.

From 2025-26 the repayment is marginal: nothing up to the minimum repayment income, then 15 cents for each dollar above it up to a second threshold and 17 cents above that, unless 10% of all repayment income is less. For 2026-27 the minimum repayment income is $69,528 and the second threshold $129,717, and 10% is the lesser amount from $186,051. For 2024-25 one percentage of the whole repayment income applied, from 1% above $54,434 to 10% from $159,664.

The boundary cases below take the inputs of the 4 worked examples on the ATO’s thresholds and rates page, read 17 November 2026, and work each one from section 154-20. For Barry’s 2026-27 repayment income of $137,064, section 154-20(2) gives 15% of the $60,189 from $69,528 to $129,717, which is $9,028.35, plus 17% of the $7,347 above $129,717, which is $1,248.99: $10,277.34 in all. For Branson’s 2024-25 repayment income of $99,736, the 5.5% rate gives $5,485.48.

## What the study and training loan repayment calculator does not compute

The calculator gives the compulsory repayment for one income year. It does not compute:

- the cap at the debt you still owe, or voluntary repayments;
- the overseas debtors repayment levy on worldwide income for a foreign resident (section 154-16);
- whether no repayment is due because your Medicare levy is not payable or is reduced under section 8 of the Medicare Levy Act 1986 (section 154-1(2));
- the amounts an employer withholds each pay for a loan, which the take-home pay calculator works for 2026-27, or indexation of the debt;
- years before 2020-21.

Confirm the figure with the ATO’s Study and training loan repayment calculator or a registered tax agent.

Business profit $20,000.00 Standard deduction on the wages $1,000.00 Taxable income $79,000 Tax on taxable income $14,220.00 Low income tax offset $0.00 Small business income tax offset $576.00 Medicare levy $1,580.00 Total tax, levies and repayment $15,224.00 Less the same on the wages alone $9,285.00 Tax to set aside for the business $5,939.00 Total to set aside for the year $5,939.00 Each quarter $1,484.75 Each month $494.92 Each week $114.21 Share of each invoice to set aside 27.00% From an invoice of $1,000.00, set aside $269.95 As a PAYG instalment rate, 27.00% of business income excluding GST covers this year’s tax on it. A return like this meets 2 of the 3 PAYG instalment entry tests; the ATO works out the third, notional tax, and decides entry. This assumes the wages’ withholding covers the tax, levy and any study loan repayment on the wages alone.

## How the sole trader tax set-aside calculator works

The calculator takes a year’s business income and expenses, any wages from a job and any tax agent fees, gifts or personal super contributions you claim. It works out the year’s income tax, the offsets, the Medicare levy, any Medicare levy surcharge and any study or training loan repayment. It then works the same on the wages alone. The difference is the tax the business adds, which nobody withholds, so it is the amount to set aside from business income.

The small business income tax offset is worked as section 328-360 sets it: 16% of the share of the tax on taxable income that the business profit makes up. On arrival the example shows it below its $1,000 cap: $20,000 of profit is 20/79 of $79,000 of taxable income, so the offset is 16% of 20/79 of $14,220, which is $576.00. The business also costs the low income tax offset the wages alone would have had, $115.00, which the difference picks up.

A business registered for GST also sets aside the GST on its income less its GST credits, paid with each activity statement. The calculator gives one share to keep from every invoice, covering both, and the year’s amount split by quarter, month and week. It also gives the tax as a share of the business income excluding GST, which as a PAYG instalment rate would cover this year’s tax on it.

## What the sole trader tax set-aside calculator does not compute

The calculator is for an Australian resident aged 18 or over with one business as a sole trader, a full year of income and no dependants. It does not compute:

- a business loss or losses carried forward; whether Division 35 defers a loss is worked out below;
- personal services income rules, which can deny deductions: see the PSI rules checker;
- GST-free or input-taxed sales, GST on a cash or accruals basis by period, or a GST refund when credits exceed the GST on income;
- other income such as interest, dividends, rent or capital gains, or partnership and trust distributions, which change both the tax and the offset’s share, or reportable fringe benefits and salary sacrificed to super from the job, which count in repayment income and income for surcharge purposes;
- work-related deductions against the wages, which reduce the standard deduction from 2026-27, or a job withheld from at the wrong rate;
- super guarantee, which a sole trader does not pay for themselves, or personal super contributions beyond entering them as a deduction;
- a family’s Medicare levy, levy reduction or surcharge, or the seniors and pensioners tax offset;
- notional tax or the instalment rate the ATO sets, or when each instalment and activity statement is due;
- a study loan debt smaller than the repayment, which section 154-20(1)(c) of the Higher Education Support Act 2003 caps at what is still owed;
- 2027-28, whose working Australians tax offset (Subdivision 61-E, added by Act No. 49 of 2026) applies from that year.

Confirm the figures with the ATO’s calculators and tools or a registered tax agent.

## How the Division 293 tax calculator works

The Division 293 tax calculator works out the extra 15% tax on concessional super contributions for one income year when income and contributions together exceed $250,000. It adds up Division 293 income, the income measure used for the Medicare levy surcharge without reportable super contributions, then takes the contributions less any excess over the year’s cap, raised by unused cap carried forward when your total super balance allows it. Those are the low tax contributions. The taxable contributions are the lesser of the low tax contributions and the amount by which they and Division 293 income exceed $250,000, so only the part above the threshold is taxed, and never more than the contributions. Each step is shown, with the room left under the threshold when you are below it.

Excess concessional contributions are not taxed by Division 293: they are added to your assessable income and taxed at your marginal rate less a 15% offset instead. A one-off event, such as a capital gain, an employment termination payment or back pay, can take you over the threshold for a single year. The ATO assesses Division 293 tax on its own notice once it has your return and your fund’s contribution reports. It is payable 21 days after the notice, and you can elect within 60 days to have it released from super.

## What the Division 293 tax calculator does not compute

The calculator covers 2021-22 to 2026-27, for contributions to accumulation interests. It does not compute:

- defined benefit interests, whose defined benefit contributions the regulations work out and whose tax is deferred to a debt account (Subdivision 293-D), or the rules for State higher level office holders with constitutionally protected funds and for Commonwealth justices and judges (Subdivisions 293-E and 293-F);
- contributions the Commissioner has disregarded or reallocated to another year, which stay in low tax contributions, or which contributions count: enter them as your fund reports them;
- contributions that count differently for Division 293 than for the cap: a super guarantee amnesty amount the Commissioner paid to your fund, which is not a low tax contribution (section 293-30(4)(c)), and a contribution refunded under section 99G(6) of the Superannuation Industry (Supervision) Act 1993, which is not a concessional contribution (section 291-25(2)(e));
- each part of Division 293 income, the unused cap or your total super balance, which you enter;
- 2027-28 and later years, whose cap is not yet known, or years before 2021-22;
- the refund for a former temporary resident who receives a departing Australia superannuation payment, interest, or the release from super itself.

Confirm the figures with your Division 293 notice from the ATO or a registered tax agent.

## How the income tests calculator works

The income tests calculator adds up the 6 income measures that the income tests section of an individual tax return feeds, from the same amounts. Each measure starts from taxable income without any assessable first home super saver released amount, then adds the parts its own definition names.

- Income for surcharge purposes, for the Medicare levy surcharge and the private health insurance rebate, adds family trust distribution amounts, fringe benefits, reportable super contributions and investment losses.
- Division 293 income, for the extra 15% tax when it and low tax contributions together exceed $250,000, is the same less reportable super contributions.
- Rebate income, for the seniors and pensioners tax offset, adds super contributions, investment losses and the adjusted fringe benefits total.
- Repayment income, for study and training loans, adds investment losses, fringe benefits, exempt foreign employment income and super contributions.
- Adjusted taxable income, for the dependant (invalid and invalid carer) tax offset, adds adjusted fringe benefits, target foreign income, investment losses, tax-free pensions and super contributions, less child support paid.
- Co-contribution total income starts from assessable income instead, adds fringe benefits and employer contributions and takes off business deductions.

The ATO’s page When you must repay your loan, last updated 13 October 2026 and read 19 November 2026, works Christina’s repayment income: taxable income of $50,420, a $1,250 net investment loss, $4,560 of reportable fringe benefits, $2,580 of exempt foreign employment income and $15,000 of reportable super contributions give $73,810. The calculator opens on her figures, with her loss taken as a financial investment loss, the benefits from an employer that pays FBT, the contributions from her employer, her target foreign income as the exempt income alone and assessable income equal to taxable income; those splits are fictional. Tom’s income for surcharge purposes of $117,000, from the ATO’s surcharge page, is among the boundary cases.

## What the income tests calculator does not cover

The calculator works the measures only. It does not decide whether an offset, the surcharge, a study loan repayment, Division 293 tax or a co-contribution applies, or work out their amounts; the income tax calculator works the surcharge and a study loan repayment. It covers a person resident in Australia for the whole of 2024-25, 2025-26 or 2026-27: a foreign resident pays no Medicare levy or surcharge and repays a study loan on worldwide income, and a part-year resident’s measures were not checked.

It does not add a spouse’s income, work out family tax benefit or child care subsidy income, which also count a partner’s, or the Commonwealth Seniors Health Card income test, which Services Australia applies. It takes each amount as you enter it: it does not decide what is a reportable fringe benefit, target foreign income or a tax-free pension, or work out excess concessional contributions. Confirm the figures with the ATO’s income tests calculator or a registered tax agent.

## How the super projection calculator works

The super projection calculator projects one accumulation super account from 2026-27 to the age you retire, a year at a time, and gives the balance then in future dollars and at its present value, in the dollars of today’s wages. Each year your employer contributes its rate of your salary, up to the maximum contribution base, and your own contributions are added. The fund takes 15% contributions tax from the employer and salary sacrifice contributions, takes out the dollar fee, the percentage fee and the premiums, and claims them as a deduction, which saves 15% of them. The return and the percentage fee are worked on the balance at the start of the year and on half the year’s contributions less the dollar fee and premiums, as they come in through the year. After the first year, your salary, contributions, fees and premiums grow at the wage growth rate.

The present value divides the balance at retirement once by 1 plus the present value rate (3.7% unless you change it) to the power of the years projected, rounded to the cent, so that it reads against today’s wages. The calculator is general information about super, not advice: it shows the effect of the figures you enter and does not recommend a fund, an investment option or a contribution.

## The assumptions and why they are reasonable

- Retirement at 67: the default ASIC’s Instrument 2022/603 sets for anyone younger. Super is preserved until 60, so an earlier age is projected to 60, as the Instrument takes the greater of the age you enter and your preservation age.
- Today’s dollars at 3.7% a year: the rate the Instrument sets, the long-term growth in wages the Treasury’s 2023 Intergenerational Report expects, so the result compares with what wages buy now.
- Wage growth of 3.7% a year for your salary, contributions, fees and premiums: the same long-term forecast, as ASIC’s guide expects contributions to rise with wages.
- A return of 6.1% a year after investment fees and tax on earnings, steady every year: ASIC’s assumption for a balanced investment option. Real returns vary and can be negative in some years; your fund’s option may have a different mix.
- Administration fees of $59 a year and 0.11% of the balance, and insurance premiums of $599 a year: ASIC’s assumptions from industry statistics. Your statement shows your own.
- Employer contributions at the 12% super guarantee on salary up to the $270,830 maximum contribution base for 2026-27, which is assumed to grow with wages.
- 15% contributions tax and the fund’s deduction for fees and premiums, as the law now stands; tax and super law are assumed not to change.
- Contributions within the 2026-27 caps, with the caps assumed to rise with wages after that.

## What the super projection calculator does not compute

The projection covers one accumulation account from 2026-27, with the rules of that year assumed to continue. It does not compute:

- defined benefit interests, or an account already paying a pension or a transition to retirement income stream;
- income in retirement, the age pension or how long the balance would last;
- the low income super tax offset, the government co-contribution or spouse contributions, which would add to the balance of someone on a lower income;
- Division 293 tax for income over $250,000, excess contributions, the nil non-concessional cap for a total super balance at the transfer balance cap, or tax on a withdrawal;
- years of good and bad returns, career breaks, or contribution, activity, switching and adviser fees, any of which can lower the balance.

Use your fund’s own retirement estimate or a financial adviser for a forecast you would act on.

## How the government super amounts calculator works

The calculator works 3 amounts from the same answers. Total income for the co-contribution is your assessable income, less any FHSS released amount, plus reportable fringe benefits and reportable employer super contributions (less any excess concessional contributions), less business deductions. Adjusted taxable income, which decides LISTO, is taxable income without any FHSS released amount, plus adjusted fringe benefits, target foreign income, investment losses, tax-free pensions and reportable super contributions, less child support paid, as the income tests calculator works it.

The super co-contribution is half your personal contributions, at most $500. Above the year’s lower income threshold the $500 falls by 3.333 cents for each dollar; at the higher threshold, $15,000 above it, none is payable. An amount under $20 is raised to $20. It needs total income below the higher threshold, at least 10% of total income before business deductions from employment or a business, a lodged return, non-concessional contributions within your cap, a total super balance below the general transfer balance cap, and an age under 71.

The year’s thresholds are $39,837 and $54,837 for 2020-21, $41,112 and $56,112 for 2021-22, $42,016 and $57,016 for 2022-23, $43,445 and $58,445 for 2023-24, $45,400 and $60,400 for 2024-25, $47,488 and $62,488 for 2025-26, and $49,293 and $64,293 for 2026-27.

LISTO is 15% of your concessional contributions, to the nearest cent, at most $500 and at least $10, where adjusted taxable income is $37,000 or less and the same 10% test is met. The ATO pays both amounts to your fund, rounded up to a multiple of 5 cents.

The spouse contribution tax offset is 18% of your contributions for your spouse, counting at most $3,000, which falls by a dollar for each dollar of the spouse’s income above $37,000. It is nil when the spouse’s income is $40,000 or more, the spouse’s non-concessional contributions exceed the spouse’s cap, or the spouse’s total super balance has reached the general transfer balance cap. The most it can be is $540.

## What the government super amounts calculator does not cover

The calculator refuses a person who held a temporary visa at any time in the year: the exceptions for New Zealand citizens and some prescribed visas are not worked out. It also refuses a person not resident in Australia for the whole year, a cap or balance answer of not known where that answer decides an amount, and nil total income where a contribution leaves the 10% test to decide.

It leaves out contributions your fund had not received by 30 June, LISTO the ATO estimates without a return, concessional contributions to constitutionally protected funds and other amounts LISTO disregards, a deceased person’s income, interest on late payments, and 2019-20 and earlier. It does not cover 2027-28, when the law changes LISTO and the co-contribution thresholds are not yet published. It takes each amount and answer as you enter them; confirm them with your fund, the ATO or a registered tax agent.

## How the transfer balance calculator works

Your transfer balance account starts when you first become the recipient of a retirement phase income stream, on 1 July 2017 at the earliest. A new income stream credits its value on the day it starts, and a repayment under a limited recourse borrowing arrangement entered into from 1 July 2017 credits the increase in value (IT(TP)A s 294-55). A commutation, a fraud or bankruptcy loss, a family law payment split or an income stream leaving the retirement phase debits the account. A negative balance has no effect.

Your personal cap is the general cap for the year the account starts: $1.6 million to 2020-21, $1.7 million for 2021-22 and 2022-23, $1.9 million for 2023-24 and 2024-25, $2 million for 2025-26 and $2.1 million for 2026-27. When the general cap rises, your cap rises by the unused percentage of the increase: 100% less your highest balance at the end of a day, as a whole percentage of your cap then, rounded down. Once your balance has exceeded your cap at the end of a day, your cap is no longer indexed.

At the end of each day the balance is above your cap, the excess earns that day’s general interest charge rate, credited to the account the next day, so it compounds. Excess transfer balance tax is 15% of the earnings for each run of days in excess, or 30% for a later run starting on or after 1 July 2018 once you have been liable for one. An income stream held on 30 June 2017 above $1.6 million but at most $1.7 million, reduced by the excess by 31 December 2017, gave no excess in those 6 months.

The excess concessional contributions charge applied to the extra income tax from an excess for 2013-14 to 2020-21, compounding daily from 1 July of the year to the day before the tax was due, at the base interest rate plus 3 points. Releasing excess non-concessional contributions adds associated earnings: the excess compounded daily from 1 July of the contributions year to the ATO’s first determination at the proxy rate, the year’s average base interest rate plus 7 points, rounded down to the dollar. The release is the excess and 85% of the earnings; the earnings are assessable income with a 15% tax offset.

## What the transfer balance calculator does not cover

The calculator refuses reversionary income streams, a child recipient’s cap, capped defined benefit income streams, structured settlement contributions, credits and debits under regulations, and the ATO’s determinations, commutation authorities and notices. It takes no determination, so it credits every day’s earnings; the ATO’s own figures stop at its determination and can differ by cents. It works days to 31 December 2026, the last GIC rate the ATO has published, and no day from 1 July 2027.

The charge ended for 2021-22 and later years; the release needs every base rate of the contributions year, so 2026-27 is not yet worked. A partial release, ENCC tax on amounts not released and the interest on unpaid amounts are not covered. Confirm the result with your fund, the ATO or a registered tax agent before relying on it.

## How the pension minimum calculator works

The minimum annual payment from an account-based pension is the account balance on 1 July times the percentage factor for your age on that day. The factor is 4% under 65, 5% from 65 to 74, 6% from 75 to 79, 7% from 80 to 84, 9% from 85 to 89, 11% from 90 to 94 and 14% at 95 or more. It is rounded to the nearest $10, and an amount ending in exactly $5 rounds up.

In the year a pension starts, the balance and age are taken on the start day, and the minimum is the same percentage of the balance times the days from the start day to 30 June over the days in the year, 366 when the year includes 29 February. A pension starting on or after 1 June, in the year’s last 30 days, needs no payment that year.

## What the pension minimum calculator does not cover

The calculator works 2024-25 to 2027-28 with the factors from 2023-24; it does not apply the halved factors of 2019-20 to 2022-23. It does not cover market-linked or other non-account-based pensions, transition to retirement maximums, the year a member dies, or payments that fall short. It takes the balance, age and start day as you enter them; confirm them with your fund, the ATO or a registered tax agent.

# 183-day residency day count

Count your days in Australia in an income year from 2020-21 to 2026-27 and check them against the 183-day test for tax residency.

Published 26 November 2026. Last checked 26 November 2026.

JavaScript is required for interactive calculations. The formula, assumptions and source links remain available below.

Your days in Australia in one income year

Income year, 1 July to 30 June 2026-27 2025-26 2024-25 2023-24 2022-23 2021-22 2020-21

Periods in Australia

Period 1 arrival day Period 1 departure day Period 2 arrival day Period 2 departure day Period 3 arrival day Period 3 departure day Period 4 arrival day Period 4 departure day Period 5 arrival day Period 5 departure day Period 6 arrival day Period 6 departure day

Enter up to 6 stays in Australia, each from the day you arrived to the day you left; both days count. Leave the arrival blank if you were already here on 1 July, the departure blank if you were still here on 30 June, and both blank to skip a row. Overlapping periods count each day once, and days outside the income year are not counted.

Is your usual place of abode outside Australia? No Yes

Do you intend to take up residence in Australia? No Yes

However many days you count, the test is not met if both are true: your usual place of abode is outside Australia and you do not intend to take up residence here. The Act leaves both to the Commissioner’s satisfaction; your answers stand in for it, and the calculator does not test them.

Calculate

Fictional example: the first boundary case below. Change the inputs and calculate your own. Inputs: 2025-26 (1 July 2025 to 30 June 2026); 2 periods in Australia; usual place of abode outside Australia: no; intends to take up residence: no. Days in Australia in the income year 229 of 365 More than one-half of the year 183 days or more Usual place of abode outside Australia and no intention to take up residence No, as you answered 183-day test Met Enough days, and the exception does not apply on your answers.

## How the 183-day residency day count works

The calculator adds up the distinct days you were in Australia between 1 July and 30 June, counting the day you arrived and the day you left as whole days. Paragraph (a)(ii) of the definition of ‘resident or resident of Australia’ in s 6(1) of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 includes a person ‘who has actually been in Australia, continuously or intermittently, during more than one-half of the year of income, unless the Commissioner is satisfied that the person’s usual place of abode is outside Australia and that the person does not intend to take up residence in Australia’. More than one-half is 183 days, or 184 in a year that includes 29 February.

The exception needs the Commissioner to be satisfied of both facts: your usual place of abode is outside Australia, and you do not intend to take up residence in Australia. The calculator takes your answers in place of that satisfaction: if you answer yes and no, it shows the test as not met however many days you spent here. TR 2023/1 says a person on an extended holiday is the usual case.

## What the 183-day residency day count does not cover

The calculator does not decide whether you are an Australian resident. The 183-day test is one of 4. You are also a resident if you reside in Australia according to ordinary concepts, if your domicile is in Australia and your permanent place of abode is not outside Australia, or if you are a PSS member or a CSS eligible employee, or the spouse or child under 16 of one (the Commonwealth superannuation fund test). Those tests turn on facts and judgements this page does not ask for; read TR 2023/1 for each. Nor does it test your usual place of abode or intention, apply a tax treaty’s tie-breaker rules for a person resident in 2 countries, or work out part-year residency or the tax that follows. Confirm your residency with the ATO or a registered tax agent.

## Use your ATO determination

In ATO online services through myGov, go to Super, then Manage, then First home saver. Follow the ATO’s steps to check your contributions and request a determination. Enter the 3 amounts from the determination. Enter the release request date for the correct income year. For a completed release, enter the gross actually released and confirm the withholding and any debt offset against your ATO records.

## Estimate the maximum from contributions

The calculator counts up to $15,000 of eligible contributions a year and $50,000 in total ($30,000 for determinations requested before 1 July 2022). It counts contributions earliest first, using non-concessional contributions first in a year that contains both kinds of personal contribution. It treats contributions on the same day as made at the same time and counts the non-concessional ones first. It adds 100% of the non-concessional part and 85% of the concessional part. It compounds daily at the ATO’s published shortfall interest charge rates, from the first day of the contribution month (1 July 2017 for 2017-18 contributions) through the determination date. Earnings round down to whole dollars per original contribution.

The verified rates support contribution ledger estimates for determinations through 31 December 2026.

In the ATO’s Jill example, this ledger method estimates $7,859 in earnings. The ATO gives $5,190 in GN 2024/1, example 6. The difference remains unresolved. Use the associated earnings on your determination for the actual release.

## How the release is taxed

The assessable amount is the gross released less the non-concessional component, floored at zero. It counts in the income year you requested the release. The 30% tax offset is non-refundable. The ATO can withhold at the estimated marginal rate including Medicare levy less 30 percentage points, or 17% where the Commissioner cannot estimate that rate. The marginal rate option here assumes the ordinary 2% Medicare levy and rounds withholding down to whole dollars. Any Commonwealth debt offset comes out after withholding.

If you do not know the withholding, calculate the assessable amount and offset first. The net release and minimum recontribution need the withholding amount.

The 20% FHSS tax and minimum recontribution figures apply conditionally under the First Home Super Saver Tax Act 2017 and Division 313. Check the contract, notification and recontribution deadlines with the ATO. For determinations made before 15 September 2024, see Treasury Laws Amendment (2023 Measures No. 3) Act 2023, Schedule 4, items 28 and 30. For an item 30 release, enter the original determination date and the amounts the ATO confirmed.

Confirm eligibility, contribution classification, any transitional treatment and the amount to report with the ATO or a registered tax agent. This calculator works the release figures you enter.

## How the work expenses calculator works

For working from home, the calculator shows each method open to you beside the actual cost and names the higher. From 2022-23 the fixed rate is your recorded hours times 67c (2022-23 and 2023-24) or 70c (from 1 July 2024). It covers energy, phone, internet, stationery and computer consumables, so only cleaning, decline in value and repairs are added beside it (PCG 2023/1). For 2020-21 and 2021-22, the 52c rate needed a dedicated home office and covered energy, cleaning and the decline in value of home office furniture; phone, internet, stationery, other assets’ decline in value and repairs went beside it. The 80c shortcut covered every working from home expense. Every hourly rate needs at least one additional running expense incurred from working from home. The actual cost is the total of the work-related amounts you enter.

For a car you owned or leased, the cents per kilometre method counts only the first 5,000 business kilometres, at 72c for 2020-21 and 2021-22, 78c for 2022-23, 85c for 2023-24, 88c for 2024-25 and 2025-26, and 91c for 2026-27 (section 28-25). The log book method takes the car expenses times the business use percentage, business kilometres over total kilometres (section 28-90). A log book serves the year it was kept and the next 4 years (section 28-115) and must cover at least 12 continuous weeks (section 28-120).

For self-education, expenses count only when, at the time you incurred them, you were employed and the study kept up or improved the skills or knowledge for your current work, or was likely to increase your income from it. For 2021-22 and earlier, a prescribed course of education reduces category A by $250, less any category C, D and E expenses (section 82A). From 2022-23 there is no reduction. Each deduction is shown to the cent and again with the cents disregarded, as the ATO’s examples show the figure for the return.

## What the work expenses calculator does not cover

The calculator refuses an expense reimbursed or paid by an employer or anyone else, or covered by an allowance. It also refuses a car you did not own or lease, a log book kept more than 4 years before the claim year, one covering under 12 weeks and one that no longer represents the car’s use. It also refuses cents per kilometre expenses in category D beside log book car expenses in category A. It does not cover occupancy expenses such as rent, mortgage interest, rates and house insurance, or decide whether your home is a place of business. It also leaves out the substantiation rules and their exceptions, occupation-specific guidance, cars taken on hire or jointly owned, a new log book after an ATO notice or an added car, and the electric vehicle home charging rate. It does not work out decline in value, apportion an expense or work out the tax saved. Years before 2020-21 and after 2026-27 are not covered: no cents per kilometre rate had been determined for 2027-28 when the calculator was checked.

Earnings this pay, cents ignored (step 1) $1,400.00 Withheld from those earnings (step 2) $277.00 The payment divided by 52, cents ignored (step 3) $17.00 Withheld from earnings of $1,417 (steps 4 and 5) $284.00 The difference, times 52 (steps 6 and 7) $364.00 47% of the payment, the limit (step 8) $423.00 Withheld from the payment, the lesser (step 9) $364.00 Total withheld this pay (step 10) $641.00 Tax and study loan repayment the payment adds to a year of this pay $423.00 Each amount withheld includes the Schedule 8 study loan component: $10 of the $277 on this pay’s earnings and $104 of the $364 on the payment. The last row is the payment’s effect on the year’s assessment, were every pay this pay; the withholding schedules do not aim to match it.

## How the bonus and back payment withholding calculator works

The bonus and back payment withholding calculator works the PAYG amount an employer withholds from a 2026-27 pay that includes a bonus, commission, back payment or similar payment, by the methods of the ATO’s Schedule 5, and shows each step by its number. Either method is acceptable, and Method B usually comes closer to the tax the payee will owe.

Method A spreads the payment over the year: it works out what the tax table withholds from this pay’s earnings, then from those earnings plus a 52nd, 26th or 12th of the payment, and withholds the difference times 52, 26 or 12, but no more than 47% of the payment. A commission or bonus for a defined period shorter than a year can be spread over the pays it relates to instead.

Method B(i) is for a back payment of earlier pays in the same financial year: each of those pays is worked again with its share of the back payment, and what was withheld from it then comes off. Method B(ii) is for back pay of an earlier financial year and for a bonus or other payment that does not relate to one pay: it works like Method A, but on the average of this year’s pays to date, and takes into account earlier payments this year worked the same way.

With a study or training loan, each tax table amount includes the Schedule 8 component, and the 47% limit applies to the two together. Under Method A the calculator also gives the tax and study loan repayment the payment adds to a year of this pay, so a payee can see whether the withholding will cover it.

## What the bonus and back payment withholding calculator does not compute

The calculator applies the 2026-27 schedules only, to a resident claiming the tax-free threshold or a foreign resident. It does not compute:

- payments made before 1 July 2026, or scales 1, 5 and 6: a resident not claiming the tax-free threshold, or one with a full or half Medicare levy exemption;
- a payee who has not quoted a tax file number, who has 47% withheld, or 45% for a foreign resident, or a working holiday maker, whose payments all fall under Schedule 15;
- a withholding variation, a withholding declaration’s offsets, or a Medicare levy variation;
- payments for a single pay period, which are added to that pay’s earnings, and unused leave or employment termination payments on termination, which are withheld under other schedules;
- back payments of earlier pays with different earnings or withholding each: Method B(i) here takes the same amounts for each, so work pays that differ one group at a time;
- the split of a back payment between this financial year and earlier ones, which you enter; lump sum E reporting; or the tax offset for a lump sum in arrears, which the ATO works out on assessment.

Confirm the figures with the ATO’s tax withheld calculator or a registered tax agent.

## How the salary packaging calculator works

The salary packaging calculator shows what packaging is worth to an employee of a public benevolent institution, health promotion charity, public or not-for-profit hospital or public ambulance service for one year. Your employer pays chosen expenses from your salary before tax. Those benefits are exempt from FBT up to the employer’s cap, measured on their grossed-up value: the taxable value times 1.8868 when the employer gets no GST credit, or 2.0802 when it does. So about $15,900 of Type 2 benefits fills a $30,000 cap and about $9,010 a $17,000 cap. Salary packaged meal entertainment and venue hire can take up to $5,000 more of grossed-up value before FBT applies.

The calculator works your tax with and without the packaging and shows the difference. It also gives the reportable fringe benefits amount your income statement will show. That amount is not taxed, but it is added back for the Medicare levy surcharge, study loan repayments and other income tests, so packaging can raise a surcharge or a repayment while it lowers your income tax. If the benefits pass the cap, the employer owes FBT on the excess and usually recovers it from your package; the calculator takes that off the saving.

## What the salary packaging calculator does not compute

The calculator covers the FBT years ending 31 March 2023 to 2027, for one employer and the salary as your only income. It does not compute:

- rebatable employers, such as other registered charities, whose FBT is reduced by a rebate of 47% up to a $30,000 cap, or ordinary employers, who pay full FBT on packaged benefits;
- benefits outside the cap, such as car parking and meal entertainment that is not salary packaged, exempt benefits such as portable electronic devices, or a novated car lease, which the novated lease calculator works;
- an ambulance service employee not predominantly involved in providing or supporting its ambulance services, whose benefits are not exempt (section 57A(3)(b));
- package fees, the cost of the benefits themselves, or whether a benefit is Type 1 or Type 2, which your employer decides;
- excluded fringe benefits, such as remote area housing, which count towards the cap but are not reportable: entered here, they would raise the reportable amount;
- salary sacrificed to super, other income, deductions, or a spouse and dependants for the Medicare levy surcharge;
- how the FBT year from 1 April to 31 March lines up with the income year from 1 July: the benefits are taken as packaged evenly in the income year.

Confirm the figures with your employer’s salary packaging provider or a registered tax agent.

# Novated lease and electric car FBT exemption calculator

Source: https://duguid.com.au/tools/individual-tax/novated-lease/

> Novated lease saving for an electric or other car, 2023-24 to 2026-27: the FBT exemption conditions, the reportable amount and the employee contribution method.

# Novated lease calculator

## How the novated lease calculator works

The novated lease calculator compares a year of a novated car lease with paying the same car costs from your after-tax pay. Under the lease your employer pays the lease and running costs from your salary, claims back the GST and passes it on, so less of your salary is taxed.

The FBT exemption for electric cars decides how the costs are split. If you are a current employee and the car is a battery electric or hydrogen fuel cell car, was first held and used on or after 1 July 2022 and no luxury car tax had become payable on a supply or importation before any of the benefits counted, the whole cost comes from your pre-tax salary with no FBT. Its value under the statutory formula, 20% of the cost price for a full year, is still reported on your income statement, grossed up. That reportable amount is not taxed but counts for the Medicare levy surcharge and study loan repayments. A plug-in hybrid kept the exemption only under a lease in place and in use before 1 April 2025.

Without the exemption, the usual approach is the employee contribution method: you pay the car’s taxable value from your after-tax pay, which leaves no FBT, and the rest of the cost from your pre-tax salary. The calculator works both ways for an exempt car, so you can see what the exemption is worth, and says which condition fails when it does not apply.

## What the novated lease calculator does not compute

The calculator covers the FBT years ending 31 March 2024 to 2027, for one car and one employer, with the salary as your only income. It does not compute:

- the lease payments themselves, the residual value, interest or fees, which come from your lease quote;
- the operating cost method, FBT left over when the costs are less than the taxable value, or an employer that does not claim GST credits;
- a vehicle designed to carry a tonne or more or 9 or more passengers, which is not a car for FBT and so not covered by the exemption;
- a car benefit for a former or future employee, which the exemption does not cover (section 8A(1)(a));
- whether luxury car tax became payable on another supply or an importation, which you answer. If it first became payable between benefits, section 8A(1)(c) treats the benefits before and after differently. The calculator needs one treatment for the year;
- a car with a value at first sale different from its cost price, or a home charger;
- the end of the lease, when you pay the residual or refinance;
- salary sacrificed to super, other income, deductions, or a spouse and dependants for the Medicare levy surcharge.

Confirm the figures with your employer, your lease provider or a registered tax agent.

## How the payroll tax calculator works

The payroll tax calculator estimates one employer’s payroll tax for the whole of 2026-27 in one state or territory. Each jurisdiction allows a deduction or tax-free threshold, which an employer that also pays wages elsewhere in Australia shares in proportion to its wages there. Victoria, Queensland, Western Australia and the Northern Territory reduce the deduction as Australian wages grow, until it reaches nil. The result shows the deduction, the amount taxed, the tax at each rate and, in Victoria and Queensland, each surcharge or levy on its own line, with the provision applied.

Where a revenue office publishes worked figures, the tests hold them. Revenue NSW: $1,500,000 of NSW wages are taxed on $300,000, and $900,000 of $3,000,000 has a threshold of $360,000. The Victorian State Revenue Office: $80 million in Victoria and $70 million in New South Wales give surcharge thresholds of $5,333,333.33 and $53,333,333.33. The Queensland Revenue Office: $1,356,789 of $1,789,776 has a deduction of $932,460 to the dollar. RevenueWA: annual wages of $1,104,000 give $6,600; its other 2 examples round the deduction to the dollar and come out 1 and 3 cents lower than this calculator. RevenueSA: $800,000 of $1,600,000 has a deduction of $300,000 and $500,000 of $2,000,000 one of $150,000. The Tasmanian State Revenue Office: $2,400,000 gives $54,400, and $2,400,000 of $3,000,000 gives $72,800. The ACT Revenue Office and the Territory Revenue Office publish no worked figures that could be read, so the tests work examples from the Acts by hand: $84,375 on $3,000,000 in the Australian Capital Territory and $41,250 on $3,000,000 in the Northern Territory. This calculator opens on Revenue NSW’s first example.

## What the payroll tax calculator does not compute

The payroll tax calculator gives one annual estimate and no advice. It does not decide which payments are taxable wages or where they are taxable, and does not cover:

- an employer that is a member of a group, whose threshold and rate depend on the group’s wages and which members share the deduction;
- an employer that paid wages for only part of 2026-27, whose threshold every jurisdiction reduces by the days it employed;
- monthly or other periodic returns, and the annual reconciliation of amounts already paid;
- exemptions, rebates and discounts, such as Queensland’s apprentice and trainee rebate and its 1% discount for regional employers, claimed in the return, and the ACT’s 6.85% cap for an eligible university;
- any year other than 2026-27.

Confirm the figure with the revenue office or a registered tax agent before relying on it.

## How the SGC and Payday Super calculator works

From 1 July 2026, under Payday Super, an employer owes super guarantee for each payday, and the employee’s fund must receive it within 7 business days, or a longer period for a first contribution, out-of-cycle pay or an ATO determination. The calculator finds that due date from the site’s business days calendar, then works out the super guarantee charge for one employee if the fund received less than 12% of qualifying earnings by then: the final shortfall still unpaid at the assessment, notional earnings at the GIC rate on the amount that was late, and the administrative uplift, which may be reduced based on the employer’s qualifying assessment and estimate history and any approved disclosure lodged before the assessment day. A contribution counts from the day the fund received it with what it needs to allocate it to the employee. If an unresolved part-day holiday changes the due date, the calculator shows the possible dates and withholds the charge. For a quarter that ended by 30 June 2026 it applies the old law instead: the shortfall at that year’s charge percentage, 10% nominal interest and the $20 administration component.

## What the SGC and Payday Super calculator does not cover

The calculator gives an estimate for one employee and one payday or quarter, and no advice. It does not cover:

- the choice loading for not meeting choice of fund obligations;
- the late payment offset under the old section 23A for quarterly contributions made late;
- bunched contributions under section 18C(2) item 4;
- a contribution made from 1 to 28 July 2026 that item 186 of the transition applies first to a shortfall for the quarter ending 30 June 2026: count only what is left of it;
- a disclosed contribution with no receipt day, whose notional earnings section 36(3) works out as if the fund received it 7 business days after it was paid;
- exemption certificates, and amounts paid that have not reached the fund;
- GIC and penalties once the charge is payable;
- Norfolk Island salary or wages, of which item 2(2) of Schedule 2 to the Tax and Superannuation Laws Amendment (Norfolk Island Reforms) Act 2015 (Compilation No. 1, 1 July 2026) for quarters to 30 June 2026, and item 189 of Schedule 1 to the Payday Superannuation Act for paydays in 2026-27, count only part, for a transitional rate of 7% to 10% for 2022-23 to 2025-26 and 11% for 2026-27 (Table 21 of the ATO’s key superannuation rates), both Acts read 19 November 2026: the calculator refuses them rather than apply the general rate;
- paydays after 30 June 2027, whose maximum contributions base is not yet known, and quarters before July 2022.

Confirm the figure with the ATO or a registered tax agent before relying on it.

Quarter July to September 2026 October to December 2026 January to March 2027 April to June 2027 Pay cycle Weekly Fortnightly Monthly First payday in the quarter

A date in the quarter’s first 7 days for weekly pay, first 14 days for fortnightly pay or first month for monthly pay. Monthly paydays fall on the same date each month, or the month’s last day if it is shorter.

## How the Payday Super cashflow calculator works

Until 30 June 2026 an employer could hold a quarter’s super guarantee until 28 days after the quarter ended. From 1 July 2026, under Payday Super, the employee’s fund must receive 12% of each payday’s qualifying earnings within 7 business days of that payday. The calculator lists the paydays in the chosen quarter of 2026-27, each payday’s super guarantee and the date the fund must receive it, and how many days earlier that is than the quarterly date would have been. The extra working capital is what has already gone to funds but would still be in the business under the quarterly rule. It builds with each payday and peaks at the whole quarter’s super guarantee from the last payday’s due date until the day before the quarterly date. The average days earlier weighs each payday’s amount by how much sooner it leaves. Both dates are when the fund must receive the money, so allow for a clearing house’s processing time before each. In the first quarter, July to September 2026, the April to June 2026 contributions, still due by 28 July 2026, also fall due alongside the first paydays under the new rule.

## What the Payday Super cashflow calculator does not cover

The calculator is an estimate for planning and gives no advice. It does not cover:

- the longer periods for a first contribution for a new employee or to a new fund, out-of-cycle pay, an ATO exceptional circumstances determination or bunched contributions: use the SGC and Payday Super calculator for those due dates;
- earnings that change from one payday to the next, extra or irregular paydays, and the April to June 2026 quarter’s contributions;
- each employee’s maximum contributions base of $270,830 for 2026-27: enter only earnings on which super guarantee is payable;
- Norfolk Island salary or wages, which have a transitional rate of 11% for 2026-27;
- the cost of the extra working capital, such as interest on an overdraft, and any super above the minimum;
- paydays outside 2026-27.

Confirm the figures with the ATO or a registered tax agent before relying on them.

## How the long service leave calculator works

Long service leave comes from each state and territory’s own Act, not the National Employment Standards. The calculator measures the service from the first day to the last, less the days you exclude, and applies the Act you choose. While employment continues, it gives the leave the employee can take now and when the next amount becomes available. When employment ends, it decides from the length of service and the reason whether the Act pays anything, works out the weeks it pays, deducts leave already taken or paid, and values the rest at the weekly ordinary pay. Each step names its provision. Victoria and the Australian Capital Territory give full leave after 7 years and the other states and territories after 10; New South Wales and the Australian Capital Territory can pay a pro rata amount from 5 years, the others from 7, and Victoria not before 7 years at all.

## What the long service leave calculator does not cover

The calculator gives an estimate under one Act for one employee, and no legal advice. It does not cover:

- which Act applies to employment in more than one state or territory, and whether an award, enterprise agreement or contract gives a better entitlement, including the long service leave terms of a pre-2010 award or agreement that section 113 of the Fair Work Act 2009 preserves;
- portable schemes, such as building and construction, contract cleaning, community services and security, and the black coal mining industry, Commonwealth and state public servants, Queensland seasonal employees in the sugar industry and meat works and other seasonal employees, and Tasmanian mining employees, who have their own rules;
- whether a break keeps service continuous, which absences count, and whether a reason for leaving qualifies, such as a pressing necessity or serious misconduct: you decide those;
- averaging pay for varied hours, casual or part-time work, commission or piece rates;
- leave taken in advance of the entitlement, cashing out, and service before 23 June 1990, which some Acts count under earlier rules;
- tax withheld from the payment.

The figures follow the Acts read 19 November 2026; Queensland, South Australia and Tasmania rechecked 24 November 2026. A future date assumes they are unchanged. Confirm the result with the state or territory’s long service leave regulator or a lawyer before relying on it.

## The average wholesale price method

Only for grape wine, and only if at least 10% by value of the tax period’s sales of grape wine of the same vintage and the same variety or blend are wholesale sales (subsection 9-25(3)). Enter that period’s wholesale sales of it, excluding WET and GST; every dealing valued by this method uses them. The form takes 4 sales: enter any more as part of one of them, adding their quantities and prices, which leaves the average unchanged.

## How the wine equalisation tax calculator works

Wine equalisation tax (WET) is 29% of the taxable value of each assessable dealing in wine (section 5-5). A wholesale sale’s taxable value is its price excluding WET and GST, and GST is then 10% of the price including WET: the ATO’s $120 dozen bears WET of $34.80 and GST of $15.48, $170.28 in all. A retail sale or own use, such as wine used for tastings, is valued at a notional wholesale selling price; own use of wine bought under quote is valued at its purchase price excluding GST (section 5-5, items AD3c and AD13c). By the half retail price method that is 50% of the retail price including WET and GST (section 9-35), so the ATO’s $140 dozen at the cellar door bears WET of $20.30. Grape wine may instead use the average wholesale price method, the weighted average of the tax period’s wholesale prices for wine of the same vintage and variety (section 9-40), but only if at least 10% by value of those sales are wholesale sales (subsection 9-25(3)); wine that is not grape wine must use half retail (section 9-30). A sale under quote bears no WET (section 7-10). Each amount is rounded half up to the cent.

A producer that meets the conditions of section 19-5 earns a producer rebate of 29% of the wholesale price, or of the notional wholesale selling price, on each dealing it is liable for, and on a sale under quote unless the quote states the buyer will use the wine in manufacture, make a GST-free supply of it or sell it on under quote. The rebates for a financial year are capped, for the producer or for its group of associated producers together: $350,000 for dealings to 30 June 2026 and $400,000 from 1 July 2026 (subsections 19-15(2) and (3)). The calculator takes the rebates already claimed this year off the cap and gives what is left. The wine tax goes to label 1C and the rebate to label 1D of the business activity statement, each in whole dollars, never netted. It reproduces the ATO’s rebate table for 2026-27: WET of $11,890 and rebates of $16,240 on its retail, wholesale, quoted and tasting dealings.

## What the wine equalisation tax calculator does not cover

The calculator works dealings in the financial years 2023-24 to 2027-28 and refuses earlier years, which carry the transitional rebate rules for 2017 and earlier vintage wine. It refuses the average wholesale price method for wine that is not grape wine or without the 10% share of wholesale sales, and a rebate on own use of wine bought under quote. It takes each price as given, so it does not work out an arm’s length price (section 27-10) or the price of wine sold with other goods; it assumes GST applies to a sale and does not decide whether a supply is GST-free.

Not covered: imports and other customs dealings, whose WET the Department of Home Affairs collects; the special valuations of section 9-45; wine tax credits other than the producer rebate, such as bad debts and overpaid WET; the reduction of a rebate for earlier producers’ rebates on wine used in a blend; New Zealand participants’ rebates; whether producers are associated (the group’s claims are taken as given); and the tax period a dealing belongs to. A value or total of $70,368,744,177,664 or more is refused, as the page cannot show it to the cent. Rebates claimed above the cap are flagged, not worked out: section 19-25 makes the excess payable as wine tax at the end of the financial year. Have a registered tax agent confirm the result before you lodge.

## Small claimant methods

A small claimant had fuel tax credits of $10,000 or less in the previous 12 months and expects the same in the current 12 months (PCG 2016/2). For the basic method alone, a business that claimed none in the previous 12 months need only expect $10,000 or less (PCG 2021/2 footnote 3).

## How the fuel tax credit calculator works

The fuel tax credit calculator works out a business’s fuel tax credits for fuel acquired in one income year from 2022-23 to 2026-27. Each line takes the rate the ATO published for the day the fuel was acquired, for its fuel and its use: a heavy vehicle travelling on a public road (fuel for a bus’s or coach’s passenger air-conditioning included) takes the rate net of the road user charge, every other business use takes the full rate, and a light vehicle on a public road gets nothing. The page adds the lines and gives the whole dollar amount for label 7D on the business activity statement, with the rate, its period and its ATO page for each line.

A small claimant can also enter a line by its cost and the average pump price instead of its litres, split one heavy vehicle’s diesel between public roads and other use by the basic method, and take every line at the tax period’s final rate when an applicable rate changes solely because of indexation. Rates for every period since 1 July 2022 are held here, so an earlier period’s credits can be worked out for an amendment.

## What the fuel tax credit calculator does not cover

The calculator does not decide whether the business is entitled to a credit: you state the facts that settle it. Nor does it decide who acquired the fuel in a hire chain, whether a road is a public road or travel on it is incidental, whether a vehicle meets the environmental criteria of section 41-25, or how fuel is apportioned between uses: you state those. It does not hold the auxiliary equipment percentages of PCG 2016/11, the ATO’s list of heavy vehicles used mainly off public roads, the consumption rates for articulated combinations, or rates for aviation fuel, packaging and supply, domestic heating or electricity generation. It does not work Division 44 adjustments, the attribution of credits to tax periods or the conversion of LPG kilograms to litres. It refuses fuel acquired before 1 July 2022, after 31 January 2027, or outside the income year chosen.

Fuel acquired after 19 November 2026, when the rates were read, carries a warning to check the ATO’s rates page for a change since. Confirm the result with the ATO’s fuel tax credit tools or a registered tax or BAS agent before relying on it.

## What each line needs

Each line is one sale, importation, adjustment or refund in the tax period. Fill the lines in order.

For a business registered or required to be registered for GST. You establish each line: that the vehicle is a car and not one the Act excludes (an emergency vehicle, a car fitted out for wheelchairs, a commercial vehicle not designed mainly to carry passengers, a motor home or campervan), that the supply or importation is taxable (no quote, not GST-free or input taxed), its luxury car tax value and its combined fuel consumption rating.

The value is the luxury car tax value, with GST and customs duty but not luxury car tax; for a price adjustment, the corrected value. Leave the litres blank for a car with no combined fuel consumption rating.

An adjustment takes the year the car was supplied or imported in. A refund left blank takes the tax period’s year; choose the earlier year for a car supplied or imported before then, and one from before 1 July 2019 is refused.

Needed only for a car rated above 3.5 and up to 7 litres, supplied or imported from 1 July 2025. Answer yes if, before that day, it was supplied or imported and used in Australia other than for a quotable purpose: the 7 litre rating then continues.

The ATO describes a refund-eligible car as a 4 wheel or all wheel drive that is either a passenger car (category MA) with a ground clearance of at least 175 mm or an off-road passenger vehicle (category MC). The claimant must be registered for GST (sections 18-5 and 18-10).

## How the luxury car tax calculator works

The luxury car tax calculator works out the tax on a tax period’s sales and importations of luxury cars in 2019-20 to 2026-27, with the price and change of use adjustments and labels 1E and 1F on the business activity statement. Each car takes the threshold for the financial year of its supply or importation, or the fuel-efficient car limit for a car rated at most 3.5 litres per 100 km from 1 July 2025 and at most 7 litres before. The tax is 33% of the GST-exclusive value over that threshold. Tax on an importation is shown apart, because it is paid to the Department of Home Affairs with any customs duty. A primary producer’s or tourism operator’s refund of the tax borne on a refund-eligible car, up to $10,000, is shown apart too, because it is claimed on the ATO’s form.

Its results match the luxury-car-tax command of Ryan Duguid’s australian-accounting calculators on the ATO’s examples and 306 test cases, refusals included.

## What the luxury car tax calculator does not cover

The calculator does not decide whether a vehicle is a car or a luxury car, whether you could quote or a supply is taxable, the value of a car sold with other goods, or whether a car is refund-eligible: you state those. It does not work bad debt adjustments, the adjustments in subsections 15-30(1A) and (3A), a public institution’s adjustment, the credit for an entity that is not registered, the refund for cars supplied before 1 July 2019, or which tax period a line belongs to. It refuses a tax period outside 2019-20 to 2026-27, a supply year outside 2012-13 to the tax period’s, and a second primary producer refund in the period. A primary producer’s refund in an earlier period of the same year also rules out another, which the page cannot see.

Confirm the result with the ATO’s luxury car tax guidance or a registered tax or BAS agent before relying on it. The vehicle classifier shows whether a vehicle is a car for luxury car tax.

Capped at 30%: lump sum A, type T $6,420.00 Long service leave before 16 August 1978: lump sum B $780.00 5% of it, assessable at marginal rates $39.00 At marginal rates: unused leave on termination (paid leave type U) $14,820.00 Assessable income $21,279.00 Withheld at 32% from lump sum A, to the nearest dollar $2,054.00 Withheld from $14,859.00 at marginal rates $4,732.00 Total to withhold from the leave $6,786.00 Marginal rate calculation: $14,859.00 over 52 pays is $285.00 a pay with cents ignored; Schedule 1 withholds $188.00 from $1,155.00 and $279.00 with it added, so $91.00 × 52 is $4,732.00.

This is the payer’s withholding under Schedule 7 and the labels for the employee’s income statement; it does not estimate the tax assessed on their return.

## How the unused leave calculator works

When employment ends, unused annual leave, leave loading and long service leave are taxed by when the leave accrued and why the employment ended. Leave for employment before 18 August 1993, and all of it from 16 August 1978 on a genuine redundancy, early retirement scheme or invalidity, is capped at 30% and withheld at 32%; it is lump sum A. Only 5% of long service leave for the period before 16 August 1978 is assessable; the whole amount is lump sum B. The rest goes through Schedule 7’s marginal rate calculation with that 5%, spread over a year of pays and withheld at the employee’s Schedule 1 rate, and is reported as unused leave on termination.

## What the unused leave calculator does not cover

The calculator gives an estimate for one employee’s unused leave paid on termination from 1 July 2026 to 30 June 2027, and no advice. It does not cover:

- splitting a payment between the periods by days of service under sections 83-95 to 83-115: enter each part;
- whether a termination is a genuine redundancy, an early retirement scheme or invalidity;
- unused leave paid after an employee’s death;
- a working holiday maker, whose payments Schedule 15 covers;
- an employee who has not claimed the tax-free threshold, or claims a Medicare levy variation or the seniors and pensioners offset (scales 1, 5 and 6), or has a withholding variation;
- a post-17 August 1993 payment under $300 with long service leave from before 16 August 1978, where Schedule 7 does not say how its limit applies;
- employment termination payments, which the redundancy and ETP withholding calculator covers.

Confirm the figures with Schedule 7 or a registered tax agent before relying on them.

## How the workers compensation premium calculator works

Every state and territory scheme bills a premium on the wages an employer estimates for the policy period and adjusts it to the wages actually paid. The calculator takes the wages, the rate your insurer gives your industry classification and the facts your scheme asks for, and applies the scheme’s published method as far as it goes for an employer whose premium does not yet turn on its own claims: icare’s small employer formula in New South Wales, the Premiums Order for a new or small employer in Victoria, WorkCover Queensland’s notice for a policy that starts in 2026-27, ReturnToWorkSA’s formula with its discount bands and claims cost cap in South Australia, and the insurer’s rate times wages in the other 4. It adds GST, and Queensland’s insurance duty, and, given the actual wages, works the premium again and shows the adjustment.

## What the workers compensation premium calculator does not cover

The calculator gives an estimate for one employer and one policy, and no advice. It does not cover:

- the industry classification or the rate, which are the insurer’s, and the wages, which each scheme’s definition decides, including whether a contractor or director counts as a worker;
- experience-rated and performance-rated premiums: New South Wales above $30,000 of basic tariff premium and the Loss Prevention and Recovery products, Victorian employers that are neither new nor small, Queensland policies in force before 1 July 2026 or carried on from an earlier policy (reinstated within 6 months, or a business taken over: sections 11 and 12 of the notice) and Queensland default assessments, which have a $500 minimum (section 4.2), and a South Australian supplementary underwriting rate;
- members of a group in New South Wales, Victoria, Queensland and South Australia, policies for less than 12 months in New South Wales, the Mine Safety Fund adjustment for mining WICs, the catastrophic claims contribution and the performance discount;
- Comcare and self-insured employers, household workers, the South Australian work health and safety fee, discounts for paying early and instalment interest;
- whether an employer is exempt from holding a policy, which the result flags where a scheme’s limit was read, and any policy year other than 2026-27.

Confirm the premium with your insurer before relying on it.

It keeps the year’s account and the franking return’s figures; it does not lodge the return or decide what may be franked.

## How the franking account calculator works

Each PAYG instalment, income tax payment and franking credit received credits the account on its day, and each franked distribution, refund and other debit takes it down. A deficit at 30 June gives rise to franking deficit tax. When you enter that deficit as next year’s opening balance, the calculator adds the matching credit on 1 July. The tax is also an offset against the company’s income tax, reduced by 30% of the part caused by its own distributions and refunds when that part is more than 10% of the year’s credits. The first distribution in each franking period sets the benchmark: one franked above it gives over-franking tax, one below it an extra debit, and a benchmark that moves too far from the last must be disclosed. A franking credit received is entered as the credit, not the dividend, and the offset is applied only when the income tax is given.

When a later refund changes the deficit tax, use the actual 30 June balance and R&D deferral for next year’s opening figures. In next year’s account, enter the refund on its receipt date and enter the additional franking deficit tax from that refund as a separate credit on that date.

## What the franking account calculator does not cover

The calculator gives an estimate for one entity’s income year from 1 July 2025 to 30 June 2026 or from 1 July 2026 to 30 June 2027, and no advice. It does not cover:

- consolidated groups, an entity that stops being a franking entity, New Zealand franking companies, pooled development funds, friendly societies, life insurance companies, exempting entities, a substituted accounting period or late balancer, and diverted profits tax;
- whether a distribution is frankable, what the company may frank it to, or whether a statement given after a distribution was allowed (s 202-75);
- a tax offset refund other than an income tax refund’s R&D part, the general interest charge on late franking tax, and the return’s amounts in whole dollars;
- the company’s tax rate and maximum franking credit from turnover, which the company tax and franking calculator works out.

Confirm the figures with the ATO’s instructions or a registered tax agent before relying on them.

## How the company tax and franking calculator works

The calculator applies the base rate entity test of section 23AA of the Income Tax Rates Act 1986 to this year’s figures: aggregated turnover under $50 million, and base rate entity passive income of no more than 80% of assessable income. A base rate entity pays 25% of its taxable income, and any other company 30% (subsection 23(2)).

The rate for franking a dividend comes from a second test. Section 995-1 of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1997 runs the base rate entity test on the previous year’s turnover, passive income and assessable income, so a company can pay tax at 30% and frank at 25%, or the reverse; a company that did not exist in the previous year franks at 25%. The maximum franking credit is the dividend times 1 over the gross-up rate, which is 100% less that rate, over that rate (section 202-60): one third of the dividend at 25% and three sevenths at 30%. A credit above the maximum is taken to be the maximum (section 202-65).

The shareholder includes the dividend and its franking credit in assessable income and gets a tax offset equal to the credit (section 207-20). Tax at the marginal rate you enter, less the offset, is the extra tax the dividend brings; where the offset is larger, an individual gets the excess refunded (section 67-25).

The calculator reproduces the outcome of each ATO example: Happy Feet (3.8% passive income, 25%), Coffee and Cake (28.6%, 25%), Best Equity (100%, 30%), SoftDev (85%, 30%) and Hats 4 Cats ($170 million of aggregated turnover, 30%). For Dillmore Manufacture’s $100,000 dividend franked at 30% it gives $42,857.14, the exact credit; the ATO rounds the gross-up rate to 2.3333 and shows $42,857.75, which is more than the section 202-60 maximum.

## What the company tax and franking calculator does not cover

The calculator does not work out aggregated turnover, assessable income or base rate entity passive income: enter figures you have established, with the turnover of connected entities and affiliates included, as the ATO’s Hats 4 Cats example shows. Taxable income gives the tax before offsets, PAYG instalments and other credits.

Not covered: the rates of RSA providers and pooled development funds (subsections 23(3) to (5)), life insurance companies (section 23A), not-for-profit companies and credit unions; corporate unit trusts and public trading trusts; and income years before 2021-22, when the base rate was 27.5% or 26%. A shareholder that is a company, trust, super fund or non-resident is outside its scope; a company shareholder cannot have excess franking credits refunded (section 67-25). Franking account balances, franking deficit tax, the benchmark rule and the holding period rule are not tested: the company tax and franking worksheets track the franking account and the benchmark rule. Have a registered tax agent confirm the figures and the result.
