## How the R&D tax offset calculator works

The calculator works one company’s research and development tax offset under section 355-100 for an income year from 2021-22 to 2026-27. The offset is worked on the notional deductions, or, where they total less than $20,000, on the part paid to research service providers that are not associates and as CRC contributions. A company with aggregated turnover under $20 million that exempt entities do not control gets its corporate tax rate plus 18.5 percentage points, and the offset is refundable. Any other company gets its corporate tax rate plus a premium of 8.5% on the part up to 2% of its total expenses and 16.5% on the part above, and the offset is non-refundable. The corporate tax rate is 25% for a base rate entity that is not an RSA provider, PDF or other company taxed at a special rate, and 30% otherwise. Notional deductions above $150 million get the corporate tax rate only.

A clawback amount is the recoupment amount you enter plus the lesser of the feedstock revenue and the feedstock expenditure. Section 355-450 works the offset again on the notional deductions less the clawback amount, and takes the clawback amount at the corporate tax rate as the deduction amount. The offset less the adjusted offset and the deduction amount, divided by the corporate tax rate for the present year, is included in assessable income in that year. Each amount is worked exactly and rounded to the cent once.

## What the R&D tax offset calculator does not cover

The calculator does not decide whether activities are core or supporting R&D activities, whether they are registered with AusIndustry, whether the company is an R&D entity, or which expenditure it can deduct. It leaves out associate expenditure and its payment (section 355-480), overseas findings and activities overseas, R&D partnerships and offsets of earlier years. You enter the notional deductions, total expenses, turnover, control and clawback amounts as established. It does not work out the recoupment amount itself, including the grant cap and repayments, balancing adjustment clawbacks or catch up deductions. It assumes no earlier clawback or catch up amount for the offset year, and covers only companies and income years starting on or after 1 July 2021. It refuses a clawback amount when the notional deductions, or the notional deductions less the clawback, are under $20,000, because the Act and the ATO’s example do not settle how the threshold applies then. It does not carry a non-refundable offset forward. Results are planning estimates: check them against your records and the ATO’s guidance.

Assessable income here is the Division 6 share, the net capital gain, the attributable franked distribution and the franking credit.

## How the trust streaming calculator works

The calculator shares a resident discretionary trust’s net income for one income year between up to 4 beneficiaries and the trustee. A beneficiary specifically entitled to part of a capital gain or franked distribution is treated as entitled to the gain or distribution times the benefit they receive over the net benefit referable to it. The part nobody is specifically entitled to is shared by adjusted Division 6 percentage: present entitlement less the amounts specifically entitled to, over trust income less all such amounts, as the ATO’s examples work it. A share of the capital gain over the gain, times the gain remaining after losses and concessions, is the attributable gain. The beneficiary has an extra capital gain of twice that for a gain the trust discounted or reduced by the small business 50% reduction, or 4 times for both, and then applies their own discount. A share of the franked distributions gives the same share of the distributions less directly relevant deductions, and of the franking credits. Where net income without franking credits is less than the net capital gain and net franked distributions together, both are reduced rateably. Division 6E takes the capital gain, franked distributions and franking credits out of income and net income, and each beneficiary is assessed on the rest of the net income in proportion to their present entitlement to the rest of the income. The trustee is assessed under section 99A at 45% on the part no beneficiary is presently entitled to, with its share of a discounted gain grossed up, and gets its share of the franking credits as a tax offset. Each amount is worked exactly and rounded to the cent once.

## What the trust streaming calculator does not cover

The calculator does not decide whether a beneficiary is presently or specifically entitled, whether the deed allows streaming, or whether a resolution was made in time: you enter the entitlements as established. It takes one capital gain and treats the franked distributions as one class (section 207-59); a trust with several gains needs each worked separately. It assumes every beneficiary is a resident not under a legal disability and assessed under section 97, so it leaves out section 98 assessments for minors, beneficiaries under a legal disability and non-residents, Division 6AA, and the trustee’s choice to be assessed on a capital gain (section 115-230). It does not apply section 99 to deceased estates or other section 99A(2) trusts, and does not cover non-resident trusts, managed investment trusts, AMITs, public trading trusts or trust losses. It does not work out the capital gain, losses, discount, trust income or net income, the 45-day holding rule or other franking integrity rules, the Medicare levy, or any beneficiary’s own tax. It gives no advice on section 100A reimbursement agreements, family trust elections or family trust distribution tax, or distributions to a bucket company and Division 7A: those are out of scope. Results are planning estimates: check them against the trust deed, the resolutions and the ATO’s guidance.

## How the deferred tax calculator works

The calculator works one company’s tax effect worksheet under AASB 112 for an income year from 2020-21 to 2026-27. Each asset’s carrying amount less its tax base, or each liability’s tax base less its carrying amount, is a temporary difference: above nil it is taxable and below nil deductible. Taxable differences give a deferred tax liability. Deductible differences and unused tax losses, less those you say have no deferred tax asset because future taxable profit is not probable, give a deferred tax asset. Both are measured at the 25% or 30% you expect when they reverse, undiscounted.

The year’s deferred tax expense is the change in the net balance, split into the rate change on the opening balances, the change in recognition, and origination and reversal. Current tax is taxable income at the year’s company rate, 25% for a base rate entity (26% in 2020-21) or 30%, less non-refundable offsets. The reconciliation starts from accounting profit at that rate and shows each reconciling line and the difference left. Every amount is exact and rounded to the cent where the worksheet rounds.

## What the deferred tax calculator does not cover

The calculator does not work out tax bases or carrying amounts, or judge whether future taxable profit is probable. You enter them as established. It refuses business combinations, uncertain tax treatments, tax-consolidated group members and tax on items outside profit or loss. It refuses a rate change it cannot split without a reversal schedule. It leaves out the initial recognition exception, investments in subsidiaries, branches, associates and joint arrangements, unused tax credits, Pillar Two top-up taxes and prior year adjustments to current tax. It covers only an Australian resident company taxed at the section 23(2) rates, not life insurers, RSA providers, PDFs, non-profit companies or credit unions, and only Australian income tax, not foreign income tax. It does not decide how the balances are presented or offset. Results are planning estimates: check them against your records, the standard and the ATO’s guidance.

# Company owner salary vs dividends calculator (2026-27)

Source: https://duguid.com.au/tools/business-calculators/salary-dividend/

> Compare a company owner's salary and super guarantee with fully franked dividends: company tax, the owner's tax, Division 293 and the split that keeps the most.

# Salary against dividends calculator

Pay a company owner by salary, dividends or both, and see what is kept after tax.

Published 19 November 2026. Last checked 19 November 2026.

JavaScript is required for interactive calculations. The formula, assumptions and source links remain available below.

Salary against dividends inputs for one owner

Income year 2026-27 2025-26 2024-25 2023-24 2022-23 2021-22 Company profit before the owner’s salary and super (AUD) Is the company a base rate entity this year and last year? Yes: tax and franking at 25% No: tax and franking at 30% Salary paid to the owner (AUD) Owner’s other taxable income (AUD)

Profit is the company’s taxable income before it pays the owner. The owner is a director and shareholder, an Australian resident with private patient hospital cover, and has no other concessional super contributions, no other labour income, no work-related deductions (which reduce the standard deduction) and nothing that Division 293 income adds to or takes from taxable income: no reportable fringe benefits, net investment losses, income taxed as a family trust distribution, released first home super saver amount or super lump sum taxed at 0% (the Division 293 calculator works those). Use the company tax and franking calculator to settle the rate.

Calculate Fictional example: the first boundary case below. Change the inputs and calculate your own. Inputs: 2026-27, company profit before the owner’s pay $200,000.00, company tax at 25% (a base rate entity), salary $100,000.00, other taxable income $0.00. Super guarantee at 12% of the salary $12,000.00 Company tax on the profit left $22,000.00 Fully franked dividend $66,000.00 Franking credit $22,000.00 Owner’s taxable income $187,000.00 Owner’s extra income tax and Medicare levy, less the franking credit $32,000.00 Contributions tax and Division 293 tax on the super $1,800.00 Cash kept after tax $134,000.00 Super kept after tax $10,200.00 Kept in all, cash and super $144,200.00 All salary, $178,571.43: kept in all $146,463.02 All dividends: kept in all $140,130.00 Most kept: salary of $178,571.43, $128,248.74 cash and $18,214.28 super $146,463.02 The split that keeps the most counts super after tax, though it stays in the fund until retirement.

## How the salary against dividends calculator works

The company pays the owner the salary you enter and the super guarantee on it, both deductible, pays company tax on the profit left and pays the rest as a fully franked dividend. The owner adds the dividend and its franking credit to other income and the salary, less the $1,000 standard deduction on the salary from 2026-27, and pays tax and the Medicare levy on the total, less the credit. The extra tax this income brings, over the tax on the other income alone, comes off the salary and dividend to give the cash kept. The super fund pays 15% on the super guarantee, and Division 293 tax applies where taxable income and the contributions pass $250,000.

With every dollar paid out and franked at the company’s own rate, salary and dividends are taxed at the owner’s rates either way: the franking credit hands back the company tax. What differs is the super guarantee. Salary moves 10% to 12% of itself into super, taxed at 15% instead of the owner’s marginal rate, so more salary keeps more in all whenever that rate, with the Medicare levy, is above 15%, and less where the tax-free threshold, the offsets or the levy’s phase-in leave it lower. The calculator compares your split with all salary and all dividends, then checks every salary at which a tax rate, an offset, the levy, the super guarantee base or Division 293 changes, and gives the lowest salary that keeps the most, to within $1.

In the example, a $200,000 profit paid as $178,571.43 of salary and $21,428.57 of super guarantee keeps $146,463.02, of which $18,214.28 is in super; paid all as dividends it keeps $140,130.00, all in cash.

## What the salary against dividends calculator does not cover

The calculator assumes the whole profit is paid out in the year. Profit kept in the company is taxed at its rate and paid out later, which this calculator does not model; nor does it test the company’s franking account or the holding period rule, or work a year in which the franking rate, set from last year’s figures, differs from the company’s tax rate. A payment or loan to the owner that is neither salary nor a declared dividend can be an unfranked deemed dividend under Division 7A: see the Division 7A calculator. Where the company earns the owner’s personal services income, the PSI rules checker says whether that income is taxed to the owner whatever the company pays. The salary counts as wages for payroll tax and may need workers compensation cover; neither is counted.

It does not cover salary sacrifice, other concessional contributions, work-related deductions, reportable fringe benefits, net investment losses, family trust distribution tax income, a released first home super saver amount, a super lump sum taxed at 0%, the low income super tax offset, the Medicare levy surcharge, study loan repayments, a spouse or dependants, a non-resident owner, more than one owner, or income years before 2021-22. Super counts at its value after tax, though it stays in the fund until retirement. Have a registered tax agent review the arrangement before relying on a result.

# Sole trader vs company tax calculator (2026-27)

## How the sole trader against company calculator works

As a sole trader the owner is taxed on the whole profit at the resident rates, less the low income tax offsets and the small business income tax offset, plus the Medicare levy. Drawings are not deductible, so the amount taken out changes nothing. Through a company the profit is split: the company pays the salary you enter and the super guarantee on it, both deductible, and pays company tax on the rest. The amount taken out less the salary is paid as a fully franked dividend from the profit after company tax, and whatever is left stays in the company. The owner pays tax and the Medicare levy on the salary (less the $1,000 standard deduction from 2026-27), the dividend and its franking credit, less the credit: the top-up tax is that tax less the tax on the salary alone, and is a refund where the credit is larger. The super fund pays 15% on the super guarantee, and Division 293 tax where taxable income and the contributions pass $250,000.

Each structure’s total adds those amounts for the one year. The 2 totals do not leave the money in the same place: the sole trader holds all the profit after tax, whilst the company structure leaves some in super and any profit not taken out in the company, whose later dividend may bring more personal tax or a refund. The calculator states each figure and the difference; it does not say which structure suits a business.

In the example, a $150,000 profit is taxed $38,570.00 as a sole trader, after the full $1,000 offset. Through a base rate entity paying a $60,000 salary and a $40,000 dividend, the total is $34,913.23, with $22,100.00 kept in the company and $6,120.00 in super.

## What the sole trader against company calculator does not cover

The calculator does not apply the personal services income rules: where the profit is mainly a reward for the owner’s personal efforts, Part 2-42 can tax it to the owner whatever the company pays (see the PSI rules checker). It does not apply Division 7A: a payment, loan or debt forgiveness to the owner that is not salary or a declared dividend can be an unfranked deemed dividend (see the Division 7A calculator). It does not cover the small business CGT concessions or the CGT discount, which a company cannot claim; state taxes such as payroll tax, land tax and duty; or the cost of running a company, such as ASIC fees, its own tax return and its accounts.

It also leaves out the tax on profit kept in the company once it is paid out, the company’s franking account and a year in which the franking rate, set from last year’s figures, differs from the tax rate; other income of the owner, a spouse or family members, trusts and partnerships; GST, PAYG instalments and losses; the Medicare levy surcharge, study loan repayments and the low income super tax offset; a non-resident owner; and income years before 2021-22. Super counts at its value after tax, though it stays in the fund until retirement. Have a registered tax agent review any change of structure before relying on a result.

## How the foreign buyer surcharge calculator works

The calculator applies the chosen state or territory’s own test of who is foreign to your answers, once for its duty surcharge and once for its land tax surcharge, as each revenue office states them. The duty surcharge is its rate times the dutiable value of the buyer’s share: 9% in New South Wales, 8% in Victoria, Queensland and Tasmania (1.5% on Tasmanian primary production land), and 7% in Western Australia and South Australia. The ACT and the Northern Territory charge none.

The land tax surcharge is for a full land tax year on the land value you enter: 5% in New South Wales, 4% in Victoria from $50,000 of taxable land ($25,000 for a trust), 3% of the value over $349,999 in Queensland, 2% in Tasmania and 0.75% in the ACT. Western Australia and South Australia charge none, and the Northern Territory has no land tax. Victoria charges a fixed trust’s surcharge on the land held for absentee beneficiaries only. The general transfer duty is worked on the whole property, for all buyers together, at the general rates.

The calculator reproduces the revenue offices’ examples: Revenue NSW’s $90,000 of surcharge purchaser duty and $39,187 of transfer duty on $1 million, and $60,000 of surcharge land tax on $1.2 million; Victoria’s $80,000 for Andrew, $16,000 for Emily’s $200,000 share and $20,000 for Clara’s half of a fixed trust’s $1 million; RevenueSA’s $42,000 and $21,000 for Peter; Western Australia’s $14,000 for Simon; Queensland’s $1,500.03 on $400,000; and Tasmania’s $8,000 on $400,000.

## Who is foreign in each state and territory

An individual who is an Australian citizen, holds a permanent visa or is a New Zealand citizen on a special category visa is not foreign for Queensland, Western Australian, South Australian and Tasmanian duty. New South Wales also requires a permanent resident or New Zealand citizen to have been in Australia 200 days of the previous 12 months (Revenue Ruling G009); Victoria gives a New Zealand citizen no exception unless they ordinarily reside in Australia for 6 consecutive months around settlement. Victorian and Queensland land tax charge absentees: non-citizens without a permanent visa who do not ordinarily reside in Australia and were away on the day or for over 6 months of the year.

A company is foreign when it is incorporated outside Australia, or foreign persons with associates hold 50% or more (more than 50% in Victoria) of its shares or votes, or in New South Wales, Queensland, Tasmania and Western Australia of its potential voting power. New South Wales instead asks whether one foreign person with associates holds 20% or more, or foreign persons together 40% or more, wherever the company is incorporated. Trusts and super funds follow the same shares of capital or members’ balances. Victorian land tax counts absentee interests instead, which you enter apart: a company pays absentee owner surcharge when absentees hold more than 50%, a fixed trust on the land held for absentee beneficiaries, and a complying super fund none. A foreign person who ordinarily lives in Australia is no absentee.

A discretionary trust is foreign in New South Wales if a foreign person could benefit, now or by amending the deed (section 104JA); in Victoria and Tasmania if foreign persons could be given more than 50%, or 50% or more, of the capital; in Queensland if foreign takers in default hold 50% or more; in Western Australia if a foreign person controls it, as a foreign trustee or appointor does, or foreign takers in default hold 50% or more; in South Australia if a trustee, appointor, named object or taker in default is foreign; and in the ACT only if a named foreign beneficiary could receive 50% or more. Victorian land tax looks only at named (specified) beneficiaries who are absentees.

## What the foreign buyer surcharge calculator leaves to you

The FIRB fee is the 2026-27 fee for one application to acquire residential land, which FIRB indexes each 1 July. The calculator does not decide whether the buyer is a foreign person under the Foreign Acquisitions and Takeovers Act 1975, whether an exception to the ban on established dwellings applies, or the lower fee rules, exemption certificates, fee waivers and the fees for agricultural and commercial land. The comparison leaves out land tax, since the land value entered is the buyer’s land in the chosen state or territory only.

The calculator does not decide exemptions, refunds or ex gratia relief, which each Commissioner grants on application. Among them are Australian-based developers and build to rent in New South Wales and Victoria, exempt permanent residents who live in the home in New South Wales, significant contributors and large developers in Queensland, and refunds when a buyer stops being foreign within 12 months in South Australia. When one is sought, it refuses. It also refuses a partner (provisional) or retirement visa holder, whom the revenue offices treat differently, and does not trace interests through other companies and trusts or decide who is an associate.

Not covered: landholder and corporate trustee acquisitions; concessions on general duty; Queensland’s absentee land tax rates, which replace the general rates; Victorian trust surcharge rates; control of a Western Australian discretionary trust by a foreign person other than its trustee or appointor, such as one whose consent a distribution needs; control of a Victorian company through its board or through influence the Commissioner finds, rather than through shares or votes; a Victorian beneficiary nomination for trust land bought before 2006, under which the surcharge starts at $50,000 rather than $25,000; joint land tax assessments; property converted to residential use later; and a surcharge charged again when a buyer becomes foreign within 3 years. The transfer duty calculator and the land tax calculator work the general duty with first home concessions and the general land tax. Confirm the result with the revenue office or a registered adviser before relying on it.

The regulations state base amounts, and ASIC raises some of them each 1 July in line with the Consumer Price Index; the table gives ASIC’s indexed amounts. A special purpose company is defined in regulation 3 of the review fees regulations; it includes a company whose constitution prohibits distributions to its members and whose sole purpose is to act as trustee of a regulated superannuation fund. A company in liquidation and an entity registered with the Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission pay no review fee (Schedule 1 Part 1 items 10 and 11).

## How the ASIC fees calculator works

For a standard fee, the calculator returns ASIC’s 2026-27 amount. For a late fee, it compares the day ASIC received the payment or document with the due date you enter, as INFO 30 sets the tiers by the day ASIC receives them. A payment or document received on or before the due date is not late. A review fee paid after its due date but within one month after it costs $102, and later $428 (Schedule 1 Part 3 of the review fees regulations); a document lodged late attracts the same 2 amounts (Schedule 2 item 14 of the fees regulations). A late fee is on top of the fee itself, and ASIC can charge more than one late fee when several obligations are missed.

The one month begins the day after the due date, which is not counted (item 6 of subsection 36(1) of the Acts Interpretation Act 1901). Under subsection 2G(1), a month runs to just before the same day of the next calendar month, or to the end of that month when it has no such day. A fee due on Tuesday 15 September 2026 is within one month if received by Thursday 15 October; one due on Monday 30 November 2026 is within one month if received by Thursday 31 December, because that month starts on 1 December.

## What the ASIC fees calculator does not cover

The calculator does not work out a due date. An annual review fee is due 2 months after the review date (subsection 1351(3) of the Corporations Act 2001), a review date can change, and a document’s lodgement period depends on the document, so you enter the due date shown by ASIC or the form’s rules. When a deadline falls on a weekend or public holiday, subsection 105(3) of the Corporations Act or subsection 36(2) of the Acts Interpretation Act may allow the next business day. The calculator does not apply that. When the due date or the last day of the first month is a Saturday or Sunday, it declines to give a tier for a received date that such a move could change, up to the following Wednesday and, after a weekend due date, the end of the month that would follow the moved date. It does not check public holidays.

Not covered: due dates and received dates before 1 July 2026 or after 30 June 2027, including a fee due in one financial year and received in the next, because the sources read do not settle which year’s indexed amount applies; upfront review fees; deregistration and the review fee exceptions in subsection 1351(4); registered schemes, notified foreign passport funds, small transferring financial institutions and CCIVs; registered Australian bodies and foreign companies; credit licensee late fees; fee waivers and reviews of a late fee; and the industry funding levy. Check the amount against ASIC’s invoice before you pay.

Calculate Fictional example: the first boundary case below. Change the inputs and calculate your own. Inputs: New South Wales, start 21 December 2026, end 4 January 2027. Business days after the start, to and including the end 7 Weekday public holidays skipped 25 December 2026 (Christmas Day), 28 December 2026 (Boxing Day / Boxing Day (observed) / Proclamation Day (observed)), 1 January 2027 (New Year's Day) Part-day and regional holidays count as business days; where a local day replaces Melbourne Cup Day or the WA King’s Birthday, the state date is still skipped.

## How the business days calculator works

The calculator skips Saturdays, Sundays and the public holidays of the state or territory you choose, using the dates confirmed for 2026 and 2027. Between 2 dates, it counts the business days after the start date up to and including the end date, so a Friday to the next Monday is 1. Forward or back, it finds the date that is that many business days after or before the start, and lists each weekday holiday it skipped.

‘Any state or territory’ skips full-day public holidays that apply throughout at least one state or territory. It counts Melbourne Cup Day and the WA King’s Birthday as business days because regions can observe them on different dates.

## What the business days calculator does not cover

Part-day holidays, such as the evenings of Christmas Eve and New Year’s Eve in South Australia and the Northern Territory, count as business days. So do regional holidays, among them the Royal Queensland Show in Brisbane, Tasmania’s Royal Hobart Regatta and Recreation Day, and show days, and days off for one group only, such as Tasmania’s Easter Tuesday for the public service. A council or region’s local substitute for Melbourne Cup Day or the WA King’s Birthday is not applied: the state date is still skipped.

The calculator covers dates through 31 December 2027. Check the applicable law for which days and which place count towards a deadline. The separate SGC and Payday Super calculator works out those due dates within its own coverage period.

## How the GST margin scheme calculator works

The GST margin scheme calculator first checks the conditions of section 75-5 of the GST Act that it can decide: what is sold, a written agreement with the buyer, and how you acquired the property. The sale must be a taxable sale (you are registered for GST, you sell in the course of your enterprise, and the sale is not GST-free or input taxed) of a freehold interest in land, a stratum unit or a lease of at least 50 years, and you must not have acquired it with GST on the whole price. The written agreement is made on or before the sale, or within a further period the Commissioner allows.

Under the GST margin scheme the GST is 1/11 of the margin. Subtract the acquisition consideration from the GST-inclusive price (subsection 75-10(2)). A nil or negative margin gives no GST. Leave building and development costs out (section 75-14). You may claim input tax credits on creditable purchases (section 11-5). For a subdivided lot, use only its share of the consideration (section 75-15), measured fairly by area, number of lots or anticipated selling price (GSTR 2006/8, paragraphs 58 to 61).

From a GST-exclusive price the calculator adds GST of one tenth of the price less the consideration, which is 1/11 of the margin on the resulting price (GSTR 2006/8, paragraph 145). Beside the margin scheme it gives the GST without it, 1/11 of the GST-inclusive price, and the difference. Each GST rounds to the nearest cent, half a cent up (section 9-90). The buyer cannot claim an input tax credit on a margin scheme sale (section 75-20), so the scheme suits a buyer who could not claim one anyway.

The calculator reproduces GSTR 2006/8’s worked examples: $20,000 on Bob’s house and land (Example 3), $4,000 on Josine’s 800 square metre lot (Example 4), $13,636.36 on Adam’s Lot 1 (Example 6) and a $100,000 GST-inclusive price from Example 14’s $96,364, here $100,000.40 to the cent.

## Approved valuation dates for GST margin scheme sales

The GST margin scheme calculator checks the date an approved valuation applies to for property held since before 1 July 2000. For a covered sale, use a valuation as at 1 July 2000 if you were registered or required to be registered for GST then. For later registration and unimproved property sold outside government, use the earlier of the effective date and the application date, or the effective date if the Commissioner registered you without an application (subsection 75-10(3) and GSTR 2006/7, paragraphs 60 and 61).

Get separate advice on the GST margin scheme valuation date if you registered or first became required to register after 1 July 2000 and the property already had improvements on that day. Items 2 and 3 of subsection 75-10(3) specify different valuation dates. The calculator also refers government supplies of property unimproved on that day for separate review under item 4. The valuer may prepare the report later than the date the valuation applies to.

## What the GST margin scheme calculator does not cover

The GST margin scheme calculator refuses a sale to your associate, because section 75-13 takes the GST-inclusive market value as the price. It also refuses property inherited, acquired within a GST group or joint venture, as a GST-free going concern, farm land or government land, or from an associate: paragraphs 75-5(3)(b) to (g), item 2A of subsection 75-10(3) and section 75-11 set their own tests and margins. It refuses property acquired partly in a sale with GST on the whole price, which has an increasing adjustment (section 75-22).

Not covered: adjustments for bad debts and for consideration paid later (sections 75-25 and 75-27), the valuation day for government land under item 4 of subsection 75-10(3), and whether the sale is taxable in the first place, such as whether residential premises are new. The calculator takes your valuation as given and does not check that it meets the Commissioner’s requirements for an approved valuation (section 75-35). Have a registered tax agent confirm eligibility and the result before you settle.

## How the GST adjustments calculator works

The calculator works one of 6 GST adjustments or tests for a tax period in a financial year from 2020-21 to 2026-27, with each condition and its authority. For a change in creditable purpose, it finds whether the tax period ending 30 June is an adjustment period: one starting at least 12 months after the tax period the acquisition is attributable to, counted to 1, 2, 5 or 10 periods by the GST exclusive value and whether it relates to business finance. Disposal or loss ends the count early (sections 129-20 and 129-25). No adjustment arises at or below $1,000, or $10,000 for business finance. The full input tax credit times the difference between the intended or former application and the actual application is an increasing or decreasing adjustment (sections 129-70 and 129-75).

Annual apportionment tests eligibility under section 131-5 and compares the credit with the election, the GST on the supply, or that times the non-input-taxed and consideration extents, with the section 11-30 credit; the difference is the section 131-55 increasing adjustment. The financial acquisitions threshold is exceeded when financial acquisitions’ credits exceed $150,000 or 10% of all credits, for the past or the next 12 months (sections 189-5 and 189-10). A going concern is GST-free when all 5 conditions of section 38-325 are met. Second-hand goods give a credit of 1/11 of the consideration, capped above $300 at the GST on your resale (section 66-10). A bad debt gives 1/11 of the amount, reduced for a partly taxable supply or partly creditable acquisition (Division 21 and Subdivision 136-A). Amounts are worked exactly and rounded to the cent once.

## What the GST adjustments calculator does not cover

The calculator does not decide the facts. You enter each fact, amount and percentage as established, and it does not judge whether an apportionment method is fair or reasonable. It refuses cars and reduced credit acquisitions for annual apportionment, and farm land and part supplies for going concerns. For second-hand goods it refuses goods divided for resupply, valuable metal and goods leased before sale. For bad debts it refuses the margin scheme and other special rules, reduced credit acquisitions and annual apportionment, and a change of accounting basis. It does not work out the tax period an adjustment or credit is attributable to, substituted or concluding tax periods, importations, or a Commissioner’s determination of fewer adjustment periods. It takes as given, without checking, that the 2 applications leave out changes in applying a thing to financial supplies unless the financial acquisitions threshold is exceeded (section 129-5(2)), that there has been no Division 130 adjustment (section 129-15), that a reduced credit acquisition’s percentages are worked as GSTR 2000/24 paragraphs 63 to 65 direct (section 129-40(3)), and that every member of a GST group is eligible before its representative member elects (section 131-15). Results are planning estimates: check them against your records and the ATO’s guidance.

Download the invoice to print

## How the tax invoice generator works

The generator makes one tax invoice from the supplier, recipient and lines you enter, in this browser: nothing is stored or sent. It checks the invoice against the 7 details section 29-70(1) requires: that it is intended to be a tax invoice, the supplier’s identity and ABN, what is supplied with its quantity and price, the extent each supply is taxable, the date issued and the GST payable. When the supplies total $1,000 or more, including GST, it also requires the recipient’s name or ABN. It refuses an invoice that lacks a required detail and names each one missing.

GST on a taxable line is one-eleventh of a price that includes GST, or 10% of one that excludes it. With 2 or more taxable lines, the total invoice rule adds the exact GST and rounds the total once to the nearest cent, half a cent up; the taxable supply rule rounds each line’s GST to the nearest cent, half a cent up, and adds them. When each supply is taxable and prices include GST, the invoice says ‘Total price includes GST’ and shows the GST. When taxable and GST-free or input taxed supplies are together, each taxable line is marked * with a statement that its price includes GST, or that GST is added, and each other line is labelled. With no taxable supply, the document is headed ‘Invoice’ and says it includes no GST, as no tax invoice is needed.

The supplier’s ABN, and the recipient’s if given, must pass ABN Lookup’s check digit test: subtract 1 from the first digit, weight the 11 digits 10, 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15, 17 and 19, and the sum must divide by 89. An RCTI is headed ‘Recipient created tax invoice’, needs both parties’ ABNs and the recipient’s name, a taxable line and your confirmation that the Determination allows it, and states that the GST shown is payable by the supplier. Download the invoice as a page with no script to print it or save it as PDF.

## What the tax invoice generator does not cover

The generator does not look up an ABN on the Australian Business Register, so it cannot show that either party is registered for GST or that the ABN is active. Only a supplier registered for GST makes a taxable supply and can issue a tax invoice. It does not decide whether a supply is taxable, GST-free or input taxed, or apportion a mixed supply: you enter each part as its own line. It does not cover adjustment notes, credit notes, discounts or negative lines, the margin scheme, wine equalisation tax or luxury car tax, GST groups and joint ventures, agents, co-owners or more than one recipient, non-monetary or foreign currency consideration, or eInvoicing through Peppol. For an RCTI it does not write, hold or check the written agreement, including one embedded in the RCTI (section 9 of the Determination), or check that the recipient may issue RCTIs. Results are review aids: check the invoice against the ATO’s guidance before you issue it.

## How the CGT calculator works

The CGT calculator works out the capital gain or capital loss from one sale (CGT event A1) for an Australian resident individual, trust, complying super fund or company, for a sale contract from 1 July 2020 to 30 June 2027. The sale contract’s date decides the income year and the 12 months held; the cost base adds the purchase price, buying costs, capital improvements, title costs, selling costs and, for an asset bought after 20 August 1991, costs of owning that were not deducted, less capital works deductions.

It then works the gain by each method the owner can use. The discount method halves the gain of an individual or trust, and takes a third off a complying super fund’s, once the asset was held at least 12 months, not counting the day bought or the day sold. The indexation method, for an asset bought before 21 September 1999 (sections 114-1 and 114-10 end it at 11.45 am that day, so a purchase on the day is refused), indexes each cost (except costs of owning) to the September 1999 quarter; a company must use it and gets no discount. Capital losses this year and then net capital losses from earlier years come off the gain before the discount, which is why indexation sometimes wins.

For a home, it counts the days of the ownership period, from settlement to settlement, when the home was not the main residence: before moving in, unless that was as soon as practicable, and each period away that is not treated as the main residence. A period away can be treated as the main residence indefinitely while empty, and for 6 years while rented, the 6 years starting again each time you move back in. The taxable share is those days over the ownership period, plus the floor area used to produce income for the days it was. If the home was first rented or used to produce income after 20 August 1996, was fully exempt until then and is now only partly exempt, section 118-192 treats it as bought then for its market value, and the method follows that date.

The result gives the amounts for question 18 of the supplementary tax return, in whole dollars as the return takes them, and for an individual an estimate of the extra tax and Medicare levy.

## How to enter a sale in the CGT calculator

Enter the dates of the contracts, not of settlement: the sale contract’s date is when the CGT event happens (subsection 104-10(3)). Put stamp duty and legal fees on buying in buying costs, with the date they were incurred; a deposit paid at the contract is part of the purchase price. Put capital improvements, and costs of defending your title, in the 2 cost rows with their dates; add 2 costs incurred in the same quarter together. Selling costs are agent’s commission, advertising and legal fees on the sale. Costs of owning are interest, rates, land tax, insurance and repairs you could not deduct, such as for a home or vacant land. Leave out any cost to the extent you deducted or can deduct it (subsections 110-45(1B) and (2)), except capital works: enter those costs in full and the deductions in their own field. Leave out depreciating assets such as carpets and appliances, which have their own balancing adjustment.

For a home, enter the settlement dates and the day you moved in, then each period you lived elsewhere before the sale. Tick ‘Rented’ for a period it was rented or available for rent, and ‘Choose’ for the periods you treat as your main residence; you cannot treat another home as your main residence for those periods (subsection 118-145(4)). A rented room or a surgery goes in the floor area fields, with the days that use ran; use that continued while you were away stays taxable (subsection 118-190(3)). Enter the market value at first use to produce income in case section 118-192 applies; the result says whether it did.

## What the CGT calculator does not cover

The calculator gives an estimate for one sale, and no advice. It does not cover:

- sale contracts from 1 July 2027, under Schedule 1 to the Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Act 2026, and before 1 July 2020;
- foreign and temporary residents, life insurance companies, collectables, personal use assets, and CGT events other than a sale;
- the test of section 115-45 for shares or trust interests held at least 10% with associates, a rented absence that ends on the day the ATO’s examples 72 and 80 count the 6 years apart, use of part of a home to produce income that began while you were away (subsection 118-190(3)), and costs of owning a home when section 118-192 applies;
- other capital gains in the same year, and splitting a parcel of shares between the methods, as example 12 of the ATO’s guide does;
- the small business concessions in Division 152, roll-overs, and the extra discount for affordable housing (section 115-125);
- the 6 months for 2 homes when changing main residences (section 118-140), land over 2 hectares, spouses with different main residences, inherited homes and building on land you owned;
- indexing capital works deductions, which come off at their face amount, capital works deductions on an asset bought before 13 May 1997 and improved after 30 June 1999 (subsection 110-45(1A)), and a substituted accounting period.

Confirm the figure with the ATO or a registered tax agent before relying on it.

## Shares or units bought in parcels

For shares or units bought at different times and sold in 2025-26 or 2026-27, the share parcels form matches each sale to its parcels, first in, first out or as you select, and works each gain or loss and the net capital gain.

## Common questions

### Which entities and contract dates does the capital gains tax calculator support?

The capital gains tax calculator supports resident individuals, trusts, complying super funds and companies for a single disposal contract from 1 July 2020 to 30 June 2027.

### Does it model the 50% CGT discount and main residence 6-year absence rule?

Yes. It applies the 50% discount for eligible assets held more than 12 months, indexation where applicable, capital losses and the main residence absence and section 118-192 rules.

# Privacy, browser data and site use

Source: https://duguid.com.au/privacy/

> How duguid.com.au handles browser calculations, cookies, hosting and feedback, with the site’s advice boundaries and software licence links.

# Privacy and site use

The duguid.com.au privacy notice explains how the site handles browser calculations, hosting and feedback.

Published 12 September 2026. Last reviewed 24 November 2026.

## Browser calculations

The website’s calculators process the figures you enter in your browser. They do not send those figures to a server or save them in browser storage. Download any results you want to keep before leaving the page. Downloaded files stay wherever you save them.

The accounting-question search also runs in your browser. It does not send search text to a search service. It does place the search term and topic in the page address so a filtered list can be bookmarked or shared, which means the term appears in your browser history and in any address you pass on.

## Cookies and analytics

The website’s own code does not set cookies or include advertising pixels. Its fonts, images and application scripts are served from this domain.

No analytics script is delivered. Cloudflare Web Analytics is switched off, so I receive no page-view reports. GitHub Pages and Cloudflare still process requests to host and protect the site, as the Hosting section below describes.

Email Address Obfuscation is disabled so email links work without scripts. The address is public in the HTML pages, their plain-text alternates and the machine-readable index. The contact page also spells it out for anyone whose browser does not open an email app.

Cloudflare also asks browsers to report network errors to Cloudflare for seven days and to prefetch pages you are likely to open next (the nel, report-to and speculation-rules response headers). Neither carries the figures you type into the calculators. A prefetched or shared page address can carry question-search terms, because the search places them in the address; do not put confidential information in a search you may share or leave in your history.

On a sample of page loads, Cloudflare adds a report-only security policy header, which asks your browser to tell Cloudflare which scripts the page loads and which connections it makes. It blocks nothing. A report includes the page address, which can hold question-search terms, but not the figures you type into the calculators. If Cloudflare treats a request as suspicious, it can answer with its own verification page, which runs Cloudflare’s code and may set a security cookie; see Cloudflare’s cookie documentation. Cloudflare makes these additions itself; they are not part of this website’s source. The calculators work out their figures in your browser without sending them to a server.

When you select Human or Machine view, your browser saves that display preference on this device. The preference is not sent to a server. You can change it with the view switch or remove it by clearing this site’s browser storage.

## Hosting

GitHub Pages hosts this website’s files, and Cloudflare delivers them to your browser. These providers process technical information about visits, which may include IP addresses, request details and security or performance data. See the GitHub Privacy Statement and Cloudflare Privacy Policy for their handling of that information.

## Feedback and external links

If you email me, I receive your email address and the content you send. Use fictional examples when reporting a problem. Do not include taxpayer information, client files or other confidential records. An email stays in my mailbox until I delete it, GitHub keeps issues public in its own systems under its terms and I cannot delete copies other people hold.

GitHub issues are public. Links to GitHub and other websites take you to services with their own privacy policies. Software you download or install has its own documented data handling; this notice covers the website.

For questions about this notice or information you have sent me, email ryan@duguid.com.au. To ask what personal information I hold, have it corrected or complain about how I handled it, email that address, or take a complaint about the handling of personal information to the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner. Other project links are on the Contact page.

## AI crawlers and citation

The site’s robots.txt names the main search, citation and training crawlers, and its default group allows every other agent. Search indexing and the fetches an assistant makes to answer or cite for a user are allowed, and Google-Extended is allowed so Gemini grounding can cite the site. No crawler is blocked: training crawlers are allowed too, including those from Common Crawl (CCBot), Bytespider, OpenAI (GPTBot), Anthropic (ClaudeBot), Apple (Applebot-Extended), Amazon (Amazonbot) and Meta (meta-externalagent). The machine-readable index and the full page text are published for citation, and robots.txt is the current policy if this summary and the file ever differ.

If an AI answer misquotes this site, email ryan@duguid.com.au with the page address and the quoted text. Use fictional examples only; do not send client records or taxpayer information.

## Using this site

Read the advice and review boundary before relying on a tool or example. Check each page’s assumptions, source links and review date, and have a qualified professional review outputs before acting on them.

The code Ryan Duguid wrote for this website uses the Apache License 2.0 and his original page text uses CC BY 4.0. His original data compilations and artwork use the Ryan Duguid Public Attribution Licence 1.0. Third-party material keeps its own terms.

Each tool page links to the licence for its release or source revision. For example, Ozzit v3.8.0 uses the Apache License 2.0. Earlier releases keep the terms they shipped with. When copying a formula or integrating a package, use the licence supplied with the version you take.

## Accessibility

I aim for this site to meet WCAG 2.2 level AA. Automated checks run on every change: axe scans each page at phone and desktop widths, and other tests cover the skip link, keyboard focus, one main heading per page and pages that fit those widths without scrolling sideways.

Automated checks find only some barriers. I have not tested the site with screen readers or on physical phones and tablets. If something stops you using a page, tell me through the contact page, naming the page and what happened.

# Profit vs cash flow: an Australian Excel worked example

Source: https://duguid.com.au/examples/profit-vs-cash-flow/

> A fictional Newcastle business holds quarterly profit at $35,957.55 AUD while one late $44,000 receipt leaves cash $25,160 short. Workbook, figures and limits.

# Profit vs cash flow: an Australian Excel worked example

How can a business report a profit and still run short of cash? Because profit records the sale and cash records the day the money arrives.

The worked example moves one receipt by 45 days: quarterly profit stays at $35,957.55 and the bank account falls $25,160 below zero.

Download the Excel example Compare the two cases

To run the experiment, open the workbook, change Assumptions!B2 from 0 to 45 and compare quarterly profit with the lowest daily cash balance. Read the full steps.

XLSX, 23,506 bytes. Source revision 386c7ff, MIT License. Needs desktop Excel with automatic calculation. The explanation and results below can be read without Excel.

Lumbridge Services is fictional. Every business, customer, invoice, balance and date here is fictional, and all amounts are Australian dollars (AUD). No client outcome is described.

Published 18 September 2026. Last reviewed 23 November 2026.

One receipt arrives 45 days late. Weekly closing cash falls to ($25,160) against a $15,000 buffer. Compare both cases. Exported from Excel on 4 November 2026; capture record.

## The business and the question

Lumbridge Services is a fictional maintenance business in Newcastle, NSW. It bills two service lines, Varrock maintenance and Falador repairs, and invoices $60,000 of work each month: $40,000 Varrock and $20,000 Falador, before GST. The forecast covers the quarter from 1 October to 31 December 2026.

The owner wants to buy equipment. The quarter shows a profit, so the money looks available. The question is whether the bank account can carry the business to the end of December if one customer pays late.

The model holds every other assumption still. Monthly materials are $12,000 and overhead $6,000. Gross wages are $24,000 a month, with $19,000 paid to employees, $5,000 of PAYG withholding and $2,880 of super. The opening bank balance, receivables, payables, GST, loan and tax instalment all come from fictional 30 September 2026 balances. The owner’s policy is to keep $15,000 in the bank.

## The one change: a 45-day delay

Invoice OPEN-V is September work for the Varrock line: $40,000 plus $4,000 GST, so $44,000 is banked. The baseline case receives it on 14 October 2026. The late case receives the same $44,000 on 28 November 2026, 45 calendar days later.

Nothing else changes. The work was performed in September either way, the invoice was issued either way and the customer pays in full either way. Only the day the money lands moves.

The workbook exposes that single control. Assumptions!B2 holds the delay in whole calendar days and accepts 0 to 120. The main comparison uses 0 and 45 days; the sensitivity table also checks 15, 30 and 60 days.

## Both cases, side by side

Same work, same customer, different receipt date. All amounts AUD.

Forecast measure | Receipt on time | Receipt 45 days late
Quarter revenue | $180,000.00 | $180,000.00
Profit before income tax | $35,957.55 | $35,957.55
October customer receipts | $66,000.00 | $22,000.00
October closing cash | $32,040.00 | −$11,960.00
First day the bank account is negative | None in the quarter | 28 October 2026
Lowest daily closing cash | $16,800.00 on 7 October | −$25,160.00 on 6 November
December closing cash | $67,320.00 | $67,320.00

The two cases end the quarter with the same cash because the delayed receipt still arrives, on 28 November. That later recovery cannot pay the wages, supplier invoices and GST that fall due in late October and early November.

Against the owner’s $15,000 buffer, the late case is $40,160 short at its worst day. A reader looking only at December closing cash, or only at profit, sees neither the shortfall nor its date.

Weekly closing cash in the late case, exported from the distributed workbook in Excel 16.0 on 4 November 2026. The 13 plotted values are $16,800, $15,600, $25,520, ($11,960), ($11,960), ($25,160), $17,640, $27,560, $49,680, $36,480, $79,280, $67,320 and $67,320, against the assumed $15,000 buffer. Capture record.

## Compare five receipt delays

A 15-day delay is enough to put this fictional business below zero for one day. Longer delays can also extend the time below zero without changing the lowest balance. These five runs move only the $44,000 OPEN-V receipt from its original 14 October date.

Daily closing cash at five receipt delays. All amounts AUD; all dates are in 2026.

Delay in days | Receipt date | Lowest cash | First date at that low | Days below zero
0 | 14 October | $16,800.00 | 7 October | 0
15 | 29 October | −$11,960.00 | 28 October | 1
30 | 13 November | −$25,160.00 | 6 November | 16
45 | 28 November | −$25,160.00 | 6 November | 16
60 | 13 December | −$25,160.00 | 6 November | 22

Quarterly profit before income tax stays at $35,957.55 and December closing cash at $67,320 in every run. Another scheduled customer receipt on 13 November explains why the 30- and 45-day cases have the same 16 days below zero. The 60-day case includes a further negative period later in November.

Days below zero counts all negative daily closing balances, including separate periods. It does not measure intraday liquidity. The comparison tests five selected delays, not every possible receipt date, and assumes no funding facility.

Calculated on 26 September 2026 with the Python model at the same captured source commit, 386c7ff. All 455 daily balances across the five runs were independently reconciled to the dated source receipts and payments; each monthly cash reconciliation was $0.00. This is a Python calculation record, not a new Excel verification. Read the results, definitions and source hashes (JSON).

## Why profit did not move

Profit is measured on the accrual basis. Lumbridge earned the OPEN-V revenue when it performed the work in September, so the sale sits in the September accounts in both cases. Moving the receipt changes the debtor balance, not the revenue, and no expense changes either. Quarterly profit before income tax is $11,985.85 a month in both cases, or $35,957.55 for the quarter.

Cash is measured on the day money moves. The payments the business owes do not wait for a customer. In the late case, October receipts fall from $66,000 to $22,000, while the same $63,960 of payments still leaves the account. Those payments include materials on 7 October, the September-quarter GST of $12,600 and a $3,000 income tax instalment on 28 October, and net wages and super on 28 October.

The model states the bridge between the two. It starts from profit, adds back depreciation of $200 a month and the non-cash leave provision of $2,254.15 a month, adjusts for the movement in gross receivables and the GST liability, then subtracts the $1,000 monthly loan principal and the tax instalment. A separate direct cash schedule ties to that bridge exactly: the model’s reconciliation difference is $0.00 in every month of both cases.

Three obligations are still outstanding at 31 December in both cases: $12,600 of GST, $5,000 of PAYG withholding and $13,200 of supplier invoices. The $67,320 closing balance is not spendable surplus.

## The decision for a person

The model does not approve or refuse the equipment purchase. It gives a reviewer three things to act on:

- Confirm the OPEN-V receipt date with the customer before committing to discretionary spending.
- Resolve the funding gap between 28 October and mid-November, which the model neither borrows nor overdraws. No overdraft, new loan or owner contribution is assumed anywhere in this forecast.
- Compare actual collections with the forecast each week, because the whole result turns on one date.

Whether the business should defer the purchase, arrange finance or accept the risk is a judgement about a real business with real customers. This example supplies the arithmetic, not that judgement.

## Open the workbook

Needs desktop Excel with automatic calculation. No Xero login, add-in, macro or AI agent is used, and the workbook contains no macros and no external links.

- Download the fictional Excel forecast (23,506 bytes).
- Download the sample pack: the same workbook, the 6 source files, model notes, the management briefing, the trial guide, the fixed CSV exports and the MIT License from revision 386c7ff.
- Read the sample record for the source commit, hash and verification.
- Open the Model and Cash 13 weeks sheets and find quarterly profit and December closing cash.
- Change Assumptions!B2 from 0 to 45. Trace invoice OPEN-V and watch the lowest daily balance and its date.
- Restore 0, then save a copy and reopen it to confirm the original figures return.

Only the workbook recalculates. The briefing, the CSV exports and the JSON summary in the sample pack are fixed exports taken at a 0-day delay: editing the workbook does not rewrite them. Rebuild from source with the matching delay when you need an export and a workbook that agree.

## Rebuild it from source

The example lives in the OzFPA repository, an Australian extension of Jeff Brines / Guiderail’s openfpa. From a checkout of the captured commit, with Python 3.11 and uv:

```
uv sync --locked --extra dev
uv run --locked --extra dev python examples/lumbridge-services/models/generated/lumbridge.py
uv run --locked --extra dev python examples/lumbridge-services/models/generated/lumbridge.py --delay-days 45
```

Each run writes the workbook, briefing and schedules to examples/lumbridge-services/output/ and verifies all 21 monthly workbook lines against the Python model before replacing the workbook. Expect quarter_profit_before_tax of 35957.55 in both runs, and minimum_daily_cash of 16800.0 on 2026-10-07 at a 0-day delay and -25160.0 on 2026-11-06 at 45. A rebuilt workbook can differ in package metadata or cache bytes from the file distributed here.

Read the source and assumptions at the captured commit.

To reproduce the additional sensitivity rows, run the same command with --delay-days 15, --delay-days 30 and --delay-days 60. Each run replaces the output files, so retain its results before starting the next one. Count values below zero in the resulting daily-cash.csv ending-cash column to reproduce days below zero.

## Limits

The Lumbridge case is a fictional demonstration, not a client result. No forecast accuracy, client outcome or time saving has been measured.

- The only supported scenario is the receipt delay, from 0 to 120 whole calendar days. Revenue, wages and operating assumptions are fixed.
- Payment dates, PAYG withholding, workers compensation, the tax instalment and the loan terms are supplied scenario assumptions, not statutory calculations. PAYG withholding is a flat $5,000 a month, not a withholding table result.
- Payroll tax is nil because annualised wages and super of $322,560 sit below the bundled $1.2 million NSW threshold for a single ungrouped employer. Grouping and interstate wages need separate assessment.
- Daily balances net everything dated on the same day. They do not establish intraday liquidity or the order in which payments clear.
- The output is not a complete forecast statutory balance sheet, and it does not calculate company income tax expense.
- The example does not test when a super fund receives a contribution. Payday Super timing covers that question.

Varrock and Falador are Old School RuneScape naming references. No game assets or prices are used. No game knowledge is needed.

## Common questions

### How can a business make a profit and still run out of cash?

Profit records revenue when the work is performed and cash records money when it arrives. In this example the September work stays in September profit whether the $44,000 invoice is banked on 14 October or 28 November, so a 45-day delay leaves quarterly profit at $35,957.55 while the bank account falls to minus $25,160 on 6 November.

### What changes between the two cases?

One date. Invoice OPEN-V, worth $40,000 plus $4,000 GST, is received on 14 October 2026 in the baseline and on 28 November 2026 in the late case. Revenue, expenses, wages, supplier terms and every other payment date are identical.

### Why do both cases end December with the same cash?

The delayed receipt still arrives inside the quarter, on 28 November, so both cases close December at $67,320. The recovery is too late to fund the payments due in late October and early November, which is why the daily view matters more than the closing balance.

### Is this a real client case?

No. Lumbridge Services, its customers, invoices and balances are fictional. No client outcome, forecast accuracy or time saving is claimed.

# Ozzit: Excel LAMBDA functions for Australian modelling

Source: https://duguid.com.au/tools/ozzit/

> A free Excel workbook of 165 native LAMBDA functions and 5 help tables for Australian modelling: GST, financial years, AASB 16 leases and amortisation.

# Ozzit

The Ozzit workbook holds 165 functions and 5 help tables for GST, financial years, depreciation, loans and leases, and every definition is visible in Excel.

Current release Ozzit v3.8.0, 24 November 2026, from the Ozzit repository. Release licence: Apache License 2.0. Published 18 September 2026. Last reviewed 24 November 2026.

Delivery

Excel workbook

Needs

Microsoft 365 or Excel 2024 or later

Boundary

Calculates only. The reviewer decides the accounting treatment and the tax position.

Download Ozzit v3.8.0 Browse worked formulas

XLSX, 553,054 bytes. Needs Microsoft 365 or Excel 2024 or later. No add-in or macro.

## Extract GST from $1,100

```
=oz.GSTExtractλ(1100)
```

100.00 displayed to two decimal places

Assumes a wholly taxable, GST-inclusive amount at 10%. Read the workings, the Excel check and the limits.

## What Ozzit is

An Excel workbook, not a program. Open it, copy a function into your own model, and the formula travels with the file. Every definition is a native LAMBDA stored as a defined name, so the arithmetic stays inside the workbook where a reviewer can read it.

The v3.8.0 workbook carries 170 named formulas: 165 LAMBDA functions and 5 help tables that document them inside the workbook. Each module also ships an editable demonstration worksheet, and the formula source is published as plain text in the repository’s src/ folder and indexed in functions.csv.

The Australian helpers cover GST addition and extraction with a 10% default rate, 1 July financial year labels, 5 ATO small business benchmark ratio helpers, modelling depreciation schedules and pools, AASB 16 lessee schedules and journals, PAYG withholding, hire purchase, CGT parcels, general income tax rates, Division 7A minimum repayments, margin scheme GST and FBT gross-up. The rest of the library is general financial modelling.

Release v3.8.0 adds 14 functions (oz.LeaseJournalλ, oz.HPScheduleλ, oz.HPJournalλ, oz.FinanceCompareλ, oz.CGTParcelsλ, oz.NetCapitalGainλ, oz.IncomeTaxλ, oz.Div7AMinRepaymentλ, oz.MarginSchemeGSTλ, oz.FBTGrossUpλ, oz.LowValuePoolλ, oz.SmallBusinessPoolλ, oz.IndexFactorλ and oz.BulletLoanλ), moves Ryan Duguid’s original work to the Apache License 2.0 and adds native workbook_source and audit CLI commands.

## Who it is for and what it needs

Ozzit suits an accountant or analyst who builds models in Excel and wants the working visible rather than hidden in an add-in or a macro. It is not a bookkeeping tool, and it never touches a ledger.

What the workbook needs. Scroll sideways on small screens.

Requires | Microsoft 365 or Excel 2024 or later, with LAMBDA and dynamic arrays
Does not run in | LibreOffice and Excel versions before 2024, which cannot evaluate the functions
Contains | No VBA, no macros, no add-in and no external link

Author | Ryan Duguid. Built from scratch, with provenance recorded in the repository

## Ten worked formulas

Open an example for its arguments, formula, expected display and limits. These examples use v3.6.0 and need Microsoft 365 or Excel 2024 or later. Enter them in the Ozzit workbook with space for any spilled result.

All ten were evaluated in Excel 16.0 build 20625 on 15 November 2026 against the unchanged v3.6.0 release workbook. Read the inputs and raw results. The check verifies these calculations, not an accounting treatment.

### Extract GST from an inclusive amount

oz.GSTExtractλ: Returns the GST contained in one or more GST-inclusive amounts.

Signature: GSTExtractλ(Amounts, [Rate]). Square brackets mark optional arguments.

```
=oz.GSTExtractλ(1100)
```

Expected display: 100.00, displayed to two decimal places.

Limits: Assumes the whole amount is taxable at 10%. The function returns an unrounded binary floating-point result. Use ROUND(...,2) where cent rounding is required; the reviewer decides the treatment.

Link to this example · Released formula source

### Add GST to an exclusive amount

oz.GSTAddλ: Adds GST to one or more GST-exclusive amounts.

Signature: GSTAddλ(Amounts, [Rate]). Square brackets mark optional arguments.

```
=oz.GSTAddλ(1000)
```

Expected display: 1,100.00, displayed to two decimal places.

Limits: Assumes a wholly taxable amount and the default 10% rate. This does not classify a supply or establish a credit entitlement.

Link to this example · Released formula source

### Label an Australian financial year

oz.FinancialYearλ: Labels dates with their Australian financial year, which starts on 1 July

Signature: FinancialYearλ(Dates, [StartMonth]). Square brackets mark optional arguments.

```
=oz.FinancialYearλ(DATE(2026,8,15))
```

Expected display: FY2027.

Limits: The default start month is July. Supply StartMonth for another year end; the function labels a date and does not determine a reporting obligation.

Link to this example · Released formula source

### Build a straight-line modelling schedule

oz.PrimeCostλ: Straight-line depreciation schedule for one asset or asset class, in whole years. A modelling schedule, not a tax calculation.

Signature: PrimeCostλ(Cost, Life). Square brackets mark optional arguments.

```
=oz.PrimeCostλ(1000,5)
```

Expected display: 200.00, 200.00, 200.00, 200.00 and 200.00; total 1,000.00.

Limits: Cost and life are supplied assumptions. This is a modelling schedule, not an ATO Division 40 tax calculation.

Link to this example · Released formula source

### Build a diminishing-balance modelling schedule

oz.DiminishingValueλ: Diminishing-balance depreciation schedule at 200% of the straight-line rate, writing the residual off in the final period. A modelling schedule, not a tax calculation.

Signature: DiminishingValueλ(Cost, Life). Square brackets mark optional arguments.

```
=oz.DiminishingValueλ(1000,5)
```

Expected display: 400.00, 240.00, 144.00, 86.40 and 129.60; total 1,000.00.

Limits: Uses 200% of the straight-line rate and writes off the remaining balance in the final year. It does not establish a tax deduction.

Link to this example · Released formula source

### Inspect the first month of a loan schedule

oz.Amortiseλ: Creates a corkscrew amortisation schedule

Signature: Amortiseλ( Principals, APRs, Terms, StartDates, [Timeline], [FinalPeriodEnd]). Square brackets mark optional arguments.

```
=TAKE(oz.Amortiseλ(100000,0.05,60,DATE(2026,7,1)),,1)
```

Expected display: Debt issued 100,000.00; opening 100,000.00; interest 416.67; payment -1,887.12; closing 98,529.54; principal repaid 1,470.46. Each figure is displayed to two decimals.

Limits: A 100,000 loan at 5% over 60 monthly payments. TAKE selects the first column of the six-row schedule. Remove TAKE to spill the full schedule; confirm the loan terms and timing separately.

Link to this example · Released formula source

### Discount three unpaid lease payments

oz.LeaseLiabilityλ: Present value of the lease payments that are not paid at the commencement date

Signature: LeaseLiabilityλ(Payments, Rate, [InAdvance]). Square brackets mark optional arguments.

```
=oz.LeaseLiabilityλ({100,100,100},0.05)
```

Expected display: 272.32, displayed to two decimal places.

Limits: The 5% rate is per payment period and the payments are in arrears. The reviewer establishes the lease term, included payments and applicable discount rate.

### Convert an effective annual rate

oz.PeriodRateλ: Converts an effective annual rate to the equivalent rate per period, the rate the lease functions take

Signature: PeriodRateλ(AnnualRate, [PeriodsPerYear]). Square brackets mark optional arguments.

```
=oz.PeriodRateλ(0.05,12)
```

Expected display: Approximately 0.4074% per month.

Limits: The input is a 5% effective annual rate. This conversion is not the same as dividing a nominal annual rate by 12.

### Calculate rates for dated periods

oz.DayCountRateλ: Interest rate for each period of a timeline under a day count convention: 30/360, Actual/360, Actual/365 or Actual/Actual

Signature: DayCountRateλ(Timeline, APR, [Convention], [EndDates]). Square brackets mark optional arguments.

```
=oz.DayCountRateλ(EDATE(DATE(2026,7,1),{0,1,2}),0.073)
```

Expected display: 0.0062, 0.0062 and 0.0060 for the three periods.

Limits: The default is Actual/365. Supply the required convention and check how the final period is inferred; the function does not choose a contractual day count basis.

Link to this example · Released formula source

### Calculate an annual return from dated cash flows

oz.IRRλ: Calculates IRR, correcting for when the first investment is not in the first period

Signature: IRRλ( Values, Dates). Square brackets mark optional arguments.

```
=oz.IRRλ({-1000,1100},HSTACK(DATE(2026,7,1),DATE(2027,7,1)))
```

Expected display: 10.00%, displayed to two decimal places.

Limits: One outflow of 1,000 followed by an inflow of 1,100 one year later. Other cash flow patterns may have multiple or no solutions; inspect the inputs and validate the result.

## One worked example

Take $1,100 that is assumed to be wholly taxable and GST-inclusive at 10%. Enter this formula in a cell of the Ozzit workbook:

```
=oz.GSTExtractλ(1100)
```

The result is 100.00. Check: 1100 / 11 = 100.00.

That is the whole of the function’s contribution: 10% arithmetic on an amount you supply.

Whether the supply is wholly taxable, whether a tax invoice supports it and whether the credit is claimable in that period are decisions for the reviewer. The function cannot see the evidence and does not classify the supply.

The 15 November 2026 native Excel record evaluates this formula against the exact v3.6.0 release workbook. It returned 99.999999999999986 before display rounding. The file hash was unchanged after the check. The repository also retains its historical v3.2.0 screenshot record.

## Download and use it

For an older workbook, check the licence at its tag. The v3.8.0 README describes releases through v3.4.2 as MIT. The v3.1.0 grant covers the tooling and documentation and excludes the workbook and formula sources. The v3.2.0 grant explicitly includes them.

Needs Microsoft 365 or Excel 2024 or later. Nothing is installed for the workbook alone, or install the workbook and CLI via Homebrew.

- Download the v3.8.0 workbook under the Apache License 2.0. The release page also publishes SHA256SUMS, a provenance record and a Sigstore attestation bundle.
- Or install via the Homebrew tap: brew tap ryanduguid/tap && brew install ozzit (installs the ozzit CLI and places ozzit.xlsx, oz.txt and functions.csv under $(brew --prefix)/share/ozzit).
- Check the file before you trust it: the v3.8.0 asset is 553,054 bytes with SHA-256 6395c321ec12a1c77ae5a62c79cb9784f3bf99a408b8c1f97df278d15b13499a.
- Read the source, guides and changelog, or start with the guide to opening the workbook and copying functions.

To use a function in your own file, copy the cell that calls it, or copy the definition from the workbook’s name manager into your model. The copied definition travels with your workbook under the licence for the Ozzit release you copied. Cite the library with the metadata in the v3.8.0 CITATION.cff, which names the release this page documents. The default branch may already carry a later version.

## Release verification

Release v3.8.0 was built from a signed tag. Its provenance record lists the static gates it passed:

- The published formula source reproduced all 170 named formulas in the workbook.
- All 170 rows of the function index matched the workbook and the source modules.
- All 162 signatures, parameter tables and example blocks described their own function.

The repository’s release process requires a native Excel run before publication to recalculate formulas, run assertions and check cached values. The published provenance records the static checks. On 15 November 2026 the ten worked formulas above returned the same results against the v3.6.0 workbook as against v3.5.0.

Those checks establish that the workbook calculates what its definitions say. They do not establish that a given accounting treatment is correct.

## Limits

The functions calculate; a person decides the accounting treatment and signs off.

- The GST helpers apply 10% unless you supply another rate. They do not classify a supply, test registration or prepare a BAS.
- The ATO benchmark ratio helpers restate the ATO’s arithmetic for amounts you supply. They ship no benchmark ranges and do not read a tax return.
- oz.PrimeCostλ and oz.DiminishingValueλ are modelling schedules. They are not ATO Division 40 methods and they do not implement immediate write-off or low-value pools.
- The AASB 16 functions are lessee arithmetic. They do not decide the lease term, what counts as a lease payment or whether an arrangement contains a lease, and they do not cover lessor accounting or the short-term and low-value exemptions.
- The library leaves out the Medicare levy, tax offsets, Division 7A interest and part-year resident, working holiday maker or special income tax schedules beyond full-year resident and foreign-resident general rates.
- The 13-week cash flow, practice calculator and retention reconciliation workbooks in the repository’s templates folder are separate templates, not functions in this library.
- Known defects are listed in the repository’s changelog and issues. Check a schedule against an independent calculation before relying on it.

## Common questions

### What is Ozzit?

An Excel workbook containing 165 native LAMBDA functions and 5 help tables for financial modelling under Australian conventions, published free under the Apache License 2.0. It has no add-in, macro or external dependency.

### Which Excel versions can run it?

Microsoft 365 or Excel 2024 or later, which support LAMBDA and dynamic arrays. LibreOffice and earlier Excel versions cannot evaluate the functions.

### Does Ozzit calculate Australian tax?

Ozzit applies 10% GST by default, labels Australian financial years, calculates PAYG withholding from supplied coefficients, and from v3.8.0 covers general-rate income tax (2024-25 to 2026-27), Division 7A minimum repayments, CGT parcels, margin scheme GST, FBT gross-up and depreciation pools. It leaves out the Medicare levy, tax offsets and tax advice.

### Where do I get the current release?

Download Ozzit v3.8.0 from the GitHub release page or the Homebrew tap (published 24 November 2026). The release includes ozzit.xlsx, SHA256SUMS, a provenance record and a Sigstore attestation bundle. Compare the downloaded workbook’s SHA-256 with the published value before use.

# Ozzit Dates functions: Excel LAMBDA reference

Source: https://duguid.com.au/tools/ozzit/functions/dates/

> Parameters and worked examples for 17 Ozzit Dates Excel LAMBDA functions: periods, timelines, schedules, overlaps and Australian financial year labels.

# Ozzit Dates functions

The 17 Dates formulas cover periods, timelines, schedules, overlaps and Australian financial year labels. Each entry gives what the workbook’s own help supplies: the signature, parameters, notes and worked examples.

Release v3.8.0. Read from the released Dates formula source, which the workbook compiles.

By Ryan Duguid. Published 20 October 2026. Last reviewed 20 October 2026.

## Using these functions

Each named formula is a native Excel LAMBDA in the free Ozzit workbook, or one of its 5 help tables. It needs Microsoft 365 or Excel 2024 or later. Enter a call in a cell of the workbook, or copy the definition from its name manager into your own model. Leave room for any spilled result.

The text below is the help each function carries in the v3.8.0 workbook. The workbook remains the authority, and a calculation does not decide an accounting treatment. Download the workbook and check its hash.

## All 17 functions

Displays this module's repository URL and function list
